div.head: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

Materials for evening dresses are very lovely and indetd the texture in many fr stances is so exquisite that beyond numeronr. tuckings and gaugings little or no additional trimming is necessary, except the touch of lace which always softens a toilette, whether it be simply or elaborately made, and ren- ders it altogether becoming. For the dresses of young girls quite the lightest and softest materials are used, and among the prettiest and newest of this season's novelties crepon de soie deserves mention as it altogether outshines its forerunners, viz., crepon and crepe de chine, being not only softer and more becoming but more durable. The prettiest style of making a simple evening dress of soft material is to have the skirt either gauged or pleated from the waist, with one .or two series of gaugings towards or round the hem, the bodice being likewise elaborated, while it is so cut as to show off the entire line of the
A DAII,
TY BLOUSE.

shoulders, being apparently held up by ropef of chenille, which pass over the shoulders, the sleeves also dropping down the arm and Clinging closely to just above the elbow, where they develop into full frills or poufs. The decolletage is finished either by a band of embroidery or a lace berthe, while a deep. close-fitting waist-band forms one of the chief features of the dress, and must fit accurately to ensure success.

The dainty blouse depicted is suited fox home dinner wear. It is made of accordion- pleated thin pink silk over a slip of a slightei deeper shade, and is trimmed with bands oi ecru lace arranged in an original fashion across the bodice and sleeves. It is simple yet very smart and would look very nice copied in pleated nun's veiling for afternoon wear, ox the more costly crepe de chine for the evening. A m.aterial which comes. as a boon to those of us who. while adoring that fragile becoming material' chiffon, have had to deny ourselves the joy of its possession owing to the fact that when soiled its career is over, is chiffon-voile, which although heavier is likewise more durable than chiffon in its original form. It also drapes into lovely soft folds and last, but not least, is washable. Those of us who have ruefully gazed upon the re-sults of an after- noon spent in washing chiffon accordkig to the

div.head: NEAT HAT
div.p: A NEAT HAT

latest methods divulged in the advice column of our favourite periodical, will rejoice in this delightful material which can emerge success- fully from such a trying ordeal. Chiffon velours is a more expensive and, of course, un- washable material, combining as it does all the softness of velvet with the beauty of chiffon. In the evening it evinces a mirrored effect and displays different colours in a won- derfully fascinating manner. The neat that sketched is suited for wear during this intermediate period between the late winter and the early spring fashions. It is made of straw, with the sides of the brim ourving closely upwards, while a couple of wings at either side are arranged flatly with the points resting on the coiffure at the back. The edge of the brim is bound with ribbed velvet. This is one of the styles which depends for its success more on the smartness of the shape than on the way it is trimmed. Its smartness of effect also depends greatly on the way it is put on the head, an art which most Frenchwomen possess naturally and a few Englishwomen have acquired. The

simplest hat arranged at just the correct angle will outshine in elegance a more elaborate and costly model of a more recent date and style carelessly put on anyhow. It is astonishing how many women overtook this and rest con- tent with the fact that their headgear is quite the latest thing from Paris, and cost a ridicu- lous • sum, and so must, they confidently assure themselves, look all right. No hat, however irreproachable in style, will do credit to itself or its wearer unless carefully adjusted on the hair. It is a mistake to pull the hat too low down on the forehead, as that style is not suited to an Etiglish style of face. while it is absurd and out of date to wear it in a fly- away manner.

The costume depicted in my last sketch is very smart, and is cut on quite the latest lines. A couple of smart little capes lie smoothly over the upper part of the arm while bands of stitcliing and embroidery form a pretty trim- ming. The material used is navy blue cloth, and the embroidery consists of red and gold spots on a cream ground. The stitching is all done in red silk, and a red waistband sur- rounds the waist. The skirt is pleated round the waist and is made over a red silk lining. The hat is of navy blue felt trimmed with long, ostrich feathers and a gold buckle. Indian embroideries are much used and are very effective, the rich colours being picked out with gold. These richly-coloured embroider- ies were first brought into use a year ago by many of the fair visitors to the Durbar, whc brought home with them fascinating speci, mens of the native handiwork.
COQUETTE.
A SMART COSTUME.

div.head: SIR PHILIP MAYLAND'S AWAKENING.
div.p: SIR PHILIP MAYLAND'S AWAKENING.
Ey J. R. LEVENSON,
Author of "The Salvation of Stephen Marston," "Captain Railton's Daughters," "The Doctor's Alarm," "The Bells of Misterley," "The Golden Cradle," &c.

The little village of Maybury was bubbling over with excitement. Never since the day that "the squire" brought home his youthful bride had the village worn such a holiday appearance. Mr. Philip Mayland, "the squire's" son was returning home accompanied by his baby boy and a nurse. Two years before Philip Mayland had quarrelled with his father, the baronet, who wished him to marry Lady Emily, and had left his home vowing that he would never' return to it so long as his father lived. Where he went none knew. He had inherited a goodly fortune on the death of his -mother. There was no need, therefore, for him to have recourse to his father for assistance; so that ttot even through his bankers could his where- abouts be discovered.

And nom, he was returning home at the end of two years, not only married, but a father and a widower! Small wonder that the inhabitants of Maybury found in this news sufficient of a pungent nature to arouse them from their lethargy..

While the villagers were all agog the baronet was reading Galig2lane s Messenger, saying as he did: "Thank God! thank God! the suspense was killing me. Let me reassure myself that my eyes did not deceive me. No, here it is: On May 10th, 1860, at Deanville, Leghorn, the wife of Mr. Philip Mayland, of a son.' July 27th, 1859, at the English church (St. Paul), Havre, by the Rev. J. Chesils, Grace Jean. to Philip, son of Sir Philip Mayland, Baronet, cf England.' "On May 12th, 1860, at Deanville, Leghorn, Grace Mayland, the beloved wife of Mr. Philip Mayland.' Sir Philip found each paragraph in its proper place, and as he read them he seemed to linger over them, a deep-drawn sigh, as of relief, escaping him as he finished reading them.

Having satisfied himself that his eyes had not played him false he unlocked a drawer in his escritoire, and placed the paper and letter from his son therein. Then, rising and crossing the room, he slipped back a panel in the wall, which revealed a small opening about a foot square. From out of this hiding-place the baronet took a paper—a blue, legal-like looking document. Twice he perused it in silence, twice he walked towards the fire-place as if about to burn it.

"No," he muttered, "not that. Who knows what may happen ? " Then he started, as if he feared being seen. "Bah!" he said to himself, as he replaced the document from where he had taken it, "I am getting as nervous as an old woman. A sharp canter will:do me good. Philip must not see me in this nervous condition."
Dinging for his horse Sir Philip was soon riding away, having satisfied himself that all was in active preparation for his son's return.

The village`of Maybury proper consisted only of a few labourers' cottages, and three or four shops where anything and everything might be obtained. Outside the village, though still within- the parish of Maybury, here and there might be found some more pretentious-looking residences. One of them was occupied by the local doctor, Dr. Fraser; another was occupied by the curate of the parish and his wife; and some were occupied by the families of those who held official positions in the neighbouring manufacturing. town, and who found it more pleasant than being surrounded by smoky chimneys. But we are only coaerned with two of these villa residences.

At Cedar Lawn resided Mrs, and Mr. George Birch, mother and son. Nobody seemed to be able to find out who they were or anything as to their past history. They had been made welcome when they first came to Maybury five years before our story opened.. Mrs. Birch had not mixed much in society; but her son had been made welcome every- where. Had not Madame Rumour endowed him with an income about ten times as large as that he enjoyed? was he not obe of the—if not the—most eligible partis in the. district? Then, too, apart from thie artificial attraction he was a general favourite—tall, dark, with a frank, open countenance. All who came in contact with him instinctively felt he was a man who could prove a true friend—one who would command respect from all, and one with whom it would not be well to trifle. The wonder was that he had remained single so long. _ _ _ _

But now, once again, Maclaine Rumoiir was busy with the affairs of Mr. George Birch. This time, perhaps, with a little more justification. Six months ago the village of 3..Jaybnry had awoke to discover the notice-aboard "To let" removed from the front of "Mon Repos"—a villa residence adjoining the grounds of Cedar Lawn on one side, and the park belonging to Mayland Hall on the other—and the place given over to workmen. One month later two ladies arrived and took up their abode thcre. As to who or what they were, whence they came, or wherefore, none could discover. The few facts,which these ladies did disclose to their visitors vere rather calculated to stimulate than satisfy their curiosity. From the agent who had negotiated the letting of "Mon Repos," it had been learnt that the place had been taken by a Mrs. Adair, who was going to live there with her daughter. Mrs. Adair who always spoke of her daughter as "my dear daughter," added to this fact the information that they had tired of a wandering life, and had determined to settle down. Beyond this neither ever vouchsafed any information. Among the first who called upon the Adairs were Mr. George Birch and Mr. Philip Mayland. At first they met at Mrs. Adair's ' • but, after a time, it was noticed that they visited only at such times as each knew the other would not be present. In this way it was that neither knew how frequent were the visits of the other. This it was, too, which gave rise to so much rumour. George Birch was daily to be seen calling on the Adairs. He usually paid his visits in the fore- noon. Sometimes he remained to lunch. At last it became apparent that his visits arose from other than purely friendly motives. He was deeply, passionately in love with 'Miss Adair. Suddenly, unexpectedly, this woman had come into his life, and awoke in him those feelings which many had hitherto tried to arouse, but in vain. So new to him was the sensation, so bewildering the feelings that animated him when in her presence, that he did not stop to see whether his love was reciprocated. Whenever, after a visit, he did try and analyse the meaning of Miss Adair's manner towards him, he failed utterly to understand it. He once took ;counsel with his mother on the subject, but she was unable to assist him in arriving at a solution. There were times when she (Madge) seemed glad to be in his society—when she did not mind his many love speeches ; and there were times when she would shrink from a tete-a-tete with him, and when, if ,he ventured on addressing her in a tone in any way borderinc, on that of a lover; she would coldly reply that such language was distasteful to her, and sometimes even quit his presence. Matters remained in this unsatisfactory Condition for,six months. One morning George Birch made. up his mind that he would end the suspense; that very day would learn his fate. Recently he had never been able to see Miss Adair alone. This morning, kowever, he had learnt accideiftally of her intention to walk into Maybury. There was only one route by which she could reach there. Ile would meet her. returning. She could not refuse the escort; and theii he would tell her of - the great love he had for her, and the desire to take her to him altogether—never to part. Thus it came about quite naturally that George Birch, walkinc, in the direction of Maybury, saw Miss Adair returning from thence. They met and shook hands, she unconcerned, be with a manner of suppressed excitement, stammering out some- thing as to "pleasure—unexpected—happy." Together they turned and passed down the lane. For some time neither spoke, she looking straight ahead, he . taking occasional glances at her face, trying to scan it as to what encouragement be would receive. Suddenly be burst out: "Madge, my Madge, now we are alone one look at you, my dear." Made drew back from him, frightened. she cried, "don't." She looked at him with fear almost. He seemed to be se altered. His face was flushed, his voice was hoarse with excitement. "You wonder to see me like this," he said. "Don't you know, Madge, that you are the cause ? He tried to seize her hand as he spoke. "Mr. Birch," said Madge, with downcast eyes, speaking for the first time and hurrying her step instinctively, "to what .purpose is all this?" _

"Why,- surely my meaning must be plain, My happiness is so bound up in you that I cannot live without you, my darling. I love you with a 100 that is part and parcel of my being. Tell me, darling, that I do not love in vain, that you will promise one day to be my own, my darling wife." Twice Madge essayed to stop he: lover's torrent of words.
"Mr. Birch, what can I say?" "Say, I love you," he broke in, once more attempting to draw her to him.
t cannot," she replied, with agitation, again hastening her steps. "Why speak any more of what can never be?"
"Listen, Madge, my darling," he began again, in a low, earnest voice, each word pulsating with meaning.
"Wiry go on this way 2" asked Madge, pleadingly. "Why set your heart on what is impossible 2"
a But why impossible? ask you to • make me happy and yourself happy tat). I believe you love me a little, though not as I love you." Madge, with averted eyes, shook her head sadly, and said:
"Indeed, indeed, it is impossible. Perhaps if thine were different-" _

"Then, perhaps it is that you do not love me ? " "You don't understand, you cannot. Oh, please do not say anything more about it. I am truly sorry, but what you ask can never, never be," said Madge, with a broken sob, looking into her com- panion's face with an expression in her eyes that made him feel how useless, how more than useless, it would be to urge further. Bewildered ansurprised, too, at his non-success, he walked along by her side in silence until they reached "Mon Repos." He opened the gate for her, and she passed in, and then turned round towards him, as he was about to follow.

"No," he said, as if divining her intention to stop him. "I don't want to come further with you now. Give me only one little word of comfort, Madge, and I will leave you." "I cannot; it would be wrong, Mr. Birch," she replied, with a sigh. He dropped her hands, raised his hat, strode away, and; turning a corner of the lane, was lost to view.'

Although, by the existence of his grandchild, the greatest motive for Sir Philip's urging his son to marry was removed, he had by no means abandoned the hope of one day seeing his son allied to Lady Emily. His heart was set upon bringing his hopes to fruition; and he lost no opportunity in urging the matter upon his son. It was, therefore, with no little dismay that sue learnt of his son's frequent visits to the Adairs. He had called once; but on that occasion he had only seen Mrs. Adair, who had apologised for the absence of her daughter on the score of a headache. It was in quite a casual manner that the matter leaked out; but it caused Sir Philip no little un- easiness, and he determined to speak to his son about it that day, "in order," as he said to himself, "to stop any such impossible nonsense before it took root."

Both father and son had that morning been engaged on matters connected with the estate, at different places; neither were in a particularly good humour; and when they met at lunch-time, both seemed inclined to eat in silence.

At last Sir Philip spoke. "I met Lady Emily and her father this morning. She said they had not seen anything of you lately; but she supposed that, like most men, you were forsaking old friends for new; and her father added that he had heard you had been seen frequently of late:in the neighbourhood of 'Mon Repos'-" "Meddling old fool!" muttered Philip, in a semi-audible tone.

"I wish, Philip, you would—" "I beg of you, sir, not to revive a subject which you know is so painful to me." "Tut, tut I my boy, you know very well that I have set my heart upon your union with Lady Emily." "You have certainly not concealed that fact from e. But surely you must know how distasteful such an idea was to me once; and snow it is im- possible." "Impossible, sir! What do you nrsean ? " asked Sir Philip, with an air of eagerness. "I hope you have not entangled yourself in any way with Miss Adair? By Heaven, sir, if I thought—" "You need have no fear on that score, sir," inter- rupted Philip. "If it will relieve you, I can assure you at once that I have not the slightest intention of marrying Miss Adair." "That admission, sir, only makes your frequent visits to those people the less justifiable; and if, your own sense of honour is not sufficient to pre- vent your continuing them, then, sir—" "You strangely forget yourself, father, when you speak to me in this tone about honour," broke in Philip, angrily, rising from the table. "It is hardly necessary for me to point out to you that your visits are the common talk of the place • and I must leave it with you to judge whether it is thoughtful to cause your name to be coupled with a lady's—and that lady one of your father's tenants.

_ "I have no doubt whatever, sir, that Miss Adair is perfectly well able to look after her own honour •' and as to the villagers, why, let them talk as they please." "Understand once and for all," said Sir Philip, whose anger was now fully aroused, "if I hear your name and that girl's coupled -together in the future' you know what to expect." "I should have thought, Sir Philip," answered his son, in a manner calculated to annr the baronet, "that you had learnt by now that''threats were useless so far as lam concerned. As to dis- continuing my visits to the Adaira, I have not the slightest intention of gratifying your wishes in that respect." With that parting remark Philip left his father, ?or whom he entertained some affection, and who he knew at heart really loved him. Left to himself, Sir Philip gave instructions that he was not to be disturbed, and that his dinner was to be served in his library. :Philip made his way to the Adairs, where he had recently spent most of his evenings, often staying to dinner, not returning to the Hall till late. This evening he remained later than usual; and he was no little surprised on returning home to find light still burning in the library, and to hear voices. Evidently his father had a visitor. Under ordinary circumstances, Sir Philip, on hearing his son come home, would call him into the library. To-night he did not do so; and Philip noticed a decided drop in the tone in which the conversation was being carried on—indeed, it had become inaudible; and if it had not been for the sound of voices he heard on passing the door on his way to his own roonii, he would have thought his father was alone and busy reading. On reaching his own room, Philip lit a cigar, and stood at the window, looking out over the park in the direction of "Mon Repos." His room was over the library. He could still hear voices speaking in hushed tones. It was impossible to distinguish anything that was said. He had nearly finished his cigar, when he thought he heard a latch lifted. Philip was not naturally of a curious disposition ; but he could not resist the temptation to try and ascertain what it meant. Yes, sure enough, somebody was leaving by the library window. It was almost too dark for Philip to discern whom; but by the aid of the light that streamed through the open window he could make out the mutfied figure of a woman, hurrying down the path leading to the wicket entrance which opened out on to the lane leading from the village. Philip heard his father close the window, heard him pass his room daor on the way to his own room, and then lie prepared to go to rest, but not to sleep. Be was too much exercised in his mind. Here was his father, who was preaching honour to him, receiving midnight visits from some woman, admitting and letting her out by the window of the library!

The nest morning, on descending to breakfast. Philip learnt that his father had not been to bed all night, that he had breakfasted early, and gone to London by the first train. Sir Philip had left Word that he would return in time for dinner. In no way concerned at the movemeits of his father, Philip breakfasted and went out. Ile would not be returning to lunch, he said, and if his father returned and inquired for him, he was to be told that lie had gone to the Quorn Meet, and might not be home until the dinner-hour. Bub l'homme.propo,se, Dieu dispose. The Quorn Meet was a very popular one. Philip, who was a general favourite, was mounted on a horse which lie prided himself lie alone dare mount. All had gone well for some time. The scent was good, and Reynard was not disposed to be easily caught. Philip, who had been riding for a long time side by side with Lady Emily, gradually drew away when she was joined by Lord Kingveston, who was supposed to be making good progress in Lady Emily's favour Philip's horse was carrying him well, when its path was crossed by a white hare that had been startled. This was enough. Philip'? horse broke

away, and going off at a fearful speed, which only increased the more Philip tried to tighten the reins, eventually ended in the horse stumbling and throwing Philip, who was dragged some distance before the animal was stopped. Two or three who saw the accident hastened to Philip's assistance. A litter was prepared, and he was taken to "Mon Repos," which happened to be the nearest place. Dr. Fraser, who was sent for, declared the injuries to be such as Philip could not recover from; and as his removal could not do him any harm, he was taken home, and carried up to his own room. Here Dr. Fraser made a more minute examination, and gave it as his opinion that the sufferer might last twenty-four hours—not longer. Philip, who seemed fully alive as to his condition, asked for his father; but it was late ere the baronet returned.

On learning the news of his son's accident from the stationmaster, Sir Philip ordered the carriage to drive round to Cedar Lawn, the residence of the Birches, where he left a pencilled note. Arriving home, he hastened at once to his son's room. Philip heard his father enter, opened his eyes and smiled. The baronet looked down, and in broken accents muttered:

"My boy! My boy ! " "He has been wishing to see you, sir," said the nurse who had left the nursery for her master's room. "He wants to speak to you." "You had better retire to the next room. If he wants anything I will summon you," replied the baronet.
The nurse withdrew, and the baronet took her seat by his son's bedside. "Father," said Philip, taking his father's hand, "father—stoop down—l have something I want to tell you—"

"Never mind, my boy," said Sir Philip, "do not distress yourself—you must keep quiet.' "But the doctor says—l have not long to live—l must tell you—raise me a little. There, that is better so. Listen, father. Five years ago you wanted me to marry Lady Emily; I refused, we quarrelled and parted— "My son, why revive these painful memories? " asked the baronet.

"Don't interrupt me, father; it makes it all the more difficult fpr me. I went away—l married—a child was born'. I sent you word I was returning a widower—father, I lied to you—my wife lives— she did not belong to our class—but, 0 God! how I loved her. I feared your insults, and so made you believe I was a widower, and my child mother- less. Now, father, I want you to send for her." Philip sank back exhausted; the effort had been almost beyond his strength. But he revived, and signalling to the baronet, who seemed almost too bewildered to know what to do, that he wanted his wish complied with, his father asked: ._ _
"Where and for whom am I to send ? " With an effort Philip replied:
"Send for Miss Adair."

Pencilling a note, Sir Philip informed Miss Adair that at his son's request he desired her presence at the Hall, accompanied by her Mother. This he despatched with all haste, sending a carriage for the ladies. He gave instructions that they were to be shewn into the library on arrival, and he to be informed immediately. Within a short time both ladies were ushered into the library, and joined by Sir Philip, who welcomed both with the subdued air of a man who had nearly borne as much as he could. Seating himself, he turned to the younger of his two auditors and saic . _

"Miss Adair, the news just imparted to me by my son has naturally come upon me as a great surprise. For his sake, however, I gladly welcome you. I beg you will not interrupt what I have to say, for I, too, have to make a confession to you, and to ask your pardon. If my son's recovery was at all likely, I should delay it; but it is not so, Sand therefore I prefer to tell you now. Your husband's death shall not affect your position. I shall provide for you as his wife, in addition to which you will enjoy the fortune he inherited from his mother. But your child can never be the future baronet and heir to the estates, which go together. • Your husband is unconscious of this, and I want him to die at peace with his father. Twenty years ago, Madge—you will let me call you Madge?" An inclination of the head was all the reply. "Twenty years ago my father quarrelled with his favourite son, my brother George. They liarted. My father altered his will, leaving the estates to me. Before his death, however, he revoked his will un- known to me, and while making provision for me, left the bulk to my brother. I was told of this by the gar- dener, who had witnessed the will, no one else being present. After my father's death, on the day of the funeral, the will produced was the one in my favour. It was the old story. I had suborned the gardener and suppressed the will under which my brother benefited. My brother never knew of his father's forgivness. Last night I was visited by a lady who told me that she was my brother's widow; she told me she had only just learnt of the way in which I had defrauded her husband; she had received through her lawyers a written con- fession from the man I had succeeded in suborning, and who on his death-bed did what he could to make reparation. To-day I have been in London. I have tested her proofs. They are genuine, and the man who should be master here to-day in my place, is Mr. George Birch." For a few minutes silence reigned, but it was broken by Madge requesting Sir Philip to conduct her to her husband's room. "You will not tell him? You will let him die happy and in peace ? " said Sir Philip, leading the way. `-` For his sake, yes," said Madge. Philip was asleep— at least, so said the nurse— when Madge and the baronet entered the room. But he soon opened his eyes, and held out a hand to each. So they sat, neither speaking, until Philip's spirit had fled to the world beyond—the world of peace and rest. After the funeral the baronet went abroad, accompanied by Mrs. Philip Mayland and his grandson, and Mrs. Adair. Mr. George Birch and Mrs. Birch took possession of the Hall. The change was a nine-days' wonder, but like most wonders, soon died out, and the village of Maybury forgot all about Sir Philip, until one day, four years later, news was received at the Hall of his death, and Mr. George was transformed into Sir George Mayland.

In the Maybury Post of 1866, appeared the following: "Mayland—Mayland.--On June 17th, at the Parish Church, Sir George Mayland, Bart., to Mrs. Philip, widow of Philip Mayland, cousin of the bridegroom." So who knows, but that after all, Philip's son may yet be the baronet?

div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Japanese Red Cross Society.—Viscountess Hagashi, the wife of the Japanese Ambassador, has made an appeal for aid for the wounded.—This appeal, I signed by herself and five other Japanese ladies, is addressed only to those of her own people who may be in this country, but these do not number very many,and unless the British public contributes, the subscriptions cannot amount to very much. There is a Red Cross Society of Japan. which is said to be as well organized as every other department of the Japanese naval and military services, but help will be welcome; and as the cause is one of common humanity, there are more than ordinary reasons why it should appeal to the generosity of the people of this country. The Royal Family and the War.—The King and Queen are greatly concerned over the war between Russia and Japan, which can hardly do otherwise than 'divide the sympathies of our Royal Family. Japan •is our ally to whom we can only wish a successful issue from the con- flict,but this can hardly result without bringing humili- ation upon Russia, and possibly disastrous consequences to her reigning,family. When therefore we remember that the Czar is the Queen's nephew, whilst the Czarina is the King's niece, and that moreover Princess Maud— their Majesties youngest daughter, is married to a cousin of the Czar, it is easy to understand that the War is the cause of considerable anxiety to our Royal Family. Nearly ten years have passed since Nicholaa 11. ascended the throne,but he has never given any evidence of a strong character, and chiefly for that reason no one ever attached much importance to his Disarmament proposals. No monarch gave these a more hearty welcome than our late Queen, but the war in South Africa promptly followed, and the outbreak be- tween Russia and Japan not only shews that the Czar has no control over Russian diplomacy, but it also makes him look ridiculous, after so deliberately making the universal cause ofi'peace his own. The Russian Royal Family's Wealth.—The Russian reiznini, house has,lit is said, greater wealth than any other Royal Family in the world. It is estimated that the revenue which the Czar derives from the Crown and State doniains, is not less than £1,600,000 a year, or more then three times as much as the allowance made to King Edward VII. In addition, more than forty members of the Imperial Family draw large incoines from property set aside by the State for that purpose. The jewels in possession of the Russian Royal Family are also unequalled in value and splendour, amongst all the reigning Houses of the world. But the Czar is not to be envied for all his wealth and possessions, and peace of mind in almost any circumstances, however bard, is better than the fear and anxiety which is the daily and constant lot of the Emperor of Russia. The Duke of Orleans.—The House of Hapsburg seems to be singularly ill-fated with family matrimonial troubles. It is scarcely ever free, from some or other scandal, and the latest to worry the aged Emperor is the reported intrigue between the Duke of Orleans, and the Princess Metternich of Austria. The Duke is married to Maria Dorothea,Archduchess of Austria,and a cousin of the Emperor Francis Joseph. He is understood to be seeking a divorce on the ground that he was forced into the marriage, but the Pope will assuredly not counten- ance such a subterfuge. The Duke was born at Twicken- ham in 1869, and has lived a great part of his life in this country, but he ill repaid the hospitality extended to the Orleans family by a certain coarse he took at the outbreak of the South African War, and he will scarcely increase his popularity of making himself the subject of further scandals. The Coming Courts.—With Lent,wethling bells which have been ringing so merrily in all directions lately, are stilled, and for the nonce luncheons and bridge parties are the principal forms of entertainment. We hear, however,a great deal about the coming Courts,and the fashion papers are full of somewhat wearisome dis- cussions anent the advisability of the train suspended from one shoulder or from both, or beginning in the centre of the back. Opinions would also seem to be divided as to the merits of the transparent train, some modistes asserting that it never does, and never can look as well as trains built of heavier fabric. Undoubt- edly these modistes are right, a brocade or velvet train does fall and spread out better than one built of airy fairy fabrics, but then another fact to be reckoned with is, that the latter can be worn without experiencing the fatigue occasioned by the former ; which couats for, a great deal. Parisian Headgear.—From Paris comes the most elaborate hats and toques, in crin, tulle, and chiffon, which, when we take the weather into consideration, strike one as particularly useless. Instead of crin, tulle, chiffon, and other diaphanous matorials, we are finding greater use just now for the new, light fancy straws, and in the place of feathers ?and flowers which adosn most of the delicate and artistic Paris headgear, ribbon rosettes, quills, bows of straw, anything that a deluge cannot utterly spoil, are distinctly to be pre- ferred. A new shape in straw's thesmartest of sailors, slightly turned up at the sides and in front, and rolled sharply up on to the crown behind. This hat is edged with a contrasting band of straw, the modish bows of straw which, in the majority of instances constitute the trimming, matching the edge of the brim. The New Tailor-modes.—From Vienna come the smartest models seen in the tailoring world and it is well to make a careful study of these before investing in thfit usual spring purchase—the coat and skirt. The little tightly fitting coat finishing just below the waist, and cut away moderately at the neck, is a favourite Viennese model, but Parisian tailors appear to be pre- ferring the bolero either reaching to the waist or end- ing just above it. The skirts of the plainer costumes clear the ground, and are ornamented like the coats and •

boleros, with elaborate braidings or stitchery. Fairly heavy makes of cloth and tweed are being used, and as regards colours, these are mostly of the quiet order, dark blues, dull greys' browns, and black, with a splash of colour at the neck. This should, of course, be repeated in the shirt or blouse, the hat, the petticoat, and also the en-tout-cas, when it is possible to venture out without the sombre but more useful umbrella. Very little exaggeration is tolerated by the Viennese tailors, neatness, and exquisite workmanship,being the points that strike one the mast, when contemplating a confection from their hands. Hands and Feet Growing Larger.—Athletic exercise, such as cycling, hockey, golf, and rowing, undoubtedly tend to enlarge the size of hands and feet, but it scarcely seems creditable that in recent years the average size of women's boots and shoes has gone up from threes to fives. Yet this is what a fashionable ladies' outfitter asserts to be the case, and whereas he never used to stock anything larger than fives, he now keeps sevens and even eights. There is, he adds, the same tendency for gloves, hosiery, and underwear, all to increase in sise. Fortunately, in the matter of footgear, the better style of boots and shoes now made, quite compensates for any actual increase in size. Much cycling, or even a great deal of walking, helps to enlarge the feet, but a well-made, good-fitting boot or shoe will render this unnoticeable. Is the Piano goinr, out of Favour.—Playing the piano has become such a plebeian accomplishment that it is thought by some people that it will gradually disappear amongst the well-to-do classes. There was a time when the matrimonial chances of a girl were considered to be at a discount if she was not an accomplished pianist, but a girl is expected to be able to do so many things that were not thought of 25 years ago, and instead of pianoforte playing being her almost sole attractive quality, it is now only one of many. Less attention is paid to it, and the perfection to which the mechanical player is fast being brought to, seems likely to diminish interest in the finger-skill accomplishment. Moreover it is said that learning to play the piano is conducive to nervous disease amongst children. This has been discovered since Board Schools have taught it, and those people who live in small houses and have to-listen to the thumping "of the instrument next door" will readily believe it. At the same time music is certainly not becoming less popular. It is simply that pianoforte playing is not thought so much of in well-to-do classes as it once was.

WARRINGTON* AND DISTRICT LEAGUE. THELIVALL V. LATCHFORD. At Thelwall on Saturday. During the first half, owing to the slippery nature of the turf, the contest- ants were tillable to do themselves justice, and chances for each side were not taken advantage of. At half- time there was no score. In the second half play went in favour of Thelwall, Maskell, however, scoring from a penalty for the visitors, but Short equalized for Thelwall from a free kick. Woods added a second, and the final result read :—Thelwall, two goals; Latchford, one.

The Manurial Value of Sewage. The Native Guano Company, Limited. 131ackfriars, London, have favoured us with a copy of their pub- lished results of the practical applicatibn of native guano in the farm and garden. This manure is extracted from town sewage, and its effects show it to be the natural manure for the soil, returning to it what has been taken from it. The sewage from which this guano can be obtained is, in many places, and especially in this district, neglected, wasted, and allowed to become a source of pollution to rivers and streams. The directors of the Native Guano Company invite the assistance and co-operation of all who are interested in the subject. It is contended that the multiplication of works for the treatment of sewage by their system would not only improve the sanitary conditions of towns, but what is- now a nuisance to towns would become a source of profit to the country generally, and especially to farmers, who would have a valuable manure produced almost at their own doors.

THE NEW ARMY COUNCIL.

The eight , members comprising the new Army Council are generally admitted very com- petent to fill the positions they have been given. Mr. Bromley-Davenport (Civil Mem- ber) has represented the Macclesfield Division of Cheshire in Parliament since 1886. He commanded the 4th Battalion of the Im- perial Yeomanry in the South African War. Colonel Sir Edward Willis Duncan Ward (Secretary) has been Permanent Under- Secretary of State since 1901. He entered the Army in 1874. He served with dis- tinction in the Soudan Expedition in 1885, was three times mentioned in despatches during the South African War, and was decorated for services rendered with the Ash,anti Expeditionary Force, 1895-96. The Right Hon. U. ,Oakley Arnold-Forster, M.P., -was appointed Secretary of State last year. He has been keenly interested in Army problems for a long time. Lieut-General the Mon. A RELIC OF THE BOER WAR.

The United Service Institution in Whitehall, built upon the site of the execution of King Charles 1., is now quite a feature of London life, and of great interest not only to the two services but also to the general public. It is a very fine building, and caters for the higher education of officers by a series of valuable and interesting lectures on naval and mili- tary topics by various authorities on subjects of immediate interest and importance. In
DE W
'ET'S HOME-MADE HELIOGRAPH

addition, it contains a fine library of books on all naval and military subjects of the utmost value for reference; and it is always a store- house of interesting relics, such as crop up from time to time. It was the United Service Institution which recently purchased the Silver statuette of Lord Nelson, upon the authenticity of which so much doubt has been recently cast. The price was five hun- dred guineas, and was raised by general sub- scription, to which the King himself contri- buted twenty-five guineas. At the present moment the Institution has on view for a short time an equally interesting relic, of the authenticity of which there is no possible question. It is nothing more nor less than De Wet's own home-made heliograph, which is a rePt; of the Boer war of the utmost value. It stands on a three-legged support, and con- sists of t )0 reflectors, connected by a sighting vane, which was originally the tangent sight of a big gun. The tangent screw is made from the base of a shell, and the pedestal :was originally part of a famous shell from I! Long Tom.l

div.head: JAPAN'S GREAT ADMIRAL
div.p: JAPAN'S GREAT ADMIRAL

Once the great naval victory with which Admiral Togo started the war in the Far East becomes generally known in Russia, its moral effect on such a superstitious people will be no mean factor in coming encounters. No one knew better than Admiral Togo the immense advantage to be gained in a first victory, and to Admiral Togo Japan, and the upholders of freedom the world over, will owe much in the end. If the serious student of the war could rely on every statement issued as he can on those of Admiral Togo, his task of following operations would be much simpli- fied; no one can fail to be struck with the honesty and modesty of the Admiral's an- nouncement of his great victory. enterprise may reasonably be expected no t

cularly unfortu-

article by the ADMIRAL TOGO, COMMANDER " Naval Expert" OF THE JAPANESE FLEET. of "St. James's Gazette" containing the following passage: "Great Britain's *benevolent neutrality' has already exercised its influence, for there can be very little doubt that the Japanese torpedo boats issued for the attack from Wei-hai-Wei." This statement was telegraphed abroad, and the accusations against England did not cease till Lord Lansdowne described the state- ment that Japan was using Wei-hai-Wei as a naval base as "entirely without foundation," and, in words which no one can think too strong, as "a mischievous fabrication."

div.head: DEADLY TORPEDO.
div.p: THE DEADLY TORPEDO.

One of the chief topics of the hour, dis- cussed at every dinner-party and dance, is the subject of torpedoes, which almost for the first time in their history are being brought into practical use. There is nothing like a great war to interest the public in general, from King to coster, in such more serious subjects, which are usually tabooed or ignored from the fact that they are too technical and scientific. By the end of the Boer war everyone possessed a certain smattering of knowledge upon the subject of tactics and strategy; but these were of the military order. Now the conversation and subject of inquiry are things naval. It was the deadly Whitehead torpedo, an automobile of the sea, which was used at the now famous night attack on Port Arthur. The latest type show a long cigar-shaped shell, covered with thin steel, which is about seventeen feet long and as many inches in diameter. The

div.head: WHITEHEAD
div.p: THE WHITEHEAD
THE SPAR.

machinery which drives it is worked by com- pressed air. It is self-steering and weighs in all about half a ton, carrying from 175 to 200 pounds of gun-cotton, which is fired by a trigger in the nose of the torpedo by contact with the ship. Its range is just under two miles and its speed approximates to thirty knots. The other kind of torpedo is the " Spar " which is, so to speak, an emer- gency torpedo, and consists of a ship's pinnace with a pole which rests on frames, fore and aft. This pole is forty-two feet long and six inches in diameter, tapering down to five inches at the point. It supports in front a water-tight metal case, containing 331 b. of wet gun-cotton and 211 b. of dry, which acts as a primer. It is fired by an electric battery and goes below the sea about seventy yards from its objective.

div.head: REUSS ROMANCE,

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, February 20, 1904.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, February 20, 1904.
THE LOT OF THE PEASANT
BY DR. B. TATARTCHEFF,

In considering 6ft:cid' abuses in isfacedoniii our attention is first turned to those com- mitted in the collection u: tithe. According to the law; 70 par cent. is‘th.3 limit on agri- cultural products in nature—and this con- stitutes the tithe in the proper sense of the term. Besides this, 1 per CHZIS. is provided for the increase of the agricultural treasury, per cant. for public instruction (out of which not a farthing is spent for the Christian schools by the Ottoman Government), and A- per cent.
1.(-;r supperting the expenses of the army. So
the toLl sum amounts to 12 per cent,

But in. reality the taxes, miscalled tithes, are much heavier, and cause many losses to the population The system is bad enough in itself, but the !wises of the people are made still heavier throng-h Turkish misrule and prejudice. The authorities, -who form the taxes, and are interested in obtaining the highest price possible, continually postpone the sale. to consequence harvesting is delayed, and the corn is often exposed for a long time on the held before it can be brought in. There it is liable to be stolen, cr.: raided by Turks, oz destroyed by rain, birds, or other enemies of the peasant There is yet more waste when the bidder, who has bought the tithes of several villages, has beer) unable to finish his work in time. However, tint losses coming from these two causes are Tiothing compared with those to which the people. are subjected in consequence of arbitrary imposi- tions on the part of the general farmers. Although the law establishes an imposition of l 2 per cent. in kind on ancr.ricultural products, d this sum is very often oubled Or trebled. The collector is aceoreparded by swarma of Albanians armed to the teeth, who feed them- selves at the expense of the poor peasants, who have no means of redress. The peasants can advance no claims of their own, not only because they fear the vengeance of the collector, who threatens their lives, but also because such claims would only involve waste of time and money at a season of the year which ought to be devoted to their everyday work. They know there is nothing to he obtained from the authorities, who are themselves interested in encouraging the rapacious instincts of the colleetors, in order that they may increase their own receipts. _

The position of these taxes is made up after a preliminary estimate by the State or by the will of a commission. • This commission, directed by government functionaries, shews the greatest partiality. The position and products of the Christians are always valued higher than those of the Mussulmans. It is in the collection of the taxes that partiality and favouritism take place, and lead to the greatest 'prejudices. The rich and influential Mussulman, who owns, as a rule, immaise and rich estates, and who conse- quently ought to pay larger sums, takes at the same time arriere taxes. On the contrary, the poor not only are forced to pay all at once, but there are also cases where they must pay or repay additional taxes under the form of contribution for different needs of the State, which they pay a year in advance. The illegal collection of taxes is the cause of great losses and awful suffering to the poor. Personal taxes and taxes on private property lend themselves to abuses equally excessive and equally iniquitous. When the practical busi- ness of collecting begins, the question is not how much a Christian village ought to pay, but how much it can pay, and that much is taken. When there is an emergency—and the Sublime Porte has an emergency once a year— peremptory commands are sent to every vilayet ordering money to be remitted to Constantinople. In favourable circumstances a Vali cannot think of improving or develop- ing a vilayet, but merely of keeping sufficient to meet such immediate needs as paying the troops. Moreover, if two witnesses can be found who will declare before the administra- tive council that the Christian is solvent, he is instantly thrown into prison. The import- ance of observing ordinary legal formalities is forgotten. Many native Christians, who really owe nothing at all, are compelled to remain in prison by the order of the collector. Deprived of work, their families suffering from hunger, they are compelled to pawn even their household utensils, or borrow at a fabulous rate of interest. The system of tax-collecting means the ruin of the poor, while the rich quietly await the issue of an irado ordering the incidence of the arri&a taxes on the so- called native taxpayers. There is no way of escape from tho clutches of. the tribute-grabbing Turk. For tribute it is—not tax, as • Europeans understand the word. In the imPositiote levying, and destina- tion of the 8.11108 de11111,11(10d the Macedonians themselves have no voice. The Turk com- mands; the Christian' must obey. Of govern- ment of the State as a thing evolved from the people, and existing for the good of the people, the Turk possesses not even a rudimentary conception. There are, •as it were, two hostile camps in the one a dcminant caste, an armed niinority; in the other a subject people, unarmed and helpless. The economic problem is that resulting from decayed feudalism The greater part of the land belongs 'either. to the Mosque (in which ease tiro profits are for the personal ae.vanti('e of trustees) or to the powerful Heys. The Christians who cultivate the land are the serfs of the Rey of the Mosque. In the former case ail the products from the land belong to the lord, and the peasants receive wages, which are not sullirrrent to keep a family of five persons They amount to something between .elO and :el ti arum:illy; The farmer finds Ids own implemerits. he 'SOWS his own BHod, but gets only one-half of the products, from which ha pays taxes to the landlord. And even this division is traned in the iniereste et tfim latter In inany eases the income of the farmer is less than that ot the mere servant Both alike must. pay from their slender earnings taxes and forced eeetrihntiona, which Mussulrnans and bands of Arnauts yearly demand from the villagers. and Which go to the maintenance of private attend:nits. tax-colleetors, gendarmes,. an the lecal troops These disciplined to ~.ers, not content with living on the labour of the lave-, eteitunt ii mu eelitieriab le atrocities on their fee sous ate] their tamilies After kh I these taxes have been deducted, there remains to the peasant an insignificant sure front which to maintain his household, lii consequence. nearly all the peasants incur debt:s. As they are never able to repay the capital, their obligations to the money-lender increase, and the latter looks after his own interests by exacting periodically ari additional 30 per cent. interest . -

The food, of the Ma.cedonian peasant is bread made of harley, rye, or Indian corn. Meat he is seldom ahle to touch, and he has nothing left with which to provide an educa- tion for his children. The .Turk has no wish to see a. development of intelligence among the population. Though Christians are taxed for the purpose, compulsory education has not yet found its way into the empire. After I have enumerated shortly the abuses of greatest importance committed by the

autnorities, yet another question presents itself. The central government has knowledge of the existence of these abuses, but what in.,;aatres has it taken to stop them? The Sultans who have during so many cen • tunes held the throne of the Khalifate bound themselves to solemn acts such as the Hati- Sherif, the Hati-Houmayoune, and the procla- mation of a constitution. They promised legal equality to all their subjects, without any dis- tinction of religion; the suppression of tithes, and their replacement by a more modern mode of taxation; the establishment of order and justice in the administration in the law- courts; and many other things which suggested the renewed • well-being of the Christians. It is already fifty years since these golden promises were given, but all of them to this day remain unfulfilled—a dead letter.

The educational work which has been going on during the last twenty-five years has created an atmosphere of contempt and hatred for the Turk which grows day by day, said has at length resulted in an open and 'Violent struggle for life—an insurrection by which the Macedonians hope to justify their existence and assert their right to the posses- sion of some measure of self-government and civic independence.

div.head: CHRISTIAN ENDEAVOURERS.
div.p: CHRISTIAN ENDEAVOURERS.
Annual Convention at Warrington.

On Saturday the annual convention in connection with the Warrington and District Cnristian Endeavour Union was held in the Rigged School, Bank-street. The afternoon meeting was presided over by Mr. J. F. Austin (vice-president of the Union) who was supported by the Revs. J. S. Hughes (president), Harry Wall and A. J. Wigley, Mr. A. Jolley (vice-president of the Union), and Mrs. A. Landon. There was a good attend- ance.

The CHAIRMAN said every endeavourer should know his definite work. It was the duty of the officers of Endeavour Societies to set their active members work, and to see that it was done. Continuing, he said they needed to create a healthy enthusiasm; not that kind of enthusiasm that evaporated in about a fortnight; but that which steadily grew with their work, and increased with intensity as the success of their labours incrc .sed. In conclusion, he said if they cultivated that enthusiasm and tried to uplift their own spiritual character, and those of their fellow men, they would best fulfil their high and holy calling. (Applause.) An address on "Christian Endeavour in relation to the Sunday School "was delivered by Mrs. A. Landen. She considered it was the duty of Christian Endeavour Societies to deal with boys and girls between the ages of thirteenand fifteen. it seemed to her that at that time children reached a crisis in their lives. It was the time when the average boy or girl left school, when they seemed to come to a place where two roads met, and where they were bound to make a decision. At this age the boys and girls left school to go into mills and factories, and them was too much responsibility thrown upon their shoulders all at once. It was then when the Endeavour Society needed to get hold of tne Sunday school scholar, and help him or her to wear in the mill or the factory "the white flower of a blameless life." (Applause.)

discugsion followed. The majority of members were of opinion that the Endeavour Society should act as an intermediary between the Sunday school and Church, but the Rev. A. J. Wigley and several others shared the opinion that the society should work hand i. hand with the Sunday school,and not as an intermediary between school and Church.

The Rev. Harry Wall delivered a helpful address on "How to increase the usefulness of a Christian Endeiv- our Society." The Rev. A. J. Wigley urged upon those 'resent the great necessity of using the powers they possessei to the full extent. After the conference tea was served.

At the public meeting, held in the evening, the chair was taken by the Rev. J. S. Hughes, who was supported on the platform by Miss Venda M Taylor (hon. secre- tary), the Rev. J. Pedlar (president of the Widnes Union), and Messrs. G. Simcock (Bury) and W. T. Moss (Lymm). There was a much larger attendance. Miss Taylor submitted her annual report. The Chris- tian Endeavour Movement, she said,was still extending in the district, for during the past twelve months they had received into the Union two new junior societies. and one young people's society, so that there wer3 affiliated with the Union nineteen young people's societies and ten junior societies, making a total of twenty-nine societies. There were also four other junior societies conducted by members of young people's societies, but they bad not as yet joined the Union. One young people's society had ceased to exist, and the total num- ber of members was 331 active and 178 associate mem- bere,making a total of 509 members. The members of the junior society numbered 560, 18 less than the pre- vious year. Of the whole of the societies of the Union the Baptists,Congregationalist and Primitive Methodisis were responsible for three each. The Reformed Church of England and the Established Church were repre- sentedy?y one society each, and there was a:. oLeun • denominational society connected with .he Union. (Applause.) Much to the reg:et of all who knew him, the Rev. Wilson Ecr! 3S, owing to his removal to Man- chPste7 in July, had been compelled tc re -gn Ole pre- sidency of the Union, but in his successor, the Rev. J. S, Hughes, they had found a very good president. (Applause.) Continuing, Miss Taylor said a substantial sum had been contributed to home and foreign missionaries. On May 23rd the societies in the town made a st-:eet collection in aid of the Warrington and District Nursing Associa- tion, when over £29 was realised. She (Miss Taylor) would close by quoting a few sentences from the letter of the President of the Lancashire and Cheshire Feder- ation of C. E. Unions, the Rev. J. E. Roberts :—" I would urge you to be loyal to the vital principle of our movement—' For Christ and the Church. Let this year be a Christian year. And a Christian yeir is a year full of Christ, Christ in the heart and therefore Christ in the home, Christ in the Church,Christ in business,Christ inlpolitics, Christ in social life, Christ b the midst;and therefore, Christ everywhere. I pray that Christ may be formed in you by the indwelling Spirit of God, then the outward life of conduct and service will be the outshining of the glory within." (Hear, hear and applause). The REV. J. S. HUGHES addressed the meeting on "The Endeavourer at Home."
Mr. G. SIMCOCK and the REV. J. PEDLAR also spoke on Christian Endeavour work.
The convention concluded by the holding of a con- secration service.

On all hands it is agreed that the feature of the 1904 bicycle is to be the two-speed gear, and already the "Fagan "has been accepted as the leading example. is extremely simple in operation, requiring but a ton of the finger to bring into action the low gear whi makes hill-climbing abirost as easy as riding on t ' level road. It is included fre3 of charge in the speei cation of the high-grade Royal Enfield bicycles, anu every rider who is fortunate enough to possess one of these handsome machines will find the new departure a great acquisition.

div.head: ANNUAL HEALTH REPORT.
div.p: ANNUAL HEALTH REPORT.

The annual report of Dr. M`Dougall, medical officer to the Urban District Council, was issued on Tuesday, and states that durirt the past year 186 cases of pr: • ventiblo disease were notified, against 257 cases during the preceding year. There were 125 cases of scarlet fever' 6 typhoid, 43 diphtheria, and 2 smallpox; 280 deaths from all causes were registered, a decrease of 9, and the death-rate for the year was 16.4—" rather a low death-rate for an industrial population." There were 561 births registered, giving a birth-rate of 33.1

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
FIRST DIVISION.
SNTUDAY'S MATIMES
WARRINGTON v. WIDE.

At Warriaqton, before 3,0)0 spectators in stormy weather. Playing against the breeze, Widhes with the aid of a series of forward rushes, forced Warrington to adopt defensive tactics, and twice Hallam had to nave Douglas had a smart drop, and following this narrow escape Warrington took up a strong position, and after Dickenson and Isherwood ha (1. been pulled up on the line, Bate made an opening i): Harris, who crossed at the right corner, Fish placing a fine goal. Warrington continued to have all the attack,but Taylor, Aspey,and Tilley exhibited a sound defence, and foiled Fish and Dickenson repeatedly. Half-time score :—Warrington 1 goal 1 try (5 points). Widnes nil. Turning round the game for a long time went in favour of the home side, and Tilley had to save twice in rapid succession. By degrees the Widnesians worked their way into the home quarters, and Do leas had a long shot at goal, which struck the upright. Vigorous for- ward play was associated with keen tackling, and each side had a player ordered off in the last few minutes. Result :—Warrington 1 goal 1 try (5 points), Widnes nil. Teams:—

Warrington.—Hallam, back; Fish, Isherwood, Dicken- son and. Harris, three-quarter backs; Bate and Evans, half backs ; Boardman, -Morrison, Cook, Swift, Jolley, Lunt, Edmondson, and Naylor, forwards. Widnes.—Taley, back; Peacock, Barber, I. Taylor and Hughes, three-quarter backs; Burnett and Douglas, half backs; G. Aspey, S. Aspey, Lynch, Leyshon, McDonald, McCabe, Curtis, and Cockram' forwards. Referee, Mr. G. Robinson, Runcorn. Touch judges, Messrs. F. Little (St. Helens), and T. L. Brimelow (Salford). RUNCORN v. OLDHAM.

At Runcorn on Saturday before 1000 spectators Houghton tamed out again for the home side who gained a good victory. Jolley scored a goal snd a try ad Farmer a goal, while Civil got a try for Oldham. The latter were thus defeated by 7 poiats to 3. SALFORD v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS

Played at Weiste, in hlivy rain, before 4,000 people From the start Sllford pressed, and Lomas and Thomas each scored, a goal also being added. In the second half Barry just failed to get over for ahe Rovers. Rhapps scored for Salford. Lomas landing a goal. Heath also ran over. Result—Salford, 2 goals 4 tiles (16 points); Hall Kingston Rovers, nil.

div.head: LEEDS V. HALIFAX.
div.p: LEEDS V. HALIFAX.

Played at Headingley, in wretched weather. In the opening half play was fairly even, but Littlewood,in the first minute, landed a pretty goal. Shortly I,efore the inteival Hewlett scored from a forward rash and.at half-time Leeds led by five points to nil. Though Halifax kept up a constant pressure in the wean(' half nothing tangible resulted. Result—Lead:. 1 goal 1 try (five points); Halifax, nil.

div.head: HULL v. BRADFORD.
div.p: HULL v. BRADFORD.

At Hull, before 8,000 spectators. Hull did most of the pressing, and Jackson almost kicked two penalty goals. The second half was contested equally as keenly as the first, Bradford having two lucky escapes. Con- sidering Hull's lowly position, they played a big game, and Bradford had to defend hard to keep their line in- tact. The game continued keen, and Hall accomplished a flue performance by making a pointless draw.

div.head: BATLEY v. HUNSLET.
div.p: BATLEY v. HUNSLET.

At Batley, Hunslet started against the wind sed rain and Batley were immediately in an aggressive position but the defence was sound, and no score resulted up to half-time. On the resumption, Hunslet immediately attached, and scrimmages followed on the Batley line. Goldthorpe had an unsuccessful attempt at goal,but, the same player shot tly after scored a converted try. Re- sult—Hunslet 5 points ; Batley, nil.

div.head: LEIGH v. SWINTON.
div.p: LEIGH v. SWINTON.

Played at Leigh, before 2000 pectators. In the first half Kirk ran grandly through the Swinton team, and scored. Then Johnson gained a try after fine dribbling. No goals resulted. In the second half play was more even, but Molyneux placed a penalty pal for Swinton. 11?sult—Leigh, 2 tries ; Swinton, 1 penalty goal.

div.head: TUESDAY'S MATCHES.
div.p: TUESDAY'S MATCHES.
WARRINGTON v. HALIFAX.

Warrington Wok a stroll team to Halifax on Tuesday to try conclusions with strong Hanson Lane brigwle. Hockenhall filled the half-back position in place of Evans while on the Halifax side Rigg came in in place of Morley. There had been a couple of inches of snow in YoAshire on Tuesday, and though the ground was cleared it was very heavy. Mr. Bruckshaw, of Stock- port, was the referee, and the teams turned out as f.l- -

Halifax: Little, full back; Wedgwood, Riley Williams and Hadwen, threequarters; Rigg and Gledhill half backs • Hammond, Bummer, Langhorn, Mallinson, Mortbn, Riley, Swinbank and Winskill, forwards. Warrington: Hallam, full back; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Maris, threequarters ; Bate and Hockenhall,half backs; Boardman,Morrison,Edmondson Naylor, Lunt, Jolley, Swift, and Cooke, forwards. _ . _

. „ Halitax won the— toss and Dickenson started for Warrington against a light breeze. Winskill mulled the return and Warrington at once gained a footing in the home half. A penalty drove them back however, and Isherwood's fielding being faulty, Hallam had difficulty in clearing. The Halifax forwards broke away with a fine dribble, and again Hallam saved his charge boldly. The home team scrummaged close in but faulty passing lost' an opPor- tunity. Bate eventually took play towards the centre and fine paqsing by Hockenhall,lsherwood, and Fish resulted in the latter running speedily to the home quarter. Bate again got hold and kicked across to Harris, who collided with Hadwen in going for the. ball. Superior forward play again put the home side on the offensive, and Wedgwood was only just sent over the homer flag after quick passing. A second effort came two minutes later, but with the same result, Dickenson making no mistake with his lengthy opponent., Fish made another run into the home half and received at. injury to his right knee in being tackled. Half-time arrived soon after with the scoresheet blank.

Halifax at once attacked on resumption, Hockenhall coming across and upsetting Wedgwood finely. Fish limped about for some time and was practic- ally a passenger. Warrington gradually worked their way to the other end by clever touch-kicking on the part of Bate, while Hallam put in same splendid work in eke rear. Warrington maintained the pressure, and the hall came across to Fish who promptly forgot, his swollen knee and raade a brilliant run almost to th 6 line. Dickenson followed suit with a strong effort, but spoiled an opening for Harris by going too far. At this stage Warrington were very dangerous, and Fish again startled the crowd by beating Wedgwood and running grandly in the home quarter. Wedgwood and Williams carried play right to the other end, where Warrington were p3nalised and Little kicked a goal from long range. Warrington rallied again, Fish planting the ball near the corner flag, but the home forwards relieved with a strong rush. Meantime Hadwen dribbled through, he and Hockenball both diving under the posts at the rame moment. Fortunately the Warrington man was vinderneath and the situation was saved. One more opportunity came for Warrington and the backs appeared nicely under way when Dicken- son got his transfer to Fish charged down by Riley. The wing man would have had a grand chaace. Final: Halifax, one goal (2 points) ; Warrington, nil.

div.head: HUDDERSFIELD v. SWINTON.
div.p: HUDDERSFIELD v. SWINTON.

This match, which was postponed from January 2, was played at Huddersfield on Tuesday, before 2,000 spectators. Huddersfield won the toss, and Preston commenced the game for Swinton. For i short time the game was Ifoueht out in neutral territory, but at length a mull by Deere enabled Swinton to reach the home quarter, where Preston took a place ond scored a goal. Then Huddersfield made a determine attack on the Swinton line, and were at length rewarded by Walton kicking a penalty goal and equalising the score. The home backs then made soma flue passing runs,and Wade was just brought down 4n time to prevent him scoring. The Swinton backs continued to tackle strongly, and they kept the home ride out till half-time_ when the score was two points each. In the second half Swinton had decidedly the best of the gone, and Burrows and Simister scored tries, bot'l of which Preston improved Holroyd scored an vnimproved try for Huddersfield, and the game ended :—Swinton, three goals and two tries (12 points) ; Huddersfield, one goal and one try (five points.)
KEIGHLEY v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS.

This match took place at Keighley, before over 3,000 spectators. Keighley commenced the game down-hill, with the wind behind them, and had most of the play, but the interval arrived without either iide having scored. After the change of ends Keighley still defended splendidly, and the game ended in a pointless dry. _
Second Division. DEWSBURY v. ST. HELENS.

At Dewsbury. In the first half Routh scored a fine try for Dewsbury. Immediately after changing ends Briers obtained a try for St. Helens. Dewsbury had the best of their opponents, though the result was a draw of one try (three points each).

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Baptist Church, Go!borne Street.

The morning service on Sunday last was taken by the Rev. J. Gardham Reed, who took for his text, "What think ye ofThrist ?" Pastor Grady preaching in the evening from the words "Seek ye first the King- dom of God and his righteousness."

div.head: St. Peter's Church.
div.p: St. Peter's Church.

Mr. Fred Webster gave an organ recital at this church after the evening service on Sunday evening. There was a fairly large attendance, and the compositions which Mr. Webster played were "Chorus of Angels," (Scotson-Clark), the Hallelujah Chorus, from the "Messiah," "Afferparie,"(Smartband "Saint D'Amour," (Elgar). Miss Anderton gage a very effective rendition of "Lord save us." The collection was in aid of the fund for providing the new church lights.

div.head: Wycliffa P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffa P.S.A. Society.

There was an average attendance at the meeting of this society on Sunday afternoon. Mr. Richard Mills, the visitation secretary of the society, presided, and in a short address he referred to the outbreak of war be- tween Russia and Japan. Both combatants, he said, would suffer great hardships, and there would be great destruction of life and property. He believed these differences between nations could be settled without the dread arbitrament of war if the nations were will- ing and desirous of doing so. He hoped this country would take the lead in the movement for submitting to arbitration international differences. The war in the far East might at any moment lead to !a great European calaclysm which would be fraught with untold disaster for this and other countries The address was delivered by Mr. Jackson, of Earles- town, who based an earnest and telling address On Jacob's power with God. Miss Allan sang two solos entitled "Ora Pro Nobis " and " The Better Land." The service was also taken part in by Mr. A. Downes (assistant secretary), Mr. J. Owen mid Mr. Healey.
Legh Street Primitive Methodist Church.

The church anniversary sermons were preached in this church on Sunday morning and evening, by the Rev. H. Dunnico and large congregations assembled. Mr. Dunnico took for his morning text, "Blessed are the pure nheart for they shall see God," and evening," On the east there were three gates, and on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates." The organ voluntaries for the day were, Holy Holy," (Handel), "Triumphal March" (Lemmens), "Festal March"( Sir G.Elvey);Aria,"Leise,Leise Tromme Weise " (Weber), contributed by the organist Mr. Fred Podmore. In the afternoon a musical service was given by the choir assisted by a number of local artistes. Miss Alice Griffiths sang "The Lord is Love " with sweetness and effect and Mrs. J. Hannan rendered "Just for to-day" and the "Lost Chord." Mr. Sam Hassall con- tributed "Then shill' rthe righteous " and "Total Eclipse," these solos being 'rendered with masterly effect. Mr. George Gough sang .` Eternal Rest "and "The Dawning Light," with deep religious feeling, The ctoir, under the conductorship of Mr. Albert Spruce, rendered "Behold the Lamb of God" (" Messiah ") and the intricate anthem "0 God when Thou appearest " (Mozart) with great effect. The reputation of the choir was fully sustained by the per- fect balance of ]parts and precision and attack with which they presented these selections. They also sang at the evening service, the anthem "Rock of Ages" (Buck). Miss Alice Bridge contributed the solo. Mr. J. Bissell presided at the afternoon service.—On Monday evening a reception tea was given by Mr. W. Crampton, to welcome the Missicner, Mr. Enoch Mil- son, who is conducting a mission at the Church. Songs were rendered by Miss Mansell sand Mr. W. Perry, and Mr. Milson gave an address to Christian workers.

div.head: HOLY TRINITY CHURCH. Congregational Tea and Entertainment.
div.p: HOLY TRINITY CHURCH. Congregational Tea and Entertainment.

Decorators had been busy at the Co-operative Hall, Sankey street, on Tuesday,and the result of their handi- work was that the hall presented a bright and inviting appearance in the evening when the annual congrega- tional tea party and entertainment in connection with Hely Trinity Church were held. The gathering was hignly enjoyable and successful, members of the con- gregation and friends assembling in strong force. A capital tea was followed by a concert of more than usual interest, the programme being pleasingly varied and reflecting general credit upon those responsible for it. Mr. J. Halton (Vicar's warden) presided and the attendance included the Vicar (Rev. E. C. E. Carleton), and the Revs. H. R. Wild and A. Inglis. The VICAR tendered his sincere thanks to all who had assisted and specially mentioned the valuable work of Mr. Hesketh, upon whom the secretarial duties had devolved. He had to thank them (his hearers) and all connected with Trinity Church for the kind help and support they had extended to him, and the clergy of the parish during the past twelve months. They had had a very satisfactory year, and had gone on quietly as usual. They had done nothing startling or sensational, and they had not made any history—in fact they did not aim at making _history,—.but ,they had succeeded. (Applause.) An efficient ladies' orchestra opened the programme with a tuneful valse aid at a later stage further added to the enjoyment of the evening with the selections "Dream of homeland "and "Whistling Rufus." Miss A. Wilson sweetly sang "Voices of the past," the violin obligato being supplied by Miss M. Leigh. Later she gave a good interpretation of "Love's old sweet song." Miss P.Houghton is a very promising vocalist,possessing a voice of good range and flexibility. She won general praise by her renderings of" Star of the twilight" and "The Nightingale's trill"and was heartily re-called. "Miss A.Longdin infused feeling into her song "Tatters," and she too was encored, responding with "The Zuyder Zee." Later she sang "Beloved it is morn." Mr. C. H. Hoult gave "Mona" in good style, and" Queen of the Earth "was creditably rendered by Mr. T. Healing. Pleasing features were the instrumental quartettes by the Misses E. and L. Pooley and A. and M. Warren. Miss K. Beesley's ability as an elocutionist is well- known to Warrington audiences and she fully main- tained her reputation. The quaint humour of" Paddy's dream "and the tragedy and pathos of Clement Scott's "Warriors of the sea "were brought home to the aud- ience with peculiar power. Mr. H.Hallard gave numer- ous sketches in his own inimitable way, and the room resounded with laughter when he held possession of the platform. Mr. Percy Randall also appeared in the role of humorist, and with great success, the ever popular recital of the difficulties encountered "When father laid the carpet on the stairs "calling forth an encore. The duties of accompanist were also discharged by Mr. Randall with customary taste and skill. The artistes were cordially thanked for their services. Afterwards dancing was indulged in until midnight.
