div.head: 'THE EXAMINER.
div.p: 'THE EXAMINER.
FEBRUARY 20th 1904.
A valuable- debate CHINESE SLAVES took place in the FOR THE RIND. House of Commons on

Wednesday night on he prop-) sod importation of Chinamen into South Africa. The British nation is slow to move, but it has been stirred to its depths by this nefarious scheme to induce slavery into a province over which floats the flag of the free. We deny that Chinamen are necessary to the development of South Africa's resources. No development pur- chased by trafficking in slaves would be worth the price. The pretence that the Chinamen are necessary for the prosperity of the country is simply a mask to disguise the antipathy of the capitalists to free men. As Mr. HERBERT SAMUEL put it, what the capita- lists want is not only cheap labour bat labour which will be hopeless and • subservient. We rejoice to say that the opposition to the importa- tion of Chinamen is not confined to opponents of the Government. Some of the most loyal Con— servatives are in this m atter in entire agreement with the Liberals. We deeply regret that Mr. DUKE, the member for Plymouth, is not of their number. His speech was a deplorable one. No one denies that the Chinaman is industrious and long suffering. Our objection to the Transvaal labour ordinance is the outco me not of. antipathy to Chinamen but of hatred of slavery. There are , very weighty reasons against the introduction of Chinamen as ordinary immigrants, because they depress the standard of life. These reasons become a hundredfold more cogent when the Chinamen come in not as free men but as practically slaves.

In his speech on Wednesday Mr. LYTTELTON does not appear to have realised that the labour ordinance is intensely repugnant to men who were Lord MILNER'S strongest supporters at the Cape. The elections in Cape Colony have returned a progressive majority, small, but probably suffi- cient, and in due c3urse, there will be a Ministry of a strongly imperial complexion. It is expected that Dr. JAMESON will be the new Premier ; but nr,body has expressed so hostile an opinion to the importation of Chinese labour as Dr. taArnsoN. He is the last man to he indifferent to dominant commercial interests of J,,bannesburg. No mine owner can regard him as an enemy or as a luke- warm friend. Dr. JAMESON has not &Ways taken a wise view of South African interests,but he may fairly be credited with impartiality when he pro- tests on behalf of the whole of South Africa against the employment of Asiatic labour in the mines. Mr. LYTTLETON cites Lord MILNER, Sir ARTHUR LAWLEY, and the Legislative Cbuncil in support of the ordinance as an economic neces- sity. He claims popular opinion in the Trans- vaal on the same side, but no satisfactory method of ascertaining popular opinion has been adopted. We hear of a petition with many thousands of signatures, but we are too familiar with the machinery of petitions in Johannesburg to be much impressed by this one. Votes are better than petitions, and a referendum on so great a question might be instituted, even in a Crown Colony. Mr. IiYTTLETON is quite alive to this,but he says that a referendum would take nine months, and the problem is too urgent for delay. Why it should take nine months to ascertain the views of the Transvaal population we cannot imagine. Mr. CHAMBEDLAIN declared at least a year ago that nothing should be done in Opposi- tion to the wishes of the Colony. Nothing has been done to form a just estimate of these wishes. As far as anybody can judge the bulk of opinion in South Africa is strongly against the new policy. In our opinion,the importation of Chinamen into South Africa will be both a blunder and a crime.
A telegram from tt USSIA AND JAPAN.. St. Petersburg

announces that a new telegraph line is to be made between that city and Port Arthur, and that the campaign against Japan will begin in etunest in about six weeks. There is a curious simplicity in this piece of news. It assumes that the next six weeks will be a period in which the Russian engineer and mobilisers will work undisturbed. The possibility that the Japanese may do something to embarrass these tranquil arrangements is not considered. if Admiral ALEXEIEFF had not been upset by the attack on Port Arthur he would pro bably have spent six weeks or more in preparing to_begin the campaign in earnest. On the Japanese side something serious is :in the wind. We get hints from Tokio that a great militaxy eaterpriae

is under weigh,and that it will repay the European Powers to study it. Our Government have appoint- ed General NICHOLSON to study it, but it is doubt- ul whether he will be in time for the opening movement. Japan is manifestly preparing to land a great force, not only in Korea but also in the Lao Tuna peninsula. Admiral ALEXEIEFF is already so much harassed by this prospect that troops which were lately sent to the Yalu, two hundred miles away, are being hastily brought back to Port Arthur. When the Japanese have sufficiently discomposed all the preliminary arrangements for the Russian campaign, they may strike at some point where they are not in the least expected. At all events, the chances that the construction of the new telegraph line from St. Petersburg to Port Arthur will be an uninterrupted job do not seem to be encouraging. Japan enjoys at present the superiority of numbers, and she may besiege Port Arthur by sea and land while she despatches a formidable army to the Yalu. With the com- mand of the sea she has a choice of positions. On the other hand the quality of her troops has still to be tested, and she is unlikely to underrate the military capacity of her enemy, as the Russians underrated her naval strength and skill. The negotiations of the Powers for the neutralis- ation of China will scarcely be aflected by the ill- humour of the Russian Press. First it was America that had egged Japan into war. Now it appears that the British Government had been working a very subtle scheme for many years. It began with the consular capitulations in Japan. England agreed to this on condition that the Mikado's Government should immediately con- struct a powerful fleet against Russia. Then Germany was compelled, against her will, to agree that her subjects should be judged by the Japanese courts. What means the British Government employed to force Germany into this position we are not told, In their relation with German diplomacy, British Ministers have generally been so weak and obliging that we cannot ever conjecture how they managed to subdue Germany to their wicked plot 'against Russia. Farther we learn that " the war. is certain to be protracted unless France should be induced to forget the lost provinces and join with Germany and Russia in punishing England's treachery." This is an invitation which ought to be apprecia- ted in Paris. The idea that France should oblige Russia by making a compact with Germany in Russian interests ought to appeal to the ironical writers of the French Press. We can imagine them suggesting that it is not very dignified for Russian journalists to appeal for help to France and Germany before the campaign against Japan has begun in earnest. It may happen that some striking success for the troops of the CZAR will beget a different temper. If not, the Russian journalists may be expected to address their appeals to civilised mankind, and especially to invoke the traditions of Poland and Finland in the name of freedom against the piracy of England I and Japan in the Far East.

Death has been painfully busy in our midst just lately. Last week we chronicled the demise of three well-known and respected townsmen, and to-day it is our sad duty to record the death of another gentleman whose lifetime has been spent usefully and honourably in the town. The circum- stances of Mr. Thomas Tunstall's death are particu- larly distressing inasmuch as he expired suddenly at the entrance to his office. No one had any inkling that his obvious indisposition was of so grave a character, and the sensation produced in the town by the publication of the news was very painful indeed. Mr. Tunstall was not a public man in the sense that he occupied platforms and looined large in the public eye, but he filled a num- ber of important offices which caused him to be widely known—and to know Mr. Tunstall was to respect him. He was a quiet, unassuming gentle- man, with the kindliest of dispositions, and his friends will, we are sure, sympathetically share the deep sorrow into which his witsow and family have been so tragically plunged.

Mr. Samuel Gough—we can no longer call him Councillor, for he ceased to hold that office on been convicted of bribery in the Tuesday—has recent election by which be was elevated to the Town Council, and thus earns for himself and for the town of Warrington Cu unenviable notoriety. " The means that prisoner took to corrupt the voters were contemptible and small" said Mr. Justice Bigharn in pronouncing judgment. Scieing how severely his Lordship summed up, and recol- lecting what exemplary punishment he was enabled by law to inflict, Mr. Gough must be accounted fortunate in escaping with a penalty of £.5. We do not suggest that it is inadequate. On the contrary we have some sympathy with the ex-Councillor and la,lieve that his punishment amply fits the crime. Our sympathy with him, however, does not lessen the serious view we take of the enormity of the offeucc for which he has been convicted. Election bribery is as much an outrage upon morality as an infringement of the law, and there can be no excuse for it. But wherein our sympathy lies is the fact that Mr. Gough has men made a scapegoat. We have no hesitation in asserting that bribery at elections in Warrington has been rampant for some years past. It may not have been generally known, but there is no doubt whatever that over a long period almost every means of influencing the elector has been em- ployed either by candidates personally or by their agents. If we could only get to know what a candidate's actual costs during an election have been, some idea could be gained of the methods employed. The official returns are a mere blind, but they satisfy the requirements of the law. Perhaps the sacrifice of Mr. Gough on the altar of purity may have the effect of checking the improper procedure which often obtains in Warrington elections. If it does not we sincerely hope some sharp-eyed informer will take proceed- ings to bring other delinquents to book. Were the truth only known, Mr. Gough would probably. be found to be one of the smallest offenders. How-. ever he has been caught and punished, and our chief regret is that a few other individuals with a prefix to their names have not been compelled to accompany him to the prisoner's bar.

There is a great deal of misconception in tbe town as no what Mr. Gough's conviction.for bribery really involves. We have made enquiries in an authoritative quarter and as a result we are able to set all doubts at rest. Mr. Gough is ipse facto disfranchised for seven years, dating from the day of his conviction. Being no longer a burgess:he is therefore no longer a Councillor, and the Town Cleric will shortly declare a vacancy in Bewsey Ward, which will have to be tillea in the ordinary way by another bye-election.

According to Parker on" Election Law[the enact- ment defining the offences of bribery, treating, undue influence, and personation,states.that. these offences "include respectively anything done before, at, after, or within respect to a municipal election, which, if done before, at, after, OD with respect to a Parliamentary election, would make the person doting the same liable to any penalty, punishment, or disqualification, for bribery, treat- ing, undue influence or personation, as the case may be, under any Act for the time being in force with respect to Parliamentary elections." The Act 46 and 47 Viet. chap. 51,, specifies that "a person convicted of a corrupt practice is guilty of a misdemeanour . . . and is subject to the following punishment and incapacitiel : (1) imprisonment with or without hard labour for oce year, or a fine of 00. If the corrupt practice be personation, then imprisonment for two Tearsovith hard labour,

(2) Incapacity for seven years of being 'registered and voting at any election. (3) Incapacity for seven years of holding ,any public or judicial office. (4) Incapacity for seven years of being 'elected to or sitting in Parliament. (5) Publication of name and offence in the

Stone's" Justice's Manual' is equally explicit and "leaves no shadow of doubt as to Mr. Gough's dis- -qualification for seven years.

A further point which we are happy to elucidate "has been raised in connection witu the vacancy which follows Mr. Gough's conviction. Many People are under the impression that Mr. Toole, the defeated candidate, succeeds Mr. Gough in the 'representation of Bewsey Ward. This is not the case, however. Had t4ere been a petition to unseat Mr. Gough, in which the petitioners claimed 'the seat, then on conviction it would have been 'within the discretion of the Judge to award the seat to Mr. Toole if he were of the opinion that sufficient votes had been affected by the corrupt Practices to prejudice the result of the election. The prosecutors, however, did not take the expensive course of lodging a petition, but satis- led themselves with a criminal prosecution, the result of which,as we have already made clear renders Mr. Gough's election void, and creates an ,ordinary vacancy to be filled at a bye-election.

To the ratepayer who is looking for some relief from his heavy burden of local taxation, which at the present moment totals up to 7s. 4d. in the £ —the highest rates ever demanded in the town the estimates of the Education Committee will not be very pleasant reading. The amount required from the Borough fund—or in other Words theratepayers' pockets—is £10,257 19s. 5d., as against .E 9,290 a year ago. A tenpenny rate Was required last year to meet the expenses of the Elucs.tion Committee and an additional Penny rate will be ne essary if this year's estimates meet with die sanction of the Town Council. There is an estimated deficiency in each of the four departments under the control of the Education Committee. Tne Fin- nce Committee anticipate an expenditure of £7,057 2s. 11d. whilst the modest sum of £lOO is set down as tlie probable income, apart from the rates. The School Management C3mmic,tee has the next highest deficien amount- ing to £1,299 Bs. 6d. Of this sum £565 is put down as the estimated expenditure on scholarships and prizes, which seems rather a large sum to ask the ratepayers to pay for such a pur- pose. The prospects of reduced rates this year are meagre in the extreme. The poor rate will certainly not be less and the recent outbreak of smallpox and the serious litigation with the Ship Canal Company will probably have an appreciable effect on the Borough expenditure and the amount required from the rates.

Great Sankey seems to be a favourite rendezvous for gipsies and others like them who travel through the country in caravansaries. They pitch their tents in the neighbourhood with great frequency, and the residents complain loudly of the presence of these unwelcome intruders. The Police officers have been asked to move them on whenever they see them, but last week end, two vans stood on the public highway for a couple of days within a stone's throw of a constable's house. There may be some ground for the complaints of depreda- tions when these wanderers have stayed awhile, but a more serious side of the question, it. seems to us, is the sanitary one. Without the conveni- ences of a home, these people live under conditions Which cannot he healthy, and there can be no doubt that they are sometimes the means by Which disease is conveyed from one disttict to another. The children are generally allowed to run wild, and rarely receive a smattering of educa- tion. In some districts strong measures are being taken against them, and the time seems ripe for restricting the number to smaller dimensions.

One of our local police officers was the victim Of a brutal attack on Saturday night, and the sentence of six months imprisonment passed Upon his assailant wai richly deserved. In- deed, it was perhips fortunate for the Prisoner that he Wa i not sent for trial on the more serious charge of unlawful wounding. The Police have quite enougli difficulties to face, with- out being subjected to sadden—though apparently Premeditated—onslaughts in dark streets. Such scenes as that which occurred in Museum-street are a disgrace to the town,and law-aoiding inhabit- ants will be glai that the principal delinquent Was arrested and made to pay the penalty for his yholence.

The stars in their courses are evidently fighting against the Protectionist agitation. The series of defeats sustained by the G wernment at the by- elections has culminated in the overthrow of the Protectionist candidate•iu Mid-Herts, a constitu- ency which has hitherto been regarded as so in • vulnerable against attack that at the last two General Elections the Liberals did not even venture to contest the seat. The Hon. Vicary Gibbs and his supporters, refusing to learn the lesson taught by more prudent tacticians in the Ayr Burghs, heartily welcomed the aid of the Tar& Reform League and its agents—indeed, as became a mem- ber of the Tariff Commission, the candidate declared himself a" whole-hogger." The reply of his former cuustituents has been to reject him by a Free Trade majority of 132 in place of the Con- servative majority of over 2,400 which was polled In 1892. There can, one would imagine, be no misinterpretation of such a result. It indicates even more clearly than the previous elections the determination of the constituencies to have nothing to do with Mr. Chamberlain's prop)sals.

Letters of excuse are still pouring hat° the un- happy Tariff Commission. This wonderful body Which was to have been hailed, according to its authors, by the commercial community as a means Of liberating British trade from the shackles of -free imports, is receiving some contemptuous !mocks from unexpected quarters. One of these IS delivered by a firm of paper-makers, who point out that some of the prominent members of the Commission were instrumental in organising an alkali ring which forced up the price of chemicals O n the home market against the consumer. A firm of printers in Lancashire has also 4` dumped" upon the Commission a reply which Will hardly be welcomed. It is as follows :—"We desire to state that we derive the greatest possible advantaae from what you term foreign competi- tion.' We are newspaper proprietors and general Printers, and find that foreign competition pre- vents English paper-makers who are already .rich Putting an exorbitant price on their productions. We used to pay a great deal more for paper, but competition has stirred up English manufacturers, Who have improved their machinery and methods to such an extent that the foreigner has not a look in' in many departments of our trade, Whilst, at the same time, our own manufacturers are making very fair profits."

Marriage at St. Albans Church. A. large congregation. assembled at St. Alban's Bewsey-street, on Tuesday afternoon, to Witness the marriage of Mr. Robert C. Brooks, 12, Bewsev-road, son of the late Mr. T. C. Brooks, and fissi May Reardon, only daughter of Mr. P. Reardon, °6, Bewsey-read. The officiating clergy were the Rev. Pather Swarbreck and the Rev. Father Polding. The bride was charmingly attired in a white silk dress, trimmed with orange blossom. She wore a Tell and wreath of orange blossom and carried a beautiful bouquet of white lilies. The bridesmaids were Miss W. Brooks (sister of the bridegroom) and Miss.'. Dumont (cousin of the bride) and they were tastefully gowned in grey voile, with -black picture hats. Their bouquets were composed 'cf tulips. The bridegrporn's gifts to the bridesmaids ai?ere a gold ring and a gold locket respectively. Mr. T. Reardon discharged the duties' of hest man. Mr. J• B. Caldwell presided at the organ and played appro- priate selections including Mendelssohn's " Wedding liarch." The re reception was held at the house of the laride's father, and later in the day Mr. and Mrs. 16!901Es departed for Matlock where the honeymoon is '''lng-Ipeut. Numerous presents were received.

We are pleased to record the success of Miss Ger trade Pickavance, on being awarded a scholarship of the Royal College of Art, South Kensington. The value of the scholarship is £63 per annum with free admission to the classes also a money grant for materials and railway journeys. Miss Pickavance is one of five selected from the students of the Royal College of Art. Miss Pickavanee was fir t a student at the Warrington School of Art and her progress led to her being appointed Art Puna Teacher till she ob- tained her admission to the Royal College of Art. Miss Pickavance has the M 11131117 of another War- rington Art Student, Miss Ethel Mottram who obtained her admisson to the , Collein and a scholar- ship,' from t'ne Cheshire County Council. It is evid- ent the instruction given at the Sohool of Art when responded to by earnest hard-working students pro- duces most satisfactory results. A New Bowling League. With the object of forming a Warrington and District Bowling League a meeting was held at the Cross Keys Hotel, Buttermarket-street on Thursday evening. Representatives attended from the Liberal Club, Penketh Tannery, "Bull's Head," " Cemetery " Inn, " Brooklands " hotel, and." Farmer's Arms." The project was taken up enthusiastically, and it was decided to form a league, the clubs represented being enrolled as members. A further meeting will be held on March lith when other clubs, which hay., not yet held their. annual meetings, will havelad an opportun- ity of deciding whether to join the league or not.

Local Shepherdry, The annual statement of accounts of the Warring; ton District .of the Loyal Order of Ancient Shep- herds has just been published. It is signed by Joseph Adams Pro. U.S., Joseph. A.shton, D.P.C.S., James Parr, district treasurer, and Peter Edgar; district secretary. These officers report that" financially, it is extremely gratifying to note that, with one excep- tion, lodges have made substantial progress by add- ing largely to their already accumulated capital. The distri ct funds amount to £5BB 12s. 7d., as against £l9l Bs. 10d, the previous year, while the total funds of the nine lodges have now a capital (well and safely invested) of .E5lll 11s. Old., as against 11790 12s. Bd. the previous year, or an actual gam 'of £320 182. 41-d. This is highly satisfactory, and can only have been attained by careful management, and the activity dis- played by many of our brethren. We are deeply sensible and grateful to those members who, year in and year out, have taken an intelligent and active in- terest in the progress and prosperity, not 'only of the Lodges they are metnbers of, but also the District they have the honour of belonging to. Numerically, however, we regret to state there has been a consider- able loss. During the year, 53 new members were admitted, while in the same period we have lost 77 through suspensions and 12 by deaths, leaving the total membership of the District at the end of the year at 905, or a loss upon the year of 36. div.head: Brick-street Independent Methodist Church.
div.p: Brick-street Independent Methodist Church.

The young men's section of the above Church gave , a miscellaneous concert on Thursday evening, in aid of the Renovation Fund. Mr. George Appleton occupied the chair, and solos were rendered by the following:—Messrs. W. Barton, James Shaw, H. Syers, H. Holt, C. Tonakinson, I. Shaw and J. Thorniley. Two choruses were rendered by the choir. Messrs. Harold Syers H. Shaw, T. LightfOot and A. Morris were responsible for the humorous items and acquitted themselves creditably. Selections on the cornet and violin were given by Messrs. H. Shaw and S. Tomkin- son. A. pianoforte solo was given by Mr. A. Mayhall, who also acted as accompanist. Refreshments were served during the interval and a most enjoyable even- ing was brought to a close by a laughable dialogue "Apartment's to let." Address to Men. At the Parish Charch last evening the first of a series of L3ntan addresses to man, arranged by the Church Society,was delivered bv the Ven. Archdeacon Hutchings, :Rector of Kirby-Misperton. The topic was "Temptation" to which the preacher said all were subject. Temptation was humiliating, protean, and life-long. Some people thought that as they rose to saintliness of life they would leave temptations at the bottom of the mountain. It was nothing of the kind, for the greate=t saints had had the fiercest tempations. The preacher urged watchful- ness for temptation, and said Christians should pray definitely against the temptations which beset. them. They must seek not only to overcome vice, but to make temptation the signal for cultivating the opposite virtue. What true men and women, lassies and lads would there be if, instead of falling like cowards before the breath of the tempter, people would, in the name of Christ and of His Cross, van- quish the foe ! The great point above all was to realize the love of Christ. That was the stronghold against temptation, and the source of true repentance and conversion.—Neat Friday evening the Ven. Arch- deacon Madden will speak on 'The marks of the 'Jesus." Ragged School Band of Hope. _ _ .

A. most successful concert was given by the mem- bers of the above, in the upper schoolroom on Monday evening, before an audience of 500 persons. Mr. Skelland presided, and his well chosen• remarks were highly enjoyed. The following pro- gramtne was rendered, Dialogue, " Mrs. Smith's new dress," Polly Higginson, Polly Green, Harold Morrison,George Johnson,and Willie Richards song, "The social glass," by nine young girls; recita- tion, "The Beggarman," Edith Brandwood ; flute solo, ,rohn Johnson, "El Capitan " ; song, " When father laid the carpet on the stairs," Bros. Wright ; dialogue, "The Lag of Mutton," by Misses L. Fillingham, A.. Higginson, Lily Filling- ham, Sarah Richards, M. Whittaker, •R, Wright, I. Masters, H. Brandtvood, W. Titchard, J. Wright, and C. Barlow; song, "You can't think of everything," Walter Wright; recitation, "How to cure a drunken husband," Polly Wainwright; solo "Right , men are wanted," Miss M. A. Titchard; recitation "The daughter's appeal," Lizzie Potts; song "Joseph Hawkins," - by seven girls; dialogue "Wanted a rich wife," Mrs. Barlow, Misses E. Makin, ' S. A. and M. A. Titchard, S. Potts, G. Buckley,Messrs. Crozier, Brandwood and the Bros. Wright. This last dialogue created roars of laughter especially the eviction of Hunter by Mr. Graggs the parts being taken by H. Wright and Mrs. Barlow respectively. Mr. Frank Owen accompanied with his usual ability. The singing of "God save the King," brought a most enjoyable evening to a close. Stockton Heath Affairs. A meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Com- mittee was held on Thursday evening. Mr. G. Pilling presided. There were also. present : Messrs. Pear- son, Whitley, Mounfield, Clarke, Pemberton, Bouehier, Mclntyre, Fairhurst, and NV. E. Hough, (clerk), J. Swinton (surveyor), and J. Farringto'n (In- spector.) . Plans were approved for 'cocoa-rooms, lock-up shops, arcade, with club and • billiard rooms above, proposed to be erected at the oorner of Old London-road and Victoria-square, by Mr. Peers Egerton Warburton, Arley Hall. Plans for a row of cottages with . corner shop, pro- posed to be erected by Mr. C. W. Davenport in Bed- ford-street were also approved.—The Clerk read a letter from the Cheshire County Council stating that the Council had acceded to the request of the Stockten Heath Authority to allow them two representatives on the Runcorn Rural District Conncil.—Mr. Whitley : (Hear, hear.)—The Clerk was requested to write to Mr. Stringer' contractor,for.the inaking of Dundonald Avenue and Kimberley Drive, asking him to pro:teed with the work, especially the footpaths.—The lighting sub-committee recommended that three new lamps be erected—one each in Roman-road, Cawdor-street and Whitefield-road. It was further suggested that London-road and Walton-road should be better lighted and the committee was asked to consider the advisa- bility of adopting incandescent lights in these roads. —The three new lamps were approved and it was decided that three lamps in Lendon-road and one- in Walton-road be provided with incandescent lights. The Work of the St. John Amhglance Brigade. This (Saturday) afternoon the annual meeting in sonnection with the North East Lancashire Corps and Divisions of the St. John Ambulance Brigade will be held at Preston. The report to be presented is of more than usual interest to Warrington members of this worthy organization as it deals almost entirely with the review held at Warrington on Ante 20th last which, the Executive Committee 'state proved in every respect satisfactory. The committee wish to express their indebtedness to Mr. J. Charlton Parr, the ex-Mayor and the local committee, as also to the chief superintendent (Captain W. Waring) and the officers and members of the Warrington Corps, for their hearty welcome and for the adthirable arrange- ments. The handsome cap presented by the War- rington Corps for first prize in the brigade squad competition (division 2) was a valuable addi- tion to the prizes to be competed for, and the com- mittee recommended that a hearty vote of thanks be accorded to the Warrington Corps for their generosity. In his report, the inspecting officer, Dr. J. Trimble, states that he was much struck by the improved appearance of all ranks on parade. The uniform was in excellent condition, and as a rule the men had learned to dress correctly and turn out clean, smart, and soldier-like. Dr. Trimble expresses pleasure that the silver cup referred to was won by the Warrington team. Presentation to a Forester:

The members of the Warrinii:ton District of the Ancient Order of Foresters assembled last evening in the Corporation Inn, Market-place, to do honour to one of their brethren who has rendered good service to Forestry. The proceedings commenced with a hot-pot supper,and after an excellent repast, a smoking concert was held. Bro. R. Thprnley,D.C.R.,occupied the chair and amongst those present were : Bro. Joseph Owen, P.C.R.' Bro.. W. Hipkiss. D.S.C.R., Bro. L. Dayies (district' secretary), Bro. J. Davies (assistant secretary), Bro. Humphey Owen and Councillor Peter Peacock. The presentation consisted of a framed emblem of the order and an emblematic sash in recognition of his 33 years' connection with the Court Mercy No. 240 and as mementoes of his services in the chair as past chief ranger for two years. In making the presentations. the Chairman said •Bro. Owen had filled the office of Chiefßanger with distinction to himself and credit and advantage to the Court. \He then invested him with Past Chie f Ranger's sash and handed to him the illuminated Emblem of the order,—ln accept- ing the presents, Mr. Owen gave some reminiscences of the court, and stated that when he joined in 1870 Bro. Humphrey Owen was Chief Ranger and Bro.. Llewellyn Davies Past Chief Ranger, both of whom were present that night. (Hear, hear.) Re:erring tp the position of Forestry Mr. Owen pointed ou,t that there were 932,827 mem- bers in the order, which was the second largest Friendly Society in the United Kingdom. He hoped that in the next report the membership would have reached one million. (Hear, hear.) In conclu- sion he said he greatly valued the gifts, and would always try to maintain the best tradi- tions of the Order. Three hearty cheers were then raised for Mr. Owen.—Several toasts were proposed, the place of honour being given to that of the King.—Conacillor Peter Peacock responded to the toast of the visiting brethren and expressed the hope that all the members would unite in making the Warrington district a still more prosperous one. During the evening, songs were contributed by Bros. Peter Smith, J. P. Birkhead, and J. P. Hignett, the last named also acting as accompanist. Mr. E. A. Sanders gave a humorous recitation. The proceed- ings were of a very enjoyable character.

WIDNES Mix's BRAVERY.

It was announced on Thursday that the bronze medal of the Royal Humane Society had been awarded to W. A. Wright, James-street, Widnes, for his pluck in saving one boy, and attempting to save another from drowning in the Mersey on January 23rd. SODDEN DEATH 0 F A WIDNES WOMAN,

A womannamed Mary Brown, wife of Alfred Brown, labourer, 3, Martley-street, died very suddenly on Thur.day morning. The deceased had not been ailing, and this morning the husband went to work leaving his wife in bed. When he came in at eight o'clock he found her dead in a chair in the kitchen. WIDNES MANUFACTURERS FINED.

On Thursday, at the Widnes Police Court,the Widnes Chemical Manufacturing Co. were summoned by Mr. R. E. Graves, H. M. Inspector of Factories, for having at their works an unfenced tank containing boiling soda liquid. Mr. Graves pointed out that on Christ- mas-day a workman named William Platt slippedinto the tank in question and was so badly scalded that he died. The Act of Parliament provided that any part or the whole of the fine might be applied for the benefit of the injured person or his family. In this case, however, the widow of the deceased had received £125. Mr. Poole appeared for the defendant company, and said they admitted the offence and were quite ready to effect the remedy. A fine of £2 and costs was imposed. RUNCORN COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTIONS. There are likely to be contests in all the divisions in ! Runcorn district at the approaching elections for ' Cheshire County Council. A joint conference of the Liberal Association and Free Church Council have de- : cided to nominate Mr. A. R. Norman,J.P., for Runcorn • North, and Mr. James Pritchard, J.P., for Runcorn South. Mr. Norman is the sitting member, and Mr Pritchardwill attack the seat now held by Mr.E.lmison J.P.,who,weunderstand,does not intendto seekre-election An assault is also to be made on the Daresbury and Frodsham divisions,both held by Unionists in the persons of Mr. John Ockleston, J.P.,and Mr. Thomas Baxter. The Liberal and progressive educationist candidates spoken of are Mr. James M. Fritti. of Runcorn, and Mr. Boston, of Frodsham, respectively.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWFON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWFON.
E ARLESTO WN SHOPBREAKING CHIRGE

At the Warrington Occasional Court on Monday', Martin Moran and James Reynolds, of no fixed resid- ence, were charged with breaking into the 'pawnshop of James Callendar, Market-street,Barlestown, on January I 14th and stealine 13 ladies' watches, a set of gold studs and links, and three dress rings.—Constable Butler stated that during the- night of January 14th he was on • duty in Market-street and heard the crash of glass. He saw the prisoners standing by Mr. Callendar's shopand , when he approached they ran away. It was found that I the shop window had been broken with a large stone and the articles named were missing. Moran was arrested at Southport where some of the watches were pledged and Reynolds was apprehended at I Walton, Liverpool.—Moran now stated that he was ' solely responsible Tor the robbery,and Reynolds strongly denied complicity.—Prisoners were committed to Liverpool Quarter Sessions. THEFT OF CLOTHING. W--ineb • 0 ' C' •rt Mrtcl bef,

, arringtou Occasiona, jourt on ......onday, before Mr. F. A. Frost, Elizabeth and Nancy Dnxbury, mother and daughter, who reside at Burtonwood, were charged with stealing two ladies' dress bodices, of the value of 55., the property of William Jones, pawnbroker, Market- street, Earlestown.—The evidence showed that the manager, genry Morris, saw the articles hanging in the .shop, with others, when the two prisoners were redeem- ing something. They were missed after. the prisoners left. P.C. Lennie was irformed and from inquiries he made, he visited the prisoners' house and questioned I them. They at first denied all knowledge of the articles ; but subsequently, on the way to the Police Station, ! they said they mightas swell tell the truth. The mother said that her daughter wanted to go into Service but had no clothes to go in, and alleged that the father did not give them enough money to live on. The girl herself said that she wanted to go into service, bat her father would not buy her any clothes.—Both prisoners were remanded to the Warrington Patty Sessions on I Wednesday when the magistrates bound them over under the First Offenders' Act. The girl promised to go t 9 a home.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
CANON WILL INK'S DEPARTURE.

At St. Helens on Monday evening there was a memorable gathering of th 3 members of the Parish Churchmen's Bible class which is on 3 of the largest Bible classes in England, to bid farewell to Canon Willink, who has been conductor and leader of the class for thirteen years, but is leaving St. Helens to become vicar of Great Yarmouth. Mr. Ashton' on behalf of the members of the class, presented to Canon Willink magnificent semi-grand piano in recognition of his work among them. Canon Willink made an affecting' reply.

div.head: STEPPED INTO A BLAZING FURNACE.
div.p: STEPPED INTO A BLAZING FURNACE.

Walter Barrow, aged nineteen, of 63, Stanley street, met with an exceedingly painful accident at Messrs. Pilkington's sheet glass works, St. Helens,on Thursday. Barrow was going about his work as usual, when as he passed over the gas flue, which carries a great volume of burning gas into the glass furnaces, the covering of the flue gave way and Barrow's leg went into it, and he was most terribly burnt. He was taken to the Provi- dance Hospital.—An elderly man named James Ceron was assisting in the construction of the timber yard ex- tendon at Messrs. Pilkington's on Wednesday when he fell into a deep sewer full of water, and was for some time in peril. He was rescued and conveyed to hospital. CRUSHED TO DEATH IN A COALPIT. DOUBLE PATAUTY AT ST. HELEN'S. _

I An accident which caused considerable .e;citement ; amongst the families of men down the pit occurred on I Thursday night at the Ravenhead Colliery. St. Helens l belonging to Messrs. Pilkington Brothers'. Two young I men, John William Platt., aged twenty-four, 'of 76, Hardshaw-street, and Thomas Grundy, aged twenty-three, of Rainford-road, were work- ing together as thy wagemen or metal-men, getting down roof for the purpose of improving a roadway. They were visited by a shot lighter. named Thomas Halliweli, and appeared to be all richt up to six o'clock. Shortly after that time Halliwell again visited the place, and found that the roof and sides had fallen in on both of the men. Help was abtained, and after a lot of the debris had been removed the dead bodies of the two men were recovered. Platt was married, and leaves a wife and one child, but Grundy was single.

div.head: TEMPERANCE MEETING AT WYCLIFFE MEMORIAL BUILDINGS. Address by Mrs. Garnett.
div.p: TEMPERANCE MEETING AT WYCLIFFE MEMORIAL BUILDINGS. Address by Mrs. Garnett.

The members of the Warrington Branch of the British. Women's Temperance Association conducted a temper- ance meeting held in. Wycliffe Memorial Buildings on Wednesday evening. The proceedings were presided over by Mrs. Garnett, president of the local branch. In her address,Mrs. Garnett pointed out that that day', was the anniversary of the death of Frances Willard, one of the founders of the British Women's Temperance Association, whose name was held • sacred and whose memory was consecrated in two hemispheres. During her too short life she accomplished a great work in connection with the temperance movement. When quite a young girl Frances Willard took a vow to be good an&in that respect she was something like the late Queen Victoria, who when informed that she was the Queen said ". I will be good." Frances Willard by her charming disposition attracted many to the temperance cause, and to-day there were many noble women trying to help the temperance cause Lady Henry Somerset was still working in the slums of London, and her descriptions of slums life were terrible reading. They could not close their eyes to the fact that three were slums in Warrington.lt was impossible to go through them witho4 feeling that there were poor little children who were sufferinc, physically because of the state in whichthey were brought into the world ; owing to the drunken habits of their parents. Many ' children were born into misery through this curse of drink. She (Mrs. Garnett) had travelled a good deal but she had never seen anything abroad to equal some of the sights which might be seen in any of the' large towns in Great Britain. In Norway she noticed that there were no seats in the inns and public- houses, but in England there were so many encourage- ments to drink. We made it very difficult for a workingman, either to get past a public-house or to get out of one when he once got in. Oftentimes the public- houses were cleaner and brighter than the men's homes, and one could only feel sorry for ttiona that they were driven to these places for brightness and society and some little enjoyment. What were they doing as temperance workers? There were more public-houses than were required but the owners were very loath to give any of them up. The Government was so blinded on this particular subject that although magistrates had had powers to restrict licences they were now threatened with a withdrawal of this magisterial power. They must be prepared to contest any restriction of the discretionary power of the magistrates. They were all able to exercise some influence in forming public opinion and they must use it. Mrs. Garnett proceeded, to speak on the importance of individual effort in the temperance cause, and although they might meet with many discouragements, she hoped they would persevere. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Short addresses were also delivered by Mrs. Simpson (secretary of the Warrington Branch of the British Women's Temperance Association) and Miss Green. Miss TAYLOR sang several songs in an efficient manner, the accompaniments being played by Miss Plinston. Selections on the phonograph were also given by Mr. C.M. A vote of thanks was tendered to all who had taken part on the proposition of the Rev. John Yonge.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
Warburton Bridge Tolls.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held at Bewsey Chambers on Wednesday, Mr. T. Halton pre- siding. There were also present:—Messzs. Brooks. Ball, Mather, Knowles, Forshaw, Houghton Backhouse, with Dr. Sellton (medical offinr of health), Messrs. J. C. Sutton (clerk), F. Kerfoot (inspector of nuisances), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), and H. H. Bumage (assistant surveyor.)
THE ESTIMATES. CALL UPON THE TOWNSHIP REDUCED.

The CLERK submitted the estimates of expenuiture for the half year ending iVfichwlmas next. He said that for the half year ending Michlmas, 1903, the call upon the townships was sixpence in the R. Serious thought had been given to the need for an extra outlay to further the remaining road improvements the Council have in view. Complete restoration of road surface damaged by recent rains needed an exceptional item to effect. The outbreak of infectious diseases, curable yet needing isolation, had caused and might continue to cause heivy hospital charges, yet the suffi- ciency of a rate of fivepence in the R for the ensuing half-year was hoped for and a call of that amount was advised. The following, calls to meet parish special expenses were estimated : Burtonwood, where the main sewer is being extended, £BO ; Penketh. for loan and interest, sewerage and lighting, £80; Poulton, lighting, £4O; Rixton, for loan and interest and Cemetery, £3O; Great Sankey. for lighting, £3O. One or two parishes, added Mr. Sutton, would probably increase in ratable value before the precepts were issued and the figures would be amended accordingly. On the motion of Mr. BROOKS, seconded by Mr. BALL, the estimates were adopted.

div.head: LIGHTING OF BI7IITONWOOD.
div.p: THE LIGHTING OF BI7IITONWOOD.

The CLERK reported that he had had correspondence with Mr. Forshaw with regard to the procedure of for ratepayers Of Burtonwooto secure the adoption the the Lighting Act in respect of that parish, and also with Mr. Webster, solicitor, St. Helens, upon his pro- cedure as returning officer for the poll on the lighting question at Burtonwood. Mr. FORSHAW said he had, communicated with the Local Government Board, and that authority said they could adopt the Act without applying to the District Council.

div.head: PROPOSED WINWICK IMPROVEMENT.
div.p: A PROPOSED WINWICK IMPROVEMENT.

The CLERK slid he had received a letter from Messrs. Myles, Jennings, White and Foster, of London. acting for the Ecclesiastical Commissioners, with reference to the arrangement as to the proposed exchange and widening of Hollins-lane, Winwick, and intimating that a draft would be forwarded for approval. At present he had not received the draft.
THE .FECES ON THE CUERDLEY ESTATE.
IS THE COUNCIL LIABLE FOR THEIR AI lIIVITNANCE ?

As instructed at the last meeting the Clerk wrote Mr. C. L. Evans, of the Cuerdley estate office, informing him that the Council disputed their liability to make good fences on the Cuerdley estate erected by the Old Highway Bard when new roads were cut to enable the Sheffield and Midland Railway Company to construct a loop line to Widnes. The CLERK now reported that Mr. Evans had replied as follows :—I regret you do not admit your liability, which your late surveyor always carried out when re- quested to do so. In the meax4ime I shall have to take advice upon the subject unless we can come to some amicable arrangement. It seems a pity that the rela- tions between yeur Council and the Cuerdley estate should become strained, owing to your surveyor not carrying out what evidently was an arrangement made by your late surveyor. The Council took no further action in the matter.
COUNTY COUNCIL MAIN ,ROADS.

The CLERK- said he had received from the deputy clerk of the County Council an agreement re the main roads and the establishment charges. The amount originally stated was £5O but as that was wrong it was amended to £BO.
HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

Pr. SEPHTON reported that for the three weeks end- in. February 17th, 11 births and 29 deaths had been notified. The death rate was 45.45 per 1,000, but as 22 of the deaths occurred in Winwick Asylum, the death rate proper for the district was 10.97. Thirteen cases of scarlet fever and two cases of diphtheria had been reported.

div.head: LOGFORI) DEPOT.
div.p: LOGFORI) DEPOT.

The INSPTOR reported that he visited the dept oil Tuesday and found the alterations were proceeding satisfactorily. The condensing tower was almost com- plete. Another vacuum pan was to be put down and it would give greater evaporating power and enable them to get through the work in a shorter time. The furnaces had been altered and the contract for the reservoir was to be let on the day of his visit. yhere was no comment on the report. WIELBURTON BRIDGO.

The SURVEYOR reported thathe Had had an interview with Mr. Thompson (County Surveydr) re the adoption by the Lancashire and Cheshire County Councils of the Warburton Bridge-road. He held out no hope of the Council getting the road accepted as main by the two counties, there being at present no definite through traffic between any two towns of at least 30,000 inhabit- ants. He, however, snegested that the best course to take would be for him (Mr. Newcombe) to approach the other two Authorities concerned with a view to their co-operation. If this could be arranged Mr. Thompson would recommend that the length within this County should be scheduled Secondary. He (Mr. Newcombe) would advise, however, that the Council should instruct him to make formal application to the two County Head Surveyors for the adoption of the road as main before suggesting co-operation of the four bodies to adopt has a secondary road, which proposal night corn* later.
Mr. FORSHA.W considered the present state of affairs to be a scandal. They ought to take the road out of the hands of private enterprise and make it a pulAlic road.
The SURVEYOR'S suggostion that the head surveyor be approached was agreed to.
FLOODING AT LONGFORD.

The StRVEYOR pointed out that Longford was at resent in a terribly flooded state. On investigating the cause he found that Sankey Brook was practically dammed up by Messrs. Crosfleld's tip. Tt was decided that the Surveyor should write to Messrs. Crostield stating that the Council had sustained damage through the brook being stopped up and that action would be taken against them unless the brook were cleaned.
COUNTY COUNCIL GRANTS.

The SURVEYOR said he had applied to the County for an increase of main roads maintenance grants, which at present amounted to £1,596, to an estimate of £2,024, and had also submitted estimates and applications for special grants for the following improvements on main roads :—Doe Green Corner ;Manchester-road Widen, ing ; Leigh-road, forming side; Liverpool-road, kerb- ing by Sankey Vicarage; Leigh-road,ilagging by Church and Wesleyan Chapel ; Newton-road, extra macadam required for strengthening.

div.head: Serious Fire in Mersey-street.
div.p: Serious Fire in Mersey-street.

A fire which did consider-able damage broke out on the lock-up premises of Hr. Henry Hough, furniture dealer, 18 and 20, Mersey-street, at 11 30 on Thursday morning. It was discovered by a carter named Patrick Fitzpatrick who informed Sergeant Evans and the fire bell was runt,. In the meantime Sergeant Evans, Police-constables .Stuart and. Whitby, and Mr. Thomas Allen endeavoured to extinguish the flames by throwing buckets of water on them, but the fire was burning too fiercely for their efforts to be of any avail. The fire brigade, under the command of Superintendent Turner, was quickly on the scene with the engine " Major " and appliances. Despite the exertions of the men the show room upstairs, which was filled with valuable furniture,was gutted. The stock in the shop was much damaged by water, .and the books in the office were destroyed. The flames spread to an adjoining house in which Mr. Hough's son .resided, and a portion of the roof fell in. The occupants had been roused and fortunately no one was injured. How the fire origin- ated is not known as the premises were left apparently secure at 11.30. The damage, which is partly covered by insurance, is roughly estimated at £lOOO. Mr. Hough was staying at Rhyl for the benefit of his health, and the business was,being conducted by his son. A Clergyman's Will. - .

The Jtwate of the Rev. John William Spencer, of the Old Parsonage, Turton, vicar of St. Anne's, Turton. since 1879, and vicar of Great Sankey, Warrington, from 1871-79, who 'died on. the 10th January last,aged 72 years, has been valued at £15,127 gross, with net personality of 5,14.577. Ile bequeathed £lOO to the vicar and Churchwardens of Turton in trust to pay the income to 12 poor widows of Turton, and, after family and other beauests, left the residue of his estate as to two-fifths in trust for his daughter Sarah Ann Laura ll'Nic3l, and as to three-fifths between his sons.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS
Ragby Football.

By " Ovalists" Since I last penned this column Warrington have played two matches, in the course of which they have tasted the sweets of success and the bitterness of defeat. Just now they are performing in the style which has distinguish3d them for years—one up and one down, so to speak. The sweets of success were obtained at the expense of the warriors from Widnes, who did not give up the spoils at all willingly or graciously. Nobody expected that they would, and truth to tell, they almost succeeded in retaining them.

I am not going to say much about the Widnes match. This is a football column, and it would be manifestly unfair to dump down anything here and call it football if it pertained to this particular game. The Widnesians did not come to play foot- ball. Bless you, what was the good of that? Oh no! their idea was to secure or share the spoils by hook or crook, and let the good old game go to the dogs. And it went. Ono of the dogs actually invaded the enclosure and shed tear § in the rear of the operations until Fish forcibly removed him. Moreover the spectators who did not weep, swore--at least they cussed both play and players in their own sweet • way. In the meantime Harris scor:d a try—thus fittingly signalising his re-appearance—and Fish kicked a goal from the touch-line which caused a genuine spasm of joyin the bosoms of the home crowd. There were no other events, beyond occasional buts of fisticuffs, which eventually ended in bunt and a Widnes forward being ordered off. The rest of the time was occupied by wallowing in the mud, and when Referee Ashton thankfully brought affairs to a co.nclusion,Warrington were accredited N% inners by five points. I know they are a better team than Widnes, but they did not prove it last Saturday. The state of the elements is perhaps some excuse.

On Tuesday, the gallant fifteen. from Warrington had to leave their pancakes and depart for Halifax. The weather was really cheerful for once, but beyond Rochdale we found the land covered with snow and the streets of hilly Halifax were sloppy in the extreme Fortunately the ground had been covered and was in very fair order, though naturally soft. High hopes were entertained of victory, for Warrington generally give a good acclunt of themselves against the blue and whites, and the team was at full strength. ,

Fate, and Referee Bruckshaw ruled otherwise, how- ever, and Warrington had to admit defeat by a beastly penalty goal to nil. This occurred about threequarter time, when Warrington were holding their own, and was the result of a very fine kick from that human catapult, W. Little. But why Referee Bruckshaw gave a penalty at this point was a mystery Somehow, I don't love the gentleman. This is the second occasion on which I have seen him give a penalty kick which has lost Warrington the match. At Swinton two years ago his decisiop, was unquestionably wrong, but I won't say as much in regard to Tuesday's match. Still it was very hard lines, for Warrington seemed sure of one point at least. The defence on .both sides was too good for the attack, which, I must admit, followed ordinary lines so closely as to be somewhat weak. A man with initiative is badly wanted in the Warrington rear division.

It is not long since I used to think the Warringtod threequarter line equal to any in the League, but my opinion is beginning to change. Broughton Rangers for instance, are much superior in this department, and chiefly owing to Wilson's genius. The Rangers' skipper is unquestionably the Gould of the Northern Union, and whether on attack or defence he is supremely good. Somehow the Warrington centres appear to have slowed dowd. .N.:ther appears as speedy as formerly and the occasions on which they ,have got away with the wing man in attendance could be numbered on one hand. Some of the blame may be attcibuted to the half backs, but the fact is beyond dispute that the centre positions are not filled as well as they might be. Ishecwood seems overworked, and. it would be in his own interests to stand down for a week or two. Who is to replace him my readers may ask ? Well, I am ready with a suggestion. Fish might glcentre and Kenyon come in on the left wing. There would be more speed and more dash in the line then than at present. Fish would have more to do, and the more work he has and better he does it. Just now we are losing matches, and some remedy for obvious weaknesses must be found.

I have another suggestion. The dream of the War- rington Committee has been to get a good strong half-back, but the dream has failed to come true. Why not make the required half-back, then ? There is material in the club. Let us see what Thomas can do behind the " scrum " instead of in it. He has proved himself a speedy, clever,footballer and I fancy he has the ability for something better than pushing and thrutching. Good forwards have Made better half-backs before now—Bob Wood, bf international fame for instance. And next to Lomas there is no man I fear more behind the pack than Tom Broadley. I should be glad if some of my readers would give me their opinion on these suggestions. Any letter to Ovalist, "Examiner " Office, will be welcomed and dealt with in this column.

To return to the Halifax game, it was quite up to the standard of the contests between the two clubs. .There was plenty, of open football and strenums forward play. As regards the latter Halifax had the best of matters, the home eight working with far more method and cohesion tlyin the Warrington octet. There can be no doubt Warrington would have won if the forwards could have held their own, for the backs did not get many opportunities, whereas the Halifax third line was always on the run, but never looked like piercing thp defence. Fish was obviously the speediest man on the ground, and notwithstanding an injury to the knee he played a good game and was unfortunate in not getting through on two occasions. Harris got very few chances on the attack, but he kept a close eye on Hadwen, who was the best man in the Halifax rear division. Chief honours for War- rington unquestionably go to Hallam who played a superb game throughout. In fact the Warrington men fielded and kicked into touch with a precision and power quite new to them. Their efforts deserved a better fate.
The, League table up-to-date, including .tlb3 defeat of Wigan at home on Wednesday by Hunslet, who scored two goals to a try is as follows :
The Widnes match resulted in an extra twe points in the the South West Lancashire League, which • stands as below : Pts.

Warrington journey to Swinton to-day, and they will have to show better form than of late to secure points. The Blues, though they went down at Leigh on Saturday-,won cleverly at Huddersfield on Tuesday, and are sure to make a big effort to avenge the 10-0 defeat at Wilderspool on October 24th. Warrington are playing the same back team as agaillst Halifax but there will be two changes forward. The fifteen will be selected from: Hallam, full back; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Harris, threequarters ; Bate and Hockenhall, half backs ; Boardman, Morrison, Edmundson, Lunt, Naylor, Swift, Jolley, Cooke, Harmer, and Thomas, forwards.

Dave Traynor will turn out for Swinton to-day and we shall all be interested in seeing how he performs. The full team will be :—Dixon; G-artrell, Traynor (Capt.), Wallwork, and Burrows; Molyneux and Williamson; Evans, Barnett, Preston, Cheetham, Smith, Simister, Pomfret, and Coletrup. I should like to remind my readers that the kick-off is at. 3.30 and not 3 o'clock.

div.head: WARRINGTON WORKS BOWLING ASSOCIATION. The Annual Meeting.
div.p: WARRINGTON WORKS BOWLING ASSOCIATION. The Annual Meeting.

The healthful game of bowls claims a host of enthusiasts in Wdrrington, and workingmen lovers of the popular pastime were given special opportunities of displaying their prowess last season by the promo- tion of competitions by the Works Bowling Associa- tion. Although it is still in its infancy this organiza- tion has flourished almost like "the green bay tree " and a very encouraging report was presented at the annual meeting held at the "King and Queen "Hotel, Padgate-lane, on Monday evening. Mr. Samuel Taylor presided over a good attendance, and Mr. J. L. Brime- low occupied the vice-chair. Mr. F. W. Scarisbrick (hon. secretary) was also present. Letterq of apology for non-attendance were read from Mr. J. Finlayson, Councillor Hulse, and Mr. C. Stanley Smith, of Croft. The last-named gentleman forwarded a cheque for one guinea.

THE REPORT. The HON. SECRETARY submitted his report. in which he said he;considered that the association had up to the present been a grand success. When they had their first meetinr, on April 22nd of last year, enthusiastic as it was, they little thought of the great interest that would be taken in the competition. A great factor of that success, was to his mind, owing to the generosity of Mr. Finlayson in presenting to them alcup.They alliknew what power a trophy of that kind had of making them. exert themselves,and he thought too much praise could not be given to Mr.. Finlayson for his very valuable gift. Thirty teams entered the cup competition repre- senting twenty-six works. The gold medals and cup were won by the London and North-Western Railway team, who bowled exceedingly well throughout the com- petition. The silver, enamel centre medals were won by Pearson and Knowles No. 1 team, a team that was looked upon from the beginning as very easy winners. The committee then decided to have a handicap con- fined to those works only that had entered the cup competition. That the idea wasa good one was proved by the magnificent entry of 292. The handicapping of so many proved veri difficult, but he thought as a whole that the handicappers gave great satisfaction. That they had a few grumblings he was aware, but he believed with one, or possibly two, exceptions, it was entirely the player's own fault that his name was scratched off. At any rate he could say this, that the committee did all in their power to please everybody. The first prize, a handsome marble clock and bronzes, had been won by Mr. W. Andrews from Orford Tannery. The second prize, a valuable marble clock, had been won by Mr. H. Daintith, and the third prize a watch, had been won by Mr. George Monks. Seventy-two prizes were given altogether. Speaking of the committee he did not think too much praise could be given to them for their untiring efforts in try- ing to make the association a success. He could not think it possible to get a more hardworking or more capable lot in the whole of Warrington. Two auditors had been appointed to go through the accounts, and he thought they deserved their very best thanks. At the presentation of prizes they had the honour of having amongst them their chairman, Mr. A. H. Crostield, who had during the season very generously sent them a donation of £lO. That his heart was with them last season, was shown by the letters he had sent. Ho hoped they would continue as they had begun. He was sure it was a great honour to them to have him as one of their vice-presidents. He then read a letter from Mr. Crosfield, promising that he would over be ready to lend assistance to the association. He thought they were also very lucky in having as President, Captain G. R. Crosfield, and with such Vice-Presidents as Mr. S. Smith, Mr. S. Taylor, Mr. Joseph Craik, Mr. C. Hulse, Mr. Brimelow and Mr. Finlayson they need not fear the result of the coming season. He thought Mr. Fred Clare, the landlord, de-, served great praise for his attention to the green, and his willingness to help them in whatever way he could. (Applause.) In conclusion, he wished the association at the beginning of this new season a continuance of that success to which he thought they were entitled. Looking back at the difficulties they had overcome,they might go forth to meet the coming season with new hopes, new courage, and new ambitions, and with an undaunted determmation to advance. (Loud applause.) He should just like to take that opportunity of thank- ing the captains of teams, the teams themselves, and the whole body of members for their courtesy and kindness to him during the whole of the last season. (Applause.) Mr. SCA.RESBRICK was warmly complimented upon his excellent resum6 of the events of the season, and the report was adopted on the propositioa of Mr. E. RANDALL, seconded by Mr. I. MAKIN.
THE FINANCES. Mr. DOOLEY' presented the balance sheet andanditors' report, which showed that there was a balance in hand of El. is. 3d.

The CHAIRMAN said they had every reason to con- gratulate themselves upon the excellent balance sheet, which reflected the greatest credit upon the officers. Mr. F. RIGBY proposed and Mr. 1. MAKIN seconded the adoption of the balance sheet, and the motion wa* agreed to.

THE SECRETARY RE-ELECTED. The CHAIRMAN said he understood their Secretary was to accept office for another year and, judg- ing from the ability with which he had discharged his duties, they could not do better than re-elect him. Although he did not believe in the sante individual serving continuouVy year after year, he considered that as the Secretary had only been in office one year. and was so well acquainted with the work, it would be a pity to make a change, at least for another season or two.
On the proposition of Mr. J. W. EVANS, seconded by Mr. J. WILSON, Mr. Scarisbrick was unanimously re- elected.

In returning thanks, Mr. S6.RISBRICK thanked the chairman for his kind words and the members generally for the confidence they had reposed in him. He would try in the future—as he had done in the past—to dis- charge the duties to their entire satisfaction, and .he felt sure that at the close of the season they would have nothing to complain about. (Hear, hear.) TREASURER AND AUDITORS. Mr. F. CL VIE was unanimously re-elected hon. treasurer on the proposition of Mr. a Holbrook seconded by Mr. J. Willett. Messrs. DOOLEY and SIMMS were re-elected hon. auditors.
TELE COMMITTEE. The election of the committee was then proceeded with.

Mr. HUMPHREYS thought there ought to be at least one representative from each works. It was pointed out that twenty six works were repre- sented by the association, and the committee would be too large if Mr. Humphreys' suggestion were acted upon. __ _ _ _

'Mr. HOLBROOK said Messrs. Rylands's employed 200 hands but had no representative on the committee. Mr. PETERS said the same remark applied to the London and North Western Railway. On a vote being taken, the following were elected:— Messrs. John Willett, H. Williams, George Ball. Joseph Harrison, John Monks, W. H. Smalley, Thomas Sitnister, Thomas Ellison, Thomas Lawton, Thomas Bridge, A. Peters and George Holbrook.

The CIIAIRNI4N announced that the old committee had been re-elected with the addition of Messrs. Bridge Peters and Hot brook. THE PRESIDENT. Mr. WILLETT said that Captain G. R. Crosfield would be pleased to again fulfil the duties of president if that was the wish of the members.

It was the general opinion that in Captain Crosfleld the association had an excellent president, and'on the proposition of Mr. G.llarlow, seconded by Mr. Wilson, he was unanimously re-elected. The Vice-Presidents were re-elected and the Secre- tary was asked to approach a number of gentlemen with a view of their becoming vice-presidents. The Chairman was cordially thanked for presiding, and in the course of his concluding remarks expressed the hope that this year's competitions would be carried through as successfully as their predecessors, and that the conduct of the members on the green would, as in the past, be irreproachable.

div.head: FUTURE OF THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
div.p: THE FUTURE OF THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL.

At the meeting of the Education Committee on INlonday evening, the School Management Committee will submit a report of the special meeting held for the purpose of meeting Nfr. A. CArdew, one of the senior examiners of the Board of Education, with refer- ence to the committee's proposals in regard to Second- ary Education. The discussion it is stated in the report,turned chiefly upon the future position of the Grammar school in its relation to the scheme for Higher Education as adopted by the committee. The question of the fees charged at the Grammar school was considered, but, whilst the representatives of the Board of Education deprecated any considerable reduction, several members of the committee felt that the present fees were too high, and the general tendency of the discussion pointed to the desirability of fixing the fees at .C 6 and £9 per annum having in view local conditions. _

The consideration of the provision of scholarships, at the schools, but more particularly at the Grammar school, led to the question of the proportion of the number of free scholars to be admitted to the latter school, and, after some discussion, Rivas resolved that, in the opinion of this Committee any scheme of scholarships should include scholarships, tenable at the Grammar school, for boys from the ele- mentary schools, but that, at present, the number of free scholars should not exceed 20 per cent of the total number of scholars in the school.

The other matters touched upon were the training and supply of pupil teachers, the prepulstory division of the secondary school, and the establishment of a girls' high school, the necessity for the latter belay, strongly , urged upon the Committee. On the motion of the Chairman of the Cotamittee a vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Cardew and H.M. In- spectorfor their presence and assistance.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. Warrington Borough Police court.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. Warrington Borough Police court.
Minor Cases.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Francomb and Smethurst, Councillor Thornton, and Messrs. Birchall, Hayward, and Wright. DISORDERLY Yorms.—Two youths, named William Parker, wireworkor, 12,Lilford-street,and Frank Brand- wood, fitter's apprentice, 22, Pierpoint-street, were summoned for having made a loud and unseemly noise in Sankey-street on Sunday the ith.—P.C. Stewart said the defendants were walkiAg down Sankey-street jostling groups of girls, and shouting.—The Chief Constable said he hated to have to bring respectable young boys like the defendants before the magistrates, but they did not seem to realize that by their conduct they were creating a nuisance.—Eac defendant was fined 55., including costs. A CONSIDERATE PRISONEIL—Patrick Richard Moran, 15, Ship-yard, a well-known character who made his 24th appearance, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Queen-street, at a quarter past ten on Sunday night.—PC. Hayes said that when taken into custody prisoner remarked: "I would not assault you." (Laughter.)—He was fined ss. and costs. LOOKING FOR THE WORKHOUSE.—Edward Fenton, of no fixed residence, was charged that, being a suspicious character, he was found frequenting Wilson Patten- street at 6 p.m. on Sunday with intent to commit a felony.—The Chief Constable saw the prisoner try the doors of several houses. On being accosted he made the strange reply that he was looking for the Work- house.—He was sent to gaol for a month. MtNort CASES.—For hiving made use of obscene language in Battermarket-street, on Saturday night, Edward Knight, of Cloth Hall-yard, was fined ss. in- cluding costs.—For a similar offence at Ship-yard on the 7th inst., Bridget Costello, 13, Lower Ship-yard, was fined a like amount, she having been before the magistrates 32 times previous!y.—Maria McDonald, 4, Knowles-yard, was bound over in the sum of £5, to keep the peace, and ordered to pay the costs, for having committed a breach of the peace, by being guilty of disorderly behaviour on the 6th inst.
TUESDAY-. —Before Aldermen Sutton (in the chair), awl Hutchinson and Air! J Rymer Young.

OB 3C ENE LANG ITA.GE. Nlary Hamblett, of John-street, was fined ss. and costs for having used obscene language in Wilson Patten-street the previous afternoon. TUESDAY.—Before the Mayor (presiding), Alderman Smethurst Councillors Roberts and Thornton, and

Mr. Hepherd. DRUNK IN CHARGE.—For having been drunk in charge of a horse and trap in Battersby-lane at 2.45 on Thursday afternoon, Wm. Harding, 50, Chorley-street was fined ss. and costs.—P.C. Johnson proved the case TRAVELLING WITHOUT A TICKET.—JaMeS WateTWOrth. 17, Legh-street, was summoned for travelling on the London and North-Western Railway from Newton-le- Willows to Warrington on January 29th without paying the fare.—Defendane admitted that he had no ticket, but said he had no intention to defraud.—Mr. Fenno, prosecuted and said that on the date in question defendant arrived at Bank Quay station with a young woman and gave up two tickets from Lymm to War- rington. He then procured a ticket for West Leigh for the young woman and on passing the collector told him that he was only going on the high level platform to see his friend off. As the collector knew him by sight he was allowed to pass without a platform ticket. It appeared, however, that he had booked to Newton and he was sent to get on the train for that place. At Newton he left the young woman, who went on to Leigh, and returned to Warrington by the next train, arriving at 8.25. On being asked for his ticket he said he had not travelled on the train, but had only been on the platform. Subsequently, he admitted that he had come from Newton without a ticket, but said he had no intention to defraud.— Evidence having been given, defendant stated that he was under the influence or drink and could not remem- ber exactly what occurred.—A fine of 10s. and costs £1 Bs. in all) was imposed.

div.head: WIDNES PASSIVE RESISTERS
div.p: WIDNES PASSIVE RESISTERS
Minister's Singular Plea.

On Thursday. at the Widnes Police court, 33 of the persons were summoned for non-payment of the educa- tion portion of the poor rate. Mr. Goff, assistant overseer, said he did not think the legality of the rate would be questioned, nor the amount disputed. The overseers had every respect for the Con- scientious objections, but it was clearly their duty to recover the balance of the rate. He was instructed to ask for distress warrants.
The Rev. Alex Harvey. Deacon-road, was summoned for Is. 9d. He said he had a legal objection. If any portion of this rate was used for Roman- The Chairman: We won't hear that.

The defendant said he had a further legal objection. In 1689 the toleration act was passed, and in 1778-9 a farther act was passed for the relief of Protestant Dis- senting ministers. The object of those acts was to give Protestant Dissenting ministers a legal status, and to relieve them of pains and penalties in consequence of their dissension. These acts had never been repealed. The Magistrates' Clerk: They don't affect these particular cases.

An order was made. The defendant caused some amusement by asking for time—viz., until after the South Birmingham election. David Lewis, a member of the To-in Council, was summoned for tle recovery of Bs. 6d. He said his legal objection was that it was an unconstitutional demand. He objected to pay for sectarian teaching. Orders were made in all the cases.

DRAUGHTS.
WARRINGTON v. ST. HELENS.

On Saturday a draughts match between picked teams representing Warrington and St. Helens was played at the St.illefens Y.M.C.A. Institute. The Warrington team was captained by the well-known international player, Mr. Frank Dunne, whilst St. tHelens had the services of Isaac Eden, their local champion,in a similar capacity. The nntch proved a very close affair, and though the Warrington top board players proved rather too heavily weighted for theirlopponents this was fully compensated by the strength of the home players lower down in the team. Just before " time " was called the score stood at 10 wins each, and one game pending. At that stage of the game the Warrington player held a winning position, but his next move was weak, and he went from bad to worse, finally losing a man end the game. ISt. Helens thus won the match by 11 wins to Warrington's 10, and three games were drawn. div.head: GOUT CURED COMPLETELY.
div.p: GOUT CURED COMPLETELY.

Miss M. L. Hammond, The Street, Compton, near Guildford, Surrey, has written a letter in which she declais positively that she has been completely cured of a ry serious case of Gout. " out three years ago I had an attack of blood poisonin which was followed by Rheumatic Gout. I was so bad that I was quite unable to walk, and the doctor said that I would always be subject to similar attacks. The following year I was seized with gout again and became worse than before: I had to keep my bed a whole month. During this time, the doctor attended me and when I did manage to getup and go about my work, I was compelled to use a stick to walk. I was seized with intense pain every time I attempted to move, and although I kept on taking medicine, I got no better, "After using Dodd's Kidney Pills a short time I found the pain was completely gone, and I am now quite cured. I can walk six miles without feeling the least pain, and considering how bad I was, it is wonder- ful and shows what Dodd's Kidney Pills will really de.'

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
The Photographic Society.

Mr. Birri!-11 presided at a-general meeting of the Warrington Photographic Society held at the Old Academy on Tuesday. A large number of interesting views—comprising the prize slides in the " Amateur Photographer "competitions—were thrown on the screen, the lantern being manipulated by Mr. H. War- burton. The treasurer of the society, Mr. J. H. Kirt- land, having resigned,it was necessary to elect another to act in his stead, Mr. Moores having been discharg- ing the duties pro tem. The meeting unanimously appointed Mr. F. G-arside to fill the vacancy.
FOR CLASS AND CIIrNA. of every description try J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Musical Society Dance.

A successful and enjoyable function was the annual dance in aid of the funds of the Musical Society which was held in the Parr Hall on Tuesday evening. The attendaxce numbered over 150 and included Mr. J Charlton Parr (president of the society),Mrs. Parr, Mr. and Mrs. R. T. Fairclough, and the Misses Fairclough, Mr. and Mrs. H. P. Mortimer, Mr. F.Crossley,and Mr and Mrs.. W. E. Atkin. Dancing commenced ht 8 p.m. and was continued with zest until one o'clock the following morning, Mr. R. H. Pearson's band supplying a capital selection of music. There were 20 items in the programme. Messrs. W. E. Atkin (hon. secretary of the society), F. H. Crossley, Mr. Gough, Mr. Bibby and Mr. Fieldhouse discharged the duties of M.C.'s.

The distribution of prizes in connection with the Christmas Billiard Handicap took place at the above club. In the absence of Mr. A. H. Crosfield, the Rev. Father Ryan presented the prizes to the . successful members, as follows :-1, parlour clock, P. Whelan; 2, handsome timepiece, E. Crank: 3, cue and case, Corless ; 4, prize, value 10s. 6d., P. Hope; break prize, pipe and case, J. Gibbons; consolation prize, bottle of whiskey, C. Mounfield. Prerious to the distribution a concert took place, before a good number .of members and friends. Songs were rendered by the following artistes, who acquitted them- selves in very good style :—The Misses A. Fair- dough, S. Eastens, and L. Fairhurst ; and Messrs. J. Gibbons, P. J. George, R.
