LADIES BEST GLACE BOOTS and SHOES, UNDER. the CLOCK. BELTD GE-STREET.—.444.7t- The New Vicar of Christ Church.

The Rev. G. C. Briggs, the newly-appointed vicar of Christ Church, Latchford, was on Monday evening the recipient of an illuminated address, a chiming clock, and a purse 'of gold from the parishioners of Si: Barnabas', Chester,among whom he worked for nearly seven years. Several eulogistic speeches were de- livered, the Rev. Canon Cooper Scott (vicar of the parent church of St. John the Baptist) presiding. In reply the Rev. G. C. Briggs said they were trying to make him as happy as they could at Latchford,and to forget them at St. Barnabas', but they would not do that. Ho hoped often to be in Chester and to see them all. (Applause.) He could not possibly express what he felt. He thanked them most heartily and sincerely for those very liberal presents, but he did not think for a moment that he deserved them. (Applause.)
H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF TONICS.-63. SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. St. Ann's Choir Social.

A successful and enjoyable social promoted by St. Ann's Church Choir was held in the schoolroom, Dannett-street, on Monday evening. A. very interest- ing programme was submitted and all the items were well received. The choir rendered several choruses and part songs and quartette parties, consisting of Messrs. P. Hardman, C. Savage and T. Gorton and Miss Hardman;and Messrs.H. Lowej Lowe,J. Johnson and J.Hewitt respectively were heard to advantage. Mr. H. A. Roberts contributed a piano solo,and songs were given by Miss Wilson, Mrs. Hannan, Mr. Gray and Mr. Thomas. There were also instrumental selections by Messrs. Bates, Clarke and Scott, a duet by Mr. and Mrs. Hannan, and humorous songs by Mr. Roberts. The duties of accompanists were discharged by Messrs. 11, A Roberts and E. A. Podmore.

BASSINETTES AND MAIL CARTS in latest art shades.—J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. The Field Club. At a special meeting of the Field Club held in the Museum Lecture Room, Mr. May, F.E.1.5., presided over a fair attendance. Mr. H. Stone, F.L.S., of Bir- mingham, lectured on " The movement of air and water in plants." He first. stated the prevalent theories of capillarity osmosis, and 'absorption, cited certain tests of the lifting power of each, and then showed that the theories, at least as generally held, are inadequate. He showed that in all trees, except the conifers, there are, in effect, minute continuous vessels from root to summit, that through these, drops of water separated by long bubbles of air, pass, and that the power necessary to raise water from the ground to the summit of the loftiest gain tree —soolt. is, if the air bubbles are fifteen times as large as the water drops, less than one atniosphere. He did not think there was evidence to justify assertion that this power arose from evaporation or root pressure. Either would suffice, but both might be contributory to the result. A. number of novel and interesting experiments illustrated the lecture. A long and vigorous discussion foUowed, and, on the motion of Mr. Deane, secmded by Mr. W. Mounfield, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer.

Warrington teams acluittel themselves with great credit at the annual competition in connection with the Cheshire Lines Ambulance Associat:on held at the Central Station, Liverpool. Eight teams competed, namely, Liverpool Central, Huskisson, Brunswick, Birkenhead, Warrington Central, Warrington Engineers Department, Warrington Stores' Department, and Manchester Central. The local teams were' composed as follows :—Central : Messrs. H. T. Williams, H. Holloway, J. Fogg, J. Robinson, and J. Blake. Engineers : Messrs. T. Downie, T. Tomlinson, J. Lee. 'D. Brownbell, and W. Clements. Stores : Messrs. E, Hughes, H. Welfare,W. Higham,W. Curtis,G. Crozier. —Surgeon G-. H. Darwin, of West Didsbury, who officiated as judge, awarded the first prize to War- rington Central, second to, Warrington Engineers' Department, and the third to the Huskisson team. The highest number of points possible was 390, and Warrington Central gained 258, Engineers' Depart- ment 232, and Huskisson 207.—This is the third con- secutive year in which Warrington Central have gained the first prize, and they are, therefore, winners of a fine silver challenge cdp. They have also the distinction of representing the Cheshire Lines at the railway ambulance competition to be held next May in London.
FIRE GRATES of every description.—J. S. GAR- LAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street,Warringion.—Advt.

Fancy Fair at Fairfield Schools. On Saturday afternoon and evening a fancy fair arranged by Mrs. R. Lowe and friends was held in Fairfield schools with the object of raising funds to assist in the building of a church in a poor district in Perth, Western Australia where the Rev. Gilbert Harding,a member of a well-known Warrington family, who was ordained to the diaconate by the Bishop of Liverpool, is engaged in ministerial work--IThe open- ing ceremony was performed by Mrs. J. D. Buckton, the Rector (Rev. Canon Willis) presiding. The following were the stallholders :—Pancy Stall: Misses J. Harding, Wilcox, F. Lowe, M. Clarke, L. Bottomley, G. Hudson, and D. Harding. Plain Stall: Miss Turner, Mrs. Bottomley, and Miss Boyle. Toy Stall : Misses Brimelow, M. Lowe, M. Brimelow, D. Hill, and E. Grounds. Refreshment Stall: Mrs. R. Lowe, Misses Harding, Wood, J. Price, M. Price, and E. Bunch. Toffee Stall : Misses Wood, M. Collins, D. Parsonage, .D. Collin. V. Collin, A. Taylor. Lucky Bag: Misses A. Collin and A. Parkinson, and Master W. Lowe.—The ilisses, F. Clarke and M. Harding had charge of a fish pond, and Miss Taylor gave exhibitions of palmistry, Several entertainments were given, the following com- mittee having made excellent arrangements : Rev G. W. Dickinson, Messrs. W. H. Payton (Mus. Bac.), Poole, Parkinson, Wood, Craik, and the Misses Hud- son, Harrison, Duckworth, and Wilkinson.—A. popular feature was a sketch entitled "Rival Lovers," the parts being very creditably taken by Messrs. Louis Wood and John Craik .(members of the Fairfield Entertaining Society). . The prcceeds of the fair amounted to nearly £33.

div.head: WARRINGTON IT THE ASSIZES.
div.p: WARRINGTON IT THE ASSIZES.
COUNCILLOR COUGH FOUND GUILTY OF BRIBERY.
By Our Own Reporter.

There were many familiar Warrington faces in the Crown Court at Liverpol Assizes on Tuesday, when Mr. Justice Bigham and a jury investigated four separate charges of bribery preferred against Coun- cillor Gough. The publication of the local police court proceedings in December last had enabled the Warrington public to. become acquainted with the facts of the case, and there was much speculatien as to the result of the trial. On Monday it became known that the grand jury had returned a true bill against Mr. Gough and the trial had been fixed for the following day. Consequently it was not surprising to find a good number of Warrington people journeying to Liverpool on Tuesday in company with the interested parties in the case. Amongst these were: Alderman and Mrs. Smethurst, Alderman Bennett, Councillors Brough, Forshaw, Pemberton and Lord, Mr. Gordon Roberts, Mr. Ebenezer England, Mr. R. Lewis, Mr.E. Cunnington. The arrival of the judges was heralded by the trumpeters who played "God Bless the Prince of Wales." Mr. Justice Bigharn, resplendent in his scarlet and ermine robe, immediately took his seat in the Crown Court. It was before His Lprdship that the ill-fated Whitaker Wright appeared in London on his memorable trial only a . month ago, and another reminder of that fact was the presence in the adjoin- ing Nisi Prins Court 'of Mr. Rufus Isaacs, K.C., who it will be remembered, conducted the prosecution of Whitaker Wright with marked ability. On the name of Samuel Gough being called, the well- known figure of Mr. Gough WAS seen straggling through the crowded court and making his way to the dock. On entering the grated enclosure he was imthediately relieved of his umbrella and hat by the warder, and accommodated with a seat. He was smartly dressed in a stylish grey overcoat and did not seem at all dejected by the surroundings in which he found himself placed. A bewigged gentleman then rose, and assuming a most serious air, read over the charge, which was a formidable document, couched in legal phrase- ology, the purport of which was that the defendant was indicted on four charges of bribing voters with the object of inducinc, them to vote for him. In answer to the charge, Mr.b Councillor Gough pleaded in a firm voice "not guilty." The Counsel then set to work. For the prosecution there appeared Mr. Sanderson, K.C., and Mr. Rigby Swift (instructed by Messrs. Brown and Co.),and on behalf of Mr. Gough there had been briefed Mr. Tobin, K.C., and Mr. John Guy Rutledge. These two last named counsel were in- structed by Messrs. Davies and Forshaw. of Suez-street. THE CASE FOR TILE PROSECUTION.

- - In opening the case, Mr. Sanderson briefly recited the facts which were disclosed at the Borough Police Court. Last November, he said, there was a vacancy in a particular ward called the Bewsey Ward, and the prisoner and a man named Owen Toole were the candi- dates. There existed at that time considerable feeling in Warrington, although he did not think it was material so far as this case was concerned, in favour of municipal trading and also against it. Mr. Gough as a matter of fact, was against it. But that was a mere matter of de- tail, and Vid not affect the case. There were four specific charges against Mr. Gough. In °mile was charged with giving 6d. to a man named Rogers two days previous to the election, and in the second case he was charged with offering 6d. to a woman named Ward. These two appeared to be doubtful voters; and it, was not certain which wa'jr they would vote. Two days before the election Mr. Gough went to solicit these people to vote for him. He went to Rogers, who opened the door of his house himself. He was a man iq a humble pasition in life, and he stood at the door talk- ing to Gough. They had a conversation and Rogers when asked for his vete said no would not give it. They shook hands, after which Rogers found sixpeace in one of his hands. He had apparently no time to consider whether he should take it or not but he did take it. Mr. Gough visited the woman Ward on the 213th Novem- ber at her house,and offered her 6d.She said she was not going to sell her vote for 6d., but that she was going to vote for Tocle. Then on the day of the election a man named Foxhall was taken to IVlr.Gough's committee room early in the morning, and after some conversation Mr. Gough asked him to vote for him and he put his hand in his pocket and handed him 6d. without any hesitation whatever. There were other people in the room at the time, but Foxhall would tell them that he thought "they were looking the other way." The other case was that of a woman named Kirkham, who was apparently an illiterate voter, and she was taken to the polling booth by Mr. Gough, who actually went to the presiding officer and told him that she was an illiterate voter. After this woman had given her vote under the' direction of the presiding officer, Mr. Gough gave her two three-penny pieces outside the place where she had voted. It appeared that the man Foxhall had since stated that he did not in fact receive the money from Mr. Gough. The man was met by a man named Baker as he was returning from his work, and finally he arrived in Cairo-street at aboat nine o'clock, when he was not in a suitable con- dition to make an admission. Therefore he (Counsel) did not attach mach importance to the statement. With regard to Mrs. Kirkham, shortly after she had received the two three-penny bitd an inquiry was instituted and apparently one of the prisoner's supporters sail to her: "Now be careful what you say ; it is a very important matter," and when she was accosted by a policeman, and asked whether she received the money she denied that she had in fact received the money. Later on she made a declaration that she had received two three-penny bits from Mr. Gough. It might appear to be Atra- ordinary that anyp3rson should be influenced by a small- coin as to the way in which he or she should vote, but the jury must remember that to these people 6d. was an important matter, and it would pay for a certain amount of liquor. He would be able to prove about foue specific charges, and he thought the jury would come to the conclusion in the circumstances that there had been a considerable amount of bribery going on. If the jury icarne to the conclusion that the four wit- nesses he should call were telling the trutk, that they had the money or had had it offered to them, he did not know what the tuaswer could be. He understood the defence would be that no money was passed at all, and that none was offered. WITNESSES FOR THE PROSECUTION. POINTS PROM THE EVIDENCE, Evidence was then called.

Mr. Stanley Wilson, deputy town clerk, produced three nominition papers lodged on behalf of Mr.GDugh. He also produced the burgess roll, showing that the four persons alleged to hive been bribed were electors in Bewsey Ward. Mr. Tobin,in cross-examination, elicited the fact that the information in the case was laid by Mr. E. A. Sanders.
Did you know that Sanders was secretary of Mr. Owen Toole's committee? Witness : No. I did not know that. His Lordship: This is immaterial. The only ques- tion is,did this man bribe or did he not.
Mr. Tobin: I perfe3tly agree that tkat is the only question we have to consider, but we have to seer whether some of the witnesses are speaking the truth or not.
WILLIAM ROGERS FINDS SIXPENCE IN HIS HAND.

William Rogers, an ironworker, living at 8, Refuge Square was then called, and spoke to Mr. Gough visit- ing his house before the election. Mr. Gough asked witness to vote for him. He said he had come to solicit his vote, and witness replied " You will not get it." (Laughter.) To that Mr. Gough replied: "We shall be none the worse friends." The prisoner then shook hands with him, andsaid ; "We shall meet again," and he left 6d. in his hand. Witness was standing at the door when this happened: Peers said to him, " You may shake bands with me with the same hand as you shookhands with Mr. Gough, and he (witness) replied " No,I will give you this (theleft)hand." Witness then offered him the left hand, because he had a sixpence in the right hand. Peers must have known that. His Lordship : .Was the 6d. a good one ?—T spent it, so it must have been a good 'tin. (Laughter.) Mr. Tobin: The Sixpence was in your hand at the time, and you say Peers must have known it. Witness: He must have known it, or why did he ask me to shake hands?
Did you say anything aborit it to the magistrates at the Police Court ?—I did not.

Did yot& forget it ?—I remember it now. For the first time ?—Not exactly for the first time. You were keen that Toole should win the election? —so, I was not. I had no more favour for one than another. At any rate you let Gough know that you were going to vote for Toole?—Decidedly so, because I had promised him my vote. And you told him several times that you had promised to vote for Toole?—Only on that one occasion. I had promised to vote for Toole, and really to goodness I could not vote for both of them. (Laughter.)

• Did you by your voice and manner indicate to Gough that nothing would induce you to vote for him ?—I did. And in spite of that you say that Gough pressed 6d. into your hand ?—Yes, while he shook hands with me. Did you expect the 61 to be pressed into your hand? —I did not. _ _

You might have known it was a bribe ?—I didn't 'know. Is that what you swear did not know what he gave it me for. His Lordship : You have no right to ask this man what the money was for. That is forthejury to decide.
MART WARD REFUSSS SIXPENCE.

Mary VVard, who described herself as a field worker, looked a pypical Irishwoman as she stood in the witness box. It was with difficulty she could keep her bonnet on her head and the manner in which she fondled her shawl seemed to indicatea disposition on her part to put it on her head. There was a broad Irish brogue when she spoke And she addressed his Lordship as "his Highness." On one occasion she shocked the whole court by making use of a course expression. Mr. Gough shesaid, asked her to vote for hiai and she said she would not. She said she was going to vote for Mr. Toole. Mr. Gough put 6d. in her hand. 5123 replied: "B—off with your sixpence I am not going to have it." Gough then picked up the money: Mr. Tobin: You don't dislike a drop of drink? Witness : Well, it is very little I can get. But if you could get 6d ?—I did not take the 6d. You are fond of a little drink ?—When I can pay for it.
And when you have money you buy it ?—I cannot buy much, your honour. I have a wench to keep, and I nave to work in the fields from Monday morning to Saturday night.
You lad irone.ised your vote for Toole ?—Yes, sir. And you told Gouglt so ?—Yes, sir. I told him right enough.
Was sOmeone in the house with you at the time ? Yes, a woman lodger named Julia Scanlon. Where is she ?—f don't know. She went away the next week.
Why did you refuse the money ?—Because I did not want it.
FOXHALL AND HIS EXPERIENCE IN THE COMAITrEE ROOM.

Henry T'oxhall an ironworker living at 6, Refuge- square, told a peculiar story of his experience. On the morning of the election, he said, he went to Mr. Gough's committee room "with a gentleman named Baker." Mr. Gough was outside when witness first went into the room, Mr. Gough came in and put his hand in his pocket and draw a 6d. out, struck it down by the ride of rue and knocked his hand against mine, straight down against the table." Witness was stand- ing by the table ; so was the prisoner. By His Lordship : You took the sixpence. By Mr. Sanderson: Before he went out Gough told him to mind who he voted for, and witness replied that he would make it all right. By Mr. Tobin: There were five or six people in the room at the time. They did not want to see what was gi vent° him;one lookedat a picture and another had his head down on his books. •

Mr. Tobin: Did you say one afternoon, or evening, in Cairo-streek, in the presence of Gough, "I never.got 6d. It is quite untrue."—Witness: Yes. I understand you now to assert that that was a lie,and that you said what you did for drink?--Yes, sir. Did you tell a lie in order to get more drink from either Gough or Baker?—Baker told me to tell the lie. Did you tall it to get more drink out of Baker?—Yes. Are you willing to tell lies to people for the sake of getti.ig drink?—Wall, I would not every week. (Laughter).

TILE PRESIDING OFFICER'S EVIDENCE. Mr. A. J. Willett, solicitor, said he acted as presid- ing officer at the election on November 30th. He re- membered two women coming into the lvoh about llo'clo3k. One was Mrs. Kirkham. A woman came in with her. Mr.Gotigh came to the entrance of the poll_ ing station and said: " Mr. Presiding OFficer,theqe two women are illiterates." During the time Mrs. Kirkham was voting the prisoner was standing at the entiance to the polling station. Helwould be about two yards from witness. When the voter left the room the prisoner also left.

div.head: 'JANE KIRKFUIf, AN ILLUERATE
div.p: 'JANE KIRKFUIf, AN ILLUERATE

Jane Kirkham, a widow, of 92,C ttherine-s4t met created much amusement by her conduct in the witness box. She made several attempts to get out, but she was promptly called back. and the counsel and his lordship sorely taxed her pttience by asking some awkward questions. She exclaimed that "she would never come here again as long as she lived." At length his lordship observed, "I think we have had enough of Mrs. Kirk- ham," and she wts th3n allowed to leave the box. In her evidence she said she went into the school- room to vote; she could not write, and she made a cross on the surnmolis. (Laughter.) She meant on the voting paper. When w:tness came out the prisoner gave her two threepenny pieces, but the prisoner did not buy her vote.

By His Lordship: It was against the Imperial where Mr. Gpugh gave her the money. Witness (to his Lordship): Have you done with me now? (Laughter.) Mr. Tobin: I want a word or two with you. (More laughter.) In answer to counsel she stated that when she left, home she had two threepenny 13s in her hand, but she" spent um." (Laughter.) She spent the money in drink as she usually did. (Laughter.) Mr. Gough did not make any secret about givins, the money. He did not- take her round the corner and slip it into her hand. She and Mrs. Kenwright afterwards went to the Imperial Hotel and spent the money. Mr. Tobin: He didn't buy the vote ?—Yes, you may well laugh. Mr. Tobin: You went and spent it in drink as you generally do ?—Yes. Mr. Tobin: Anything for a drink ?—Yes. Mr. Tobin : When the policeman saw you outside the Imperial, didn't von tell him that you had not got any money ?—Yes. t had spent it. I called for three beers. The policeman walked in after; us and said "I see you Ere all right." (Laughter.) Mr. Tobin: Then you must have told a lie .when you said you had not got any money. Will you explain why you told a lie? Witness : What lie have I told?
His Lordship: Your version is that you got the money after you had voted, and that you had not 1.333 n bribed?
Witness : Yes, sir. THE DEFENDANT'S CASE. :NIR. GOUGH IN THE WITNESS BOX.

This concluded the case for the prosecution, and Mr. Tobin at once called the defendant. Mr. Gough, in his evidence, said he was a house i furnisher and had been n business for 25 years. During the whole of that time he had never been charged with an indictable offence. He remembered going to Rogers's house on Saturday, November 28th, at from 6 to 6.30. William Peers and William Woodcock went with him. They were both present that day. He went to solicit Rogers's vote. He used several arguments why Rogers should vote for him, instancing what he had done in public life. He tried to induce Rogers to vote for him but he would not be convinced. He did not show the slightest sign of wavering in witness's favour. There was not a word of truth in the story that he gave Rogers 6d. He could see no advantage in doing so. The charge was absolutely untrue. He remembered calling at Mrs. Ward's house on the same round. He tried to convince her by argument to vote for him, but she would not be convinced, and gshe showed no sign of wavering. He did not. present her with 6d.; there was nota word of truth the charge. He could see no advantage he could possibly derive from doing so. He did not know Foxhall before the election. There was a certain number of clerks in the committee room. These was not a word of truth in the statement thathe took 6d, out of his pocket and slipped it into Foxhall's hand by his side. He should never think of doing that in the presence of anyone. Mr. Tobin : Have you given a single penny to any- one for a vote in connection with the election? Witness: No.

_ continuing, he said he did not hand Kirkham two threopennyfbits outside the polling station. The police officer was there as well as Mr. Toole, Mr. Pemberton and others. ft was a moral impossibility to have given reoney away without it 'being seen. The policeman asked Kirkham whether she had received any money and she said no, and said it emphatically too. She was Indignant about the matter. "POOR MEN EASY TO BUY."

Mr. Sanderson: Do you swear on your oath that you did not give any money to Rogers ?—I did not give any money to him or any other voter in the ward. I would not think of doing it in the presence of any- body.
-Why ?--Because I know it would bea greater offence to do it in the presence of anyone._
His Lordship- asked witness ilk. he knew anything against Rogers. Witness: I know he is a man given to drink, awl one who does not always pay his debts. He has owed orne money for years.
His Lordship: How many years is it since you last asked him for it.
Witness: I cannot say. He went away from the By Mr. Sanderson: Didn't you say at the Police Court "I know nothingagainst Rogers." Witness : I don't remember.

Can you give any reason why Rogers should go and make this false statement against you ?—Men who are given to drink are easily led away. You know that from experience ?—Not by experience. It is the habit that leads them to do it. poor men given to drink are easy to buy ?—Yes. Do you know Mrs. Ward ?—I know she is a woman who might be easily bought. His Lordship: How do you know that? Because she is addicted to drink. -Questioned as to Foxhall, the witness said he was prepared to swear that he did not see Foxhall in the committee-room. Counsel closely cross-examined witness with reference to the Kirkham incident. Witness said he had no knowledge that he spoke to her on that day. His Lordship: Didn't you hear Mrs. Freer say to Mrs. Kirkham outside the Imperial Hotel, "Now don't tell lies; you have had two threepenny bits."—Witness: I never heard it. His Lordship: Didn't you hear her evidence in the Police Court ?—Witnes4: No. CORROBORATIVE EVIDENCE.

William Woodcock and William Peers, both of whom accompanied Mr. Gough whilst he was canvassing in Refuge-square, gave evidence bearing out Mr. Gough's statement. Ernest Allen, and Georg 3 Howl, a striker, also gave evidence on behalf of the defendant. The last named was the only witness who did not give evidence at the Police Court. He was assisting, he said, in Mr. Gough's

committee room. Mr. Gough did not go into the com- mittee room while Foxhall was there. He never saw the prisoner hand any money to anyone. His Lordship: A thousand people could say that; you might call me. Witness (continu:ng) said he saw Foxhall and Baker in Cairo-street. Foxhall was never asked to sign a paper. Mr. Gough said to Foxhall "Did I give you anything for voting for me?" and he replied" You did not, and I shall never say so, but I had been made drunk and got to sign it as such but isitall sign nothing no more." (Laughter.)

div.head: CLOSING SPEECHES. MR. TOBIN AND MEE DRINKS.
div.p: THE CLOSING SPEECHES. MR. TOBIN AND MEE DRINKS.

Mr. Tobin made a powerful address to the jury. No maa knew better than the prisoner, he said, that the offence with which he was charged was a 'serious one because it rendered a man liable to imprisonment for a certain length of time and involved him in the loss of civil rights for seven years and also the loss of public office. Mr. Gough had been 20 years in business in War- rington and he was elected by a majority the repre- sentative of the Bewsey ward, and that fact showed that he was respected by the majority of the people who lived in the ward; yet he was charged with committing an offence which he knew to be grave and criminal, but to bribe openly and in the presence of persons, was it likely on the face of it? Were the witnesses for the prosecution people upon whom they could rely in a criminal case or not? Were they tainted witnesses or not? Three out of the four, all of them except Mrs. Ward, admitted that they took money either in respect of a vote to be given or a vote already given. In a sense they were tainted witnesses, and therefore not to be relied upon unless corroborated. Drink would do a good many things, and free drinks would persuade a man sometimes to say things about another the gravity of which was not appreciated at the time. The jury had been told that some of the w;tnesses took the money without a protest, and therefore they did notappreciate the gravity of the charge they were making against a man who had been for so many years in the service of the town. Might not all this have been done for drink or for political spite, or for a thousand and one reasons that actuated the minds of people? Having once made a statement, people were pinned to itaand they were obliged to repeat it in open court. In Zilch of the four cases was there one tittle of corrobation ? Each witness spoke to his own facts and no one was brought to corroborate them. But how was that met by the prisoner? Peers and Woodcock corroborated him, and three or four persons were called for the de- fence, all of whom denied that any money was passed. Were they not to attach weight to the evidence of the prisoner himself? He had stood in the dock, but he hoped the minds of the jury would not be prejudiced against him in consequence, for every man was pre- sumed to be innocent until he had been found guilty. He was entitled to as much credit as any of the wit- nesses. He had told his story like a man. It was alleged that he had put sixpences into the hands of people, although he knew they were not going to vote for him. He could understand that being done in the case of wavering voters, but not in a case like that he had mentioned, and he, therefore, asked the jury to disbelieve the evidence for the prosecution, which he contended was absolutely unsafe. MR. SANDERSON'S REPLY.

Mr. Sanderson replied to the criticisms of Mr. Tobin. There was practically only one question for considera- tion, he said, and that was whether Mr. Gough did or did not give the !money mentioned to the four witnesses for the prosecution, or to one of them, for one was sufficient in the case of a prosecution. If money was given or offered it could be only for one object, namely to induce people to vote. He (counsel) recognised that this was a serious case all through as it rendered the prisoner liable to a fine or imprisonment, and it was for that reason he objected to Mr. Tobin's remarks about the demeanour of the witnesses. They had dealt with material facts and he contended that they had given their evidence in a perfectly straightforward manner, and that it was to be relied upon. There was corrobora- tion, and that of a most remarkable kind, as four persons has been found to give evidence. It certainly spoke for itself. If there had been only one case one might have said "We cannot rely upon it, and we must accept Mr. dough's denial," but when they got four in lependent witnesses having no connection with each other, all of whom had come forward to say that they had reeeived or had been offered money, there was no reason in the world why they should not be believed. He did not wish to press the case unduly but he did not think the comments of Mr. Tobin were justified by the facts.

div.head: STRONG REMARKS BY THE JUDGE.
div.p: STRONG REMARKS BY THE JUDGE.

His Lordship, in summing up, said that he quite agreed with- counsel that the case was one of import- ance, it was of grave importance. The legislature had thought proper to entrust the conduct of local affairs to people whom they had seen before them, and it must have occurred to the jury that such people could be very easily tampered with. It was therefore of grave import- ance that when anyone was found tampering with these people justice ought to be brought home to him. These elections to sit on local bodies were of considerable local importance. The candidates elected had the management of local affairs ; they were the people to whom this) management was entrusted and they had the control of the public money. It was essential therefore,that the representatives of the people should be honestand also that they should be fairly and properly elected. Therefore he agreed that the case was of considerable importance. The defendant was charged under statute with the offence of bribery, and the section of the Act under which proceedings had been taken, stated that if found guilty a person could be sent to prison for a term not exceeding a year, or fined in a sum not exceeding .£2OO. The punishment inflicted might be a fine or it might also be imprison- ment. That was, however, a matter for the judge to decide, and the jury were not to acquit the prisoner because they might contemplate he would be sent to prison. The question of his guilt was essentially one for the jury—twelve Imen of commonsense—who bad heard the evidence which had been given, and he suggested to them that if they believed the evideace of any one of the witnesses, eertainly any one of the three ; witnesses (he was leaving out Mrs. Kirkham) there was ample evidence on which to find the prisoner guilty. In commenting upon the evidence of these witnesses, his Lordship said Rogers appeared to be a respectable man, and why should he come there to tell a lie? Was it conceivable that some people had entered into a 'wicked plot to induce him to commit perjury ? If they did so they would make themselves liable to a far more serious charge than that which was brought against Gough. It was urged that the people who were with Gough at the time never saw him hand any money to Rogers. But these things were not intended to be seen ; they were intended to be secret. The question really was this. Did they be- lieve Rogers was there to perjure himself? If he had not come to perjure himself, an offence had been brought home to the defendant. Then with regard to Mrs. Ward. It was said she had invented a lie to thus per- jure herself on this occasion. Did the jury think so? If they believed she had spoken the truth it appeared to him that the charge was brought home to the defendant. Then it was said there was another woman in the house at the time and that the prosecution would not call her. He would advise the jury to dismiss that from their minds. The wontan MS a lodger who left the week after the alleged offence and the jury must not be led away by the suggestion that if she had been called she 'would have told the jury something different from that given by Mrs. Ward. Proceeding to review the evidence of Foxhall, his Lord- ship said it had been brought out in evidence that a friend of Mr. Gough—a Mr. Baker, who for some reason had not been called—got at Foxhall and induced him to deny that he had received sixpence. On that point he would ask the jury to exercise their commonsense. It was only when they took Foxhall's evidence in conjunction with that of the other wit- nesses that they could weigh its value. With regard to Mrs. Kirkham, he believed she intended to say a good word for Mr. Gough. She declared that her vote hadinot'been'bought :and that;what Gough did was quite straight and open. Therefore to that extent she was a witness in his favour, but she did say this that immediately she had given her vote two three- penny pieces were slipped into her hand by him. If the jury believed that was so and that it was really a payment for the vote, the importance of her evidence was to be found in these circumstances, coupled with the evidence of the other people. There was a good deal of dispute as to what happened. Appar- ently there was some suspicion at the polling booth that money had been given to this woman, for there was some dispute afterwards as to what took place. When brought out of the Imperial Hotel by the police constable, she denied that sheihad received any bribe or any money,and it was said that Mrs.Kenwright then said to her "Don't tell lies; you know you have had two threepenny bits." Unless the jury were satisfied that the offence had been committed, Mr. Gough was not guilty. It was essentially a case in which the jury must exercisel their commonsense. They must ask them- selves the question, where does the truth lie ; where is it to be found?

div.head: VERDICT.
div.p: THE VERDICT.

After an absence it:o--m the Court for about half an hour, the jury found prisoner guilty. His Lordship said he had no doubt himself that the verdict was a right one. The means that prisoner took to corrupt the voters were contemptible and small, and although he regarded his offence as a serious one, he thought he would sufficiently vindicate the law by im- posing upon him a small fine. The prisoner would be fined £s,whigh he (the judge) thought: would be a suffi- cient warning to all persons in prisoner's position to refrain fromtrying to induce these poor people to do that which they ought not to do—to sell their votes.
THE ORIGIN OF THE PROSECUTION. QUESTION OF' COSTS.

The Judge askdd if the prosecution had been pro- moted by one of the two political parties. Mr. .Sanderson said no except in so far,as that it had been promoted by Mr:Sanders, as secretary to Mr. Toole, who was the opposition candidate. It was felt that in this case there had been a considerable ameunt of bribery, and if these four cases could be proved Mr. Toole and Mr. Sanders decided that the prosecution should be taken.
His Lordship-a- sked about the costs. He thought they might have proceeded on petition to unseat Mr. Gough. Mr. Sanderson, said they might have done that but it would have been more costly.
The' Judge said that if they had done that, and succeeded, they would likely have had to pay their own costs.

Mr. Sanderson' said no doubt they would have to pay some of them. Be had either to proceed that way or upon indictment; and having regard to the latter fact, he asked that the law should be allowed to take its own course. It was very impertant that these cases should be dealt with when discovered.
His Lordship agreed, and said that he would not interfere.

div.head: VIOLENT POLICE ASSAULTS. Dastardly Attack in Museum Street. ATTEMPTED RESCUE OF A PRISONERMAXIMUM SENTENCE.
div.p: VIOLENT POLICE ASSAULTS. Dastardly Attack in Museum Street. ATTEMPTED RESCUE OF A PRISONER- MAXIMUM SENTENCE.

Assaults on police officers are, unfortunately, no in- frequent occurrences at Warrington and several cases, including one of unusual seriousness, have been dealt with by the magistrates this week. On Monday, before the Mayor and other justices, ;John Baxter, 40, New road, and Charles Turner, 64, Ellesmere street, were charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Arpley road at 9.30 on Saturday night. Baxter twas further charged with assaulting P. S. Barnett in Wilson Patten street.

The sergeant stated that the prisoners and eight or nine other men, nearly all of whom were drunk, were using bad language. He requested them to desist, but Baxter would not and he was taken into custody. A number of the men followed them along Wilson Patten street and Turner caught hold bf witness from behind, evidently to try and release the prisoner. Baxter com- menced to kick and fight, and a struggle ensued on the ground. Baxter kicked witness several times on the chest and he also received several blows from behind. Sergeant Williamson ultimately came upon the scene and the crowd dispersed Turner persisted in molesting witness:all the way to the Police Station. The dis- turbance, he believed, originated in a foot race that was taking place in Arpley road. In the struggle, witness's whistle was damaged. The Chief Constable said this sort of conduct was becoming very prevalent on Saturday nights,and he could not help thinking that the recent boxing shows in the town had a great deal to do with it. Men got to com- paring their prowess in boxing, racing and other sports at street corners or in public houses'.; they adjourned .near Arpley cannons to settle disputes; and when the police interfered they were immediately set upon. Baxter was fined 10s. and costs and Turner had to pay ss. and costs.

THE 'CHIEF CONSTABLE AND BOXING SHOWS. Michael Jennings, 2, Ship Yard, was charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting in the Market Place at 11.5 on Saturday night and also with assaulting P.C. Johnson. The Chief Constable said prisoner was one of the so- called pugilists who had been brought into the town by the boxing shows at the circus. The music licence had been taken away from the building because the magistrates thought it was not a suitable place, and he (the Chief Constable) had now reported it to the Borough Surveyor as a building unfit to hold public entertainments in. What the Borough Surveyor was going to do he did not know but he might say, for the information of the public and the lessees,that the police had their eyo upon the building and there might be developments later on. Constable Johnson's evidence showed that the prisoner engaged in a fight near the Market in the presence of about two hundred people. When taken into custody he became violent and kicked the officer on the knee. The Chief Constable: This is the outcome of the boxing business. Boxing is a very fine sport, but when it makes half-fed gutter snipes aggressive, it begins to be a nuisance. A fine of 10s, and costs was imposed.

div.head: SERIOUS CASE
div.p: A SERIOUS CASE

CONSTABLE MUSKETT "FELLED LIKE AN 0..X.1 Patrick Dodd, 14, Ellesmere-street, was charged with assaulting P.C. Gibbs at Market Gate at 11.15 on Satur- day night. The Chief Constable said this was a rather more serious case. Gibbs, it appeared, was on duty at Market Gate and prisoner and several other men who had been turned out of public houses commenced to quarrel, obstruct the road, and make a great noise. He requested them to go away, and many of them did so. Prisoner who was incited by another man, remained, and on again being spoken to, made a "sort of running puncti " at the officer. He was taken into custody and became violent. P.C. Muskett came to Gibbs's assistance and a large crowd, many of whom were very hostile, followed them along Sankey-street, down Bold-street and into- Museum-street. When they reached the last named street which was dark, one of the crowd said to Gibbs "Nor loose him, or we will make you." Gibbs turned round to get hold of the man who had said that, leaving Muskett in charge of the prisoner. The moment Gibbs turned round, a voice was heard in the crowd saying to the prisoner "Are you ready Paddy?" Prisoner replied Yes" and immediately someone ran up to Muskett and struck him on the head with some weapon. The thud was heard for yards and the constable fell like an ox in the shambles. He was carried into Dr. Smith's surgery and remained unconscious for some time. Dodd was released from custody by the officer falling, and ran away, as did the officer's assailant. Although there must have been at least one dastardly coward in the crowd, there were some brave men who followed Dodd and helped the police to re-arrest him and take him to the Police Station. They would probably be able to bring before the Bench the man who so seriously injured Muskett. 'These assaults were becoming a daily occurr- ence, and he was afraid life would be lost if something were not done to stop them. Fortunately the officer's skull was not fractured.

The Chief Constable expressed cordial thanks to the following who assisted the police :—Walter Holford, 46, Walker-street; William Boardman, 14, Garabaldi- street ; Thomas Balmer,33, Factory-yard ; John Richard Mason, 40, Mill-lane; and George Ed. Brown, Brick- street. He added that if he were alone with a prisoner in any part of Warrington he would not be afraid. Al- though there were black sheep, it was generally found that the bra hearts predominated. Dodd was fined 20s. and costs, or in default a month's imprisonment.

div.head: ASSAILAti f ARRESTED. Sent to Gaol fop Six Months.
div.p: THE ASSAILAti f ARRESTED. Sent to Gaol fop Six Months.

There was a sequel to the above case on Tuesday when John Moore of Stoney-yard, appeared before Alderman Sutton and other magistrates on the charge of assaulting Constable Muskett in Museum-street at. 11.20 on Saturday night. ' The Chief Constable said the prisoner was originally charged with unlawfully wounding the officer, but in order that the case might be dealt with summarily, the charge had been reduced. Mr. Talbot proceeded to relate the facts as stated on Monday. Describing the attack on Muskett, he said Moore was seen to strike the officer a terrific blow on the side of the head with some instru- ment—it was not definitely known what it was—but the police presumed it was the large stone produced which was found on the spot. The officer dropped as though he had been shot. He was streaming with blood,and he was cairied unconscious into Dr. Smith's surgernsuffer- ing from concussion of the brain. Had the blow been a little nearer the temple it might probably have had fatal results. Immediately Muskett fell, the prisoner was seen to follow the man Dodd and they both ran off together. Some civilians—to whom he could hardly adequately express his gratitude—followed Dodd and held,him until the police came on the scene and arrested him. They also assisted in carrying P.C. Muskett and attending to him in every possible way. Evidence was then given by Constables Muskett and, Gibbsj; Walter Howard, Mason-street ; Richard Lathey Ellesmere-street ; Joseph Barton (late of the Army Medical Corps), Winwick-road ; Thomas Balmer, Factory-yard and John Monks, Wakefield-street. Lathey identified the prisoner as *being the man who struck the blow.—Joseph Barton stated that before the assault was committed prisoner had asked witness and his friends if they would help him to rescue Dodd, but they would not. Constable Muskett's head was swathed in bandages. He appeared very unwell and was accommodated with a chair in the box.

Dr. Smith said that when Muskett was brought to his surgery he was unconscious and suffering from slight concussion. He had a nasty, jagged wound at the back of the head which bled profusely and was so large that one could place two fingers in it. It would probably be a fortnight before he would be able to resume duty. Prisoner said he "never laid a hand "on the officer. The magistrates considered Moore was guilty of a brutal and cowardly assault and sent him to prison for the maximum term of six months.
The civilians who assisted the officers were cordially thanked and awarded 2s. 6d. each.

div.head: BY A TENANT FARMER
div.p: BY A TENANT FARMER
Ma. CHAMBERLAIN refuses to allow tenant farmers to be represented on the Tariff Com- mission.

Agriculture is still the nation s greatest industry, and its interests should be considered first in any scheme of Tariff reform; but now, as ever the claims of the tenant farmer are to he made subservient to the demands of wealthy manufacturers, in whose interests Mr. Chamberlain has propounded his policy.

div.head: FARMERS SHOULD CONSIDER.-
div.p: FARMERS SHOULD CONSIDER.-

1. That Mr. Chamberlain offers to the manufacturer Protection to the amount of ten per cent. on every article he produces, while to the farmer he offers five per cent. only, and that on but a few of his products. Bacon. is to he left out. Maize (competing with English beans, peas, oats, and barley) is to come in free; while Mr. Chamberlain has promised Messrs. Ind, Coope, and Co. that he will not tax foreign barley or any other article without consulting the heads of the industries affected. Colonial Competition. FAUMERS Must ALSO CONSIDER.—

`2 That Mr. Chamberlain's aim is to increase the supply of rtyricultural produce from abroad, and not to restrict it. .While his scheme will protect manufacturers from their most dangerous rivals in Germany, France, and America, it leares the farmer exposed to increasingly severe competi- tion from Canada, Australia, India. and Egypt. Such a scheme will not protect the farmer, but will make his last state worse than tho first. Mr. lan Malcolm, a Suffolk .(Stowmarket) Unionist M.P., writes that " Mr. Chamberlain's scheme offers no escape for British agriculturists from the prospect of seeing the home market flooded not only with corn from the United States, but also ( Ini(ler preferential treatment) from Canada and Australia in illimitable quantities."
Mr. Chamberlain has,snid. a That hi $ scheme Will not be of the ,li.t/htest use to the tenant .farmer.
Writing from Highbury, December lab, 1903, the right lion. gentleman says

There is no reason whatever to believe that the small taxot::on I prvosg will increa,se the price 41f either corn or maize. And again: The slight preference given to Colonial ~Ard . . . would not raise the price clt. feud, but woad tenet to keep prices to 110- consumer down. —Tariff Reform Leaflet No. i. Farmers v. Manufacturers. CRAMDEP.S of Agriculture have long been, engage,' in an attempt to defeat a ring of British manufacturers who have s.ought to impose unfair conditions-on the agrieulter al implement trade, to the injury of the British farmer.

These efforts have been only partially successful, because American machites have been, offered by firms outside the ring of British makers. If Mr. Chamberlain succeeds in his attempt to protect makers of agricultural machinery, a self-binder now costing £35 will cost SAO to -5:45. The difference will come out of the farmer's pocket ; all other machinery will bu proportionately dearer, the profits of great manufacturing firms will increase, and those of the .farmer Even snouict tins scheme be adopted, the town workman would very soon agitate for the removal of any tax that increased the cost of his food, and the farmer would find himself compelled to pay more for his machinery and to take less for his produce. Farmers' Just Demands.
THESE absurd and injurious proposals are intended to divert attention from those reforms which fariuers_may justly demand.

Railway Rates : Mr. Chaniberlain and his friends have been in power since -1895 without attempting to deal with the prrferen- tial rates given to foreign produee by our great railway companies. These rates are a direct tax kvied on the farmer for the benefit of the foreigner.
Here are some examples Eggs--

Russia to London Ireland to London 94s. Od. per ton. Apples— Folkestone to London Normandy .to Folkestone Dead Meat Liverpool to London— Foreign English. , 40s. Od. per ton. Our 'railways charge. French produce vitt Boulogne and Folkestone as follows : Butter, 95. ; eggs, 20s. ; onions, 88. Bd. ; potatoes, 4s. 6d. ; cabbages, 4s. ; meat, 14s. -per ton less than they charge Jim the same produce if En.;:lish .from Folkestone to London. The railway companies have thus with the assistance of Mr. Chamberlain secured a monopoly of the town market for foreign produce, end when an English farmer sends goods to _London he is heavily taxed for doing so. FARMERS WILL DEMAND THAT THIS MONOPOLY SHALL BE BROKEN DOWN AT ONCE. AND AT ALL COSTS.

Land Law Reform. THE enormous benefits conferred On the Irish farmer by this Government at the expense of the British taxpayer are not less remarkable than its neglect of the just claims of the British farmer, who has ever been a law-abiding and loyal citizen. The British faimer wants : Absolute freedom in regard to cultivation and sale of crops. Security of tenure or compensation for disturbance. Compensation for improvements, free from the harassing restrictions of existing Acts. Protection from adulteration of British and foreign butter, milk, and beei.hy unscrupulous producers and merchants. There are further questions relating to rating and land government which also call for attention. Farmers must remember that the present Government imposed on them an enormous ar O. increasing burden in the shape of an Education rate. If Mr. Chamberlain's policy is adopted all other reforms will be put aside in favour of a measure which its author defends on the Izround that it will not raise the price of farm produce, .but tend to keep prices down. WHAT FARMER IN HIS SENSES WOULD VOTE FOR SUCH A POLICY AS THIS? Remember. FINALLY, let farmers remember four things: 1. Mr. Chamberlain seeks to assist the Colonial farmer, vot to protect British agricul- ture. 2. Mr. Chamberlain proposes to give to manufacturers more than double the advantages which he would allow to the farmer. 3. Mr. Chamberlain refuses to allow the intends of tenant farmers to te represented on the Tariff Commission. 4. Protection is proposed in the interest of landlords and capitalists, and to blind farmers to the necessity of reform in railway rates, local taxation, and the land laws.

div.p: A VETERAN'S LONG WALK.

He hopes to completehis journey at John O'Groats in 27 days, nearly 1,000 miles in 24 walking days. "Dr." Deighton, like many other •athletes, finds Bovril so i useful as a sustainer n long distance walks that he in- variably trains upon it. It may be temembered that the" Doctor" completed his self-imposed task last summer of walking from London to Newcastle-on- Tyne in six clays,a distance of 300 miles.

div.head: market.
div.p: The market.

Sir,—ln walking through the market one cannot 'help being struck with the :large amount of draper, old clothes, boots and shoes, man almost everyother article which are imported into it, and the large amount of money which is taken away by these strangers must be enormous. lam told there is one man.—l think 'from 31anchester—who takes away somewhere about eighty or ninety pounds in one day; therefore, what must be the whole amount that is taken away by all who come? Shopkeepers everywhere are grumbling about slackness of trade and cannot pay their way, and yet these people ate encouraged to come and are made comfortable at the ratepayers' expense. The Markets Committee boast that the Market is paying well. Personally. I would rather it did not pay so well, because then I should know that the shopkeepers were getting the money. I can hear of one or two persons holding as many as eleven or more stalls. If so, what arrangements are made with regard to payment? Should not each stall be let by auction as in other towns? It appears to me that the town is not getting the full alue for them But I repeat again that these people should not be encouraged to come, and enter into competition with our heavily- rated shopkeepers. I have often wondered why the latter have not memorialized the Town Council and made a dead set against it. There are members of the Markets Committee strongly- opposed to these people coming from other towns. I wovdd like to have the opinion of the shopkeepers on the question. Your,&c. RATEPAYER.

div.head: Mr. Councillor Gough.'s Conviction.
div.p: Mr. Councillor Gough.'s Conviction.

Sir,—Although Mr. Gough has solemnly assured me he is entirely innocent, and altimigh the evidence against him seems far from convincing, his trial has resulted in his conviction' and I therefore consider he is morally bound to retire from the Council. The Non-trading candidates at the outset at any rate, did not seek personal victories ; their sole object was to afford the ratepayers the opportunity of voting "yes" or "no "on the question of improper trading by mem- bers of the Council with the Corporation. Any attempt i to unduly influence any elector n order to secure a merely personal success,or indeed to secure what were con ceived to be worthy results, would have been considered entirely contrary to the bases of the non-trading move- ment, and any resort now to such methods by any con- scientious adherent is to me inconceivable! Better a thousand defeats at the poll than .a single victory gained by questionable means or resulting in a sullied lag, and the mere fact, and it is a fact, that certain leaders of the political parties in the Orford, Bewsey and St. John's Wards, in connection with the recent elections in these wards, literally debauched a large proportion of the electorate, could not justify the slightest departure from the most absolute purity on she part of any one of the Non-trading candidates. ' The verdict of the judge and jury who tried Mr. Gough, indicates that he has failed to sustain the high ideals of our movement, and that being so, although lam not now a member of the Non-trading Association, lam bound to denounce his conduct, and to publicly call upon him, as I now do, to immediately vacate his seat. Of course if the convic- tion has voided the election, there is an end of th matter.—l am yours etc,
JAMES DODDS.

div.head: Class Legislation : War.
div.p: Class Legislation : War.

Sir,—War, in its nature and effects, is so horrible that it is difficult to believe that it is a natural product of human nature. But alas, both revelation and the universal experience of mankind in all ages confirm the fact. In describing the internal qualities of man, the Founder of Christianity gives murder a prominent place, and war is neither more nor less than murder on a large scale. And from the days of Cain until now the history of the world has been largely made up of the history of war. But there is one redeeming feature in connec- tion with his subject,and it is that men, whether savage or civilised, when left alone to pursue the natural and essentially peaceful occupations of life they are slow to make aggressions upon one another. Quarrels and even murders for causes trivial or otherwise are unfortunately, only too common amongst them. But their evil passions must be greatly excited and fanned by sinister and selfish ringleaders before they can be induced to take part in the horrors and carnage of the battle field. And who are the people in this country who thus operate on the baser nature of their fellow creatures, and hound them on to make war upon men, whom they have never seen, and against whom they ' can have no personal grievance whatever? Not the quiet and industrious cultivators of the fields; not the workers in our mills and other industries; notthe activeand obliging trades- men who supply our legitimate wants ; nor even the unhappy men whom modern civilisation and a spurious Christianity have relegated to the miseries of slum life. Dreams of military glory at the point of the sword have no ' charms for any of these people. and their natural sense of justice is sufficiently strong to prohibit them from entertaining schemes for empire building on the ruin of their fellow workers in other lands. The movers and ringleaders of all our wars and punitive expeditions are to be found on the highest platform of the classes; yea, even among the idle, educated and exalted patriots who have deprived the people of their inheritance in the land, and estab- lished the public houses to still further impoverish them for the benefit of the liquor dealers and the national war chest. Yes, it is to these people that we owe the fact that to-day the land is burdened with hired and amateur soldiers, armed with the deadliest weapons that the genius of cruelty can devise for the destruc- tion of life and property; and war ships are patroling the seas with the same object in view. But we are gravely told that all this demonstration of military and naval power is necessary for our protection! Never since the 10th of June, 1667, when a "Dutch fleet des- troyed Sheerness, burned the ships lying off Chatham, and sailed up the Thames as far as Tilbury Fort," has this country been subjected to the humiliation of an in- vasion. Are we expecting one now, and from what quarter? Has some continental power threatened to make war upon us, burn our homesteads, and imprison our wives and children to avenge our similar treatment of the Dutch farmers in South Africa? If so, I have never yet heard or read about it. But suppose we were confronted with such a calamity have we no defence but brute force? Are we not a Christian nation and pay many millions a year to professional teachers whose duty it is to exhort us to put our trust in tha Almighty and-not in men. If we cannot or will not do this would it not be better to devote the money thus apparently wasted to the noble and Christian duty of helping the poor and needy amongst us who cannot help themselves. The truth seems to be that our huge armaments are kept up more for offensive than for de- fensive purposes. There are but few countries in the world where the British sword has not been weilded with awful effect in past times; and to-day the same dia- bolical work is going on vigourously in many distant places. Some wars are waged for maintaining what the politicians call "the balance of power" amongst the larger nations ; some for the avowed object of seizing the territories of weaker States ; some for settling Court quarrels; and some to avenge a real or imaginary insult to "the flag." The punitive expeditions, although they do not aspire to the dignity of war, are often more cruel and vindictive than even war itself. And it is generally upon savage tribes that' these out- rages are perpetrated. For some of these tribes having suffered the horrors of foreign invasion will often dare to rebel against their oppressors in the hope of regain- lag the freedom so dear to them. But alas for their hope! The rising of these wild children of nature will not bring deliverance, but only a repetition of the slaughter and burning inflicted upon them before! In short, were it possible to portray the evil passions and disorder, the destruction of life and property, and the sorrows and destitution of bereaved widows and orphans which'have resulted From our war policy in the last hundred years only, the picture would be too awful for human contemplation! Nor can I discern in the present temper of our class legislators any hope that they will abandon their cruel I and tyrannical methods in the future. On I the contrary, the enormous and alarming increase of I expenditure for war purposes now going on seems to point to a still larger development of the policy of des- truction at no very distant date. What then can be done to prevent the waste of money and niaterials, and stay the flow of blood? This is a question of Vital importance to every working man in the country, and the response to it should be unanimous and emphatic. For it is from the working classes chiefly that the victims of war are drawn, and it is their'earninas that provide the price of blood. Let them then tell their rulers through the polling booths that no supplies will be granted for extending the terrible roll of British wars.—Yours truly, lONA. February, Viol.
Great Sankey.
W. FURNESS.

Mr. Browne said Mr. Forshaw never heard from Miss Fox and, in fact, did not know her. He received instructions from ,Mrs. Algayer to prepare the conveyance, and subsequently read over the docu- ment to her. She fully understood what it was. Mr. Forshaw offered to go to Lymm to have the assignment executed, but plaintiff said Miss Fox was an eccentric old lady, and she (plaintiff) would take the document . herself. The first Mr. Forshaw heard about Messrs. , Robert Davies and Company, was when plaintiff brought back the conveyance, and said Miss Fox would not sign it and he' must send it to Messrs. Davies and Compan 37 . He at once did as requested. Mr. Forshaw wanted to repudiate the vile aspersions made on his character,and that was why the case was being fought. , Mr. W.'.l. Forshaw was then called and bore out this statement. At plaintiff's request he obtained thedeeds from Liverpool, perused them, and advised her. On October 6th plaintiff informed him that .she had sold the property to Miss Fox for £6BO and instructed him to prepare a purchase deed. In plaintiff's presence he dictated instructions respecting the deed to Mr. Dil- worth, his clerk. Plaintiff asked what the • charges would be,and he told hershe must leave that to him. Plaintiff promised to let him know the full name of Miss Fox in order that it might be inserted in the deed. When plaintiff again called on October 15th he fully explained the conveyance to her and,to all appearances, she quite understood it. He did not tell her that it was a document relating to the payment of ground rent. He told plaintiff that Miss Fox's signature was necessary because she had covenanced for the payment of ground reht and other matters. The first time he heard of Messrs. Robert Davies and Company in con- nection with the case was when plaintiff brought back the deed. He believed all the time that he was acting for both parties as was done in scores, in fact hundreds of cases. If he had onlyacted for the vender the account would have been the same. THE QUESTION OF CHARGES. Dr. Atkinson: When she asked you what your charges were, why didn't you tell her? Mr. Forshaw: I told her if she would leave it to me. I thought she would be perfectly satisfied. I am not in the habit of contracting. I never do say what my charges are. Dr. Atkinson: Haven't you scale fees for some of these things? Mr. Forshaw: We don't get scale fees in Warrington. Dr. Atkinson: Did you tell her that the amount would be very trifling, or that you wculd not charge her much? Mr. Forshaw: No. I asked her to 'leave it to me and I was sure she would be perfectly satisfied. Dr. Atkinson: Did you intend to give her the im- pression that she would get off lightly? , Mr. Forshaw: 'I gave her the impression she would not be over-charged. Dr. Atkinson: Did you intend to give her the im- pression that she would gain by leaving it to you?—No I don't know that I did. Dr. Atkinson: Why should you ask her to leave it to you unless you intended to give her that impression? --I can only say I am not in the habit of telling people' what my charges are. 1 Further examined, Mr.. Forshaw said that when plaintiff instructed him to prepare the purchase deedl she told him that Miss Fox knew all about it and war aware that plaintiff was consulting him. He explained to Mrs. Algayer that it was the purchaser's business to prepare the deed. He. however, considered that he was acting on behalf of Mrs. Algayer and his charges were against her. When the account was made out and plaintiff complained, he told her that Miss Fox was liable for it unless they had come to some understanding That was the first occasion on which the question of Miss Fox's liability was mentioned. Plaintiff said she would get the money from Miss Fox. Mr. Forshaw ad- mitted that in a letter to Messrs. Robert Davies and Company defendant spoke of their "charges against Miss Fox." Mr. DILWORTH gave corroborative evidence as to the instructions to prepare the deed. THE IMPORTANCE OF THE CASE: Dr. Atkinson addressed the Court and said the judge had to consider that on the one hand there was the plaintiff who could not be described as a business woman. On the other hand was a solicitor who was supposed to be acting onher behalf and inhor interests. , His Honour knew the very high degree of care and the great duty devolved upon a solicitor in dealing with a client. All transactions between them boy which the solicitor gained any benefit to himself must be capable of being put in the clearest possible light. It must be clearly shown that the client fully appreciated and understood the whole thing. Dr. Atkinson criticised Mr. Forshaw's evidence in detail. If what he said in reference to Miss Fox's liability was true, he (the speaker) could , not understand any solicitor—a man who was accustomed Ito weigh his words and write what he meant—writing a letter like that in which defendants spoke of their "charges against Miss Fox." Even if plaintiff gave instructions for the deed to be prepared, unless the solicitor fully explained it to her before it was executed and made it clear to her that it was work which she had no business to do and which Miss Fox ought to pay for, he was not doing his duty and had been guilty of negligence, and therefore could not charge for the work. THE JUDGE FINDS FOR THE DEFENDANTS. His Honour said that although the amount at issue was very small, there were questions arising which affected the professional character and reputation of one person, and the veracity, more or less, of the other. The law, and the Courts administering the law, were naturally and properly very jealous of the acts of those who practised under their protection, and they were bound to exert unusual care that no one should be mis- led in the course of any business transactions that occurred betweed solicitors and clients. Plaintiff seemed to him to be a lady of great physical and still greater intellectual capacity, and to have a keen sense of business relations, and of the advantages and dis- advantages which attended the transfer of pro- perty. Speaking generally, without any disrespect to solicitors, he should say that she would be a perfectly capable match for any ordinarily. equipped solicitor in business relations. (Laughter

THE DIRECTOR'S SALARY.

The Finance Committee considered the salary of the Director, and the remuneration to be paid to the Borough Treasurer and the Borough Surveyor for the services rendered by them to the Committee, in accord- ance with the instructions of the Education Committee at their meeting on the 18th January, 1904. In view of the fact that the Town Council had, •in the interval, increased the salary of the Borough Surveyor by £lOO per annum, the committee did not deem it necessary to make any recommendation with regard to that officer. After some discussion, it was resolved, that the increment of the Director's salary on the Ist April, 1904,and annually thereafter, be .Z5O instead of £25, until the maximum be reached, also that, in view of the great additional responsibility placed upon the Borough Treasurer as Accounting Officer of the Education Com- mittee, the Council be requested to consider the desirability of increasing his salary. It was further resolved that the salary of Mr. I. C. Pharaoh, statistical clerk, be increased from £65 to £75 pei annum. as from the Ist April, 1904. EXCESS OF SCHOOL FEES. At a meeting of the Finance Committee, notifications from the Board of Education, with reference to the reduction made in the fee grant of the following schools, in respect of excess of school fees received during the past twelve months, were submitted, viz. : Fairfield, Z 9 18s. 7d. ; Latchford, St. James', .£l5 19s. 5g.; and Ladies' School of Industry, .21 163. 10d., and intimating that, during the current school year, the fees charged should not exceed an average • rate of 7s. 81d., 3s. 4,1 d., and is. 81d. per annum, respectively. —A letter was also submitted from the managers of the Ladies' School of Industry, intimating that, for the futureond with a view'to meeting the excess to which attention is drawn by the Board of Education, no fees will be charged in respect of the children in standards 6 and 7, and the action of the managers of that school was approved. THE CLASSES FOR ACTING TEACHERS. A report having been presented to the School Management Committee as to the classes held for acting teachers, the Director was requested to write to those teachers who had neither joined the classes ner answered the communication sent to them in accord- ance with the decision of the committee at their meet- inc, on the sth November last asking for an explan ttion of their non-attendance at the classes. THE SINGING OF A HYMN. _

A report of the sub-e4mmittee appointed to consider as to the desirability of singing a hymn on the daily opening of the Secondary school, recommending a selection of hymns to be used, was submitted and approved. LACK OF SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION.

The School Management Committee considered the annual reports of the Board of Education on the various elementary schools, and noticing that, in many, the ad- verse comments were due to the lack of school accom- modation, it was resolved that this committee urge up- on the Sites and Buildings Committee the necessity of proceeding immediately with the provision of further school accommodation. •

div.head: WORK OF' PUPIL TEACHERS.
div.p: THE WORK OF' PUPIL TEACHERS.

The CH.A.TRMAN having reported that, together with the Director, he had had an interview with H. M. In- spector, in the course of which the latter had com- plained that,in several schools,dnejattention had notbeen given to the superintendence of the work of the pupil teachers by the head teachers, it was resolved that the head teachers be informed that it is their duty to instruct the pupil teachers in the art of teaching, and that each head teacher in a school in which pupil teachers are apprenticed must see that each pupil teacher gives a lesson at least once each week under the guidance of the head teacher or a certificated assistant, and that a report book be kept in each school, which will be sub- ject to inspection by H. In conclusion he asked the assembly to drink the toast of "The Warring- ton District." In responding Mr. W. RATHBO'NE (district secretary) said that was the largest meeting of bakers that had ever been held in Warrington and district. He had fulfilled the duties of secretary for the past seven years, and during that period the increase of membership had been :—Warrington, 20; St. Helens, 19; Altrincham, 14; Runcorn, 6; Leigh, 8; Earlestown (which had no branch when he was elected), 16. That showed a total gain for the district of 93. Although there had been a great depression in the trade ilurine the past few months and they had suffered more thouglilacie of employment in the past six months than perhaps they had ever done before, there was not in the district one "laggard," or undesirable, among the whole of the men out of work. Mr. Rathbone paid a tribute to the work of the branch secretaries and went on to refer to the good feeling existing between masters and men. During his period of office there had not been a single effort to bring about a strike. i Hear, hear.) He felt certain that the good feeling would long continue and that so long as they had good, upright men in their Union, their em- ployers would have no cause to complain of the way in which they did their duty. (Applause.) The banner is beautifully worked on silk in red, blue and gold. It bears the arms of the Order illustrating the production of bread and confectionery, with the words "By the sweat of thy brow shall man eat bread." The toast of "The Amalgamated Union" was pro- posed by Mr. J. NIMMO, who referred to the improve- ment in the conditions of employment which the Union had been instrumental in bringing about. When the organization was founded in 186 f, pale, haggard men were working for mere pittances, in fact his father only oarnedl24s. par week,and worked very long hours. Ever since the formation of the Union the bakers had been prospering. 'Mr. J. JENKINS (general secretary) responded. He pointed out that in Warrington the conditions were not yet as good as they might be. Night work had not yet been abolished, and he was afraid the sins were not all on Ile heads of the masters. Slowly but surely a considerable number of employers had encroached upon their past privileges, and it was a wonder to him if , they were in as good a position in regard to the aboli- tion of night work as they were years ago. (A Voice : "Worse.") That was partly due to the individual selfishness of some bakers. He conten- ded that if employers insisted upon night work they I ought to pay time and a half for it. (Hear, hear.) Re- ferring to the general conditions, the speaker said bakers ought to be paid sufficient to enable them to provide for old age and keep them outside the Work- house. The toast of "The Mayor and Corporation " was honoured on the proposition of Mr. BARNES. Councillor James EVAN'S responded and expressed his aPpreciation of the efforts'of the operative bakers to bring about a better understanding between employ era and employed. In regard to the hours of labour, he had,during the whole of the time he had been connected with the trade, failed to see why bakers could not com- mence Work in the morning like the ordinary artizan It often seemed as if there was very little in the baker's life beside work and sleep. He thought he was voicing the feelings of the master bakers present when he said that they were quite willing for consideration to be given to this matter in a friendly spirit. For a:nunaber of years he had not allowed anyone employed by him to work on Bank Holiday and he had been in Docket as the result. There was nothing but sentiment in the taste of the multitude that bread should be baked at four o'clock in the morning to be eaten the following day. If the mastersand men of Warrington combined he saw no reason why next Monday morning the employees in the bakehouseshould not commence work at six o'clock with an eight hours day and fair remuner- ation. (Applause.) He suggested that a step in the right direction would be for the Master Bakers' Association to arrange a dinner and invite represent. tires of the operative bakers. Referring to the Corporation, Councillor Evans said he hoped they would rule justly and in righteousness and wisdom all their days, whoever they might be. He had a little better hope to-day than he had when he first went into the Council. He was then a "speckled bird." He was the first man who went there with a kindred feeling, and there were more of them now. Unfortunately they used to think that a man who worked did not know any- thing. Now they were finding out that the working men could take their corner and disouss what came for- ward, even in the Corporation. Mr. HIGGINBOTHAM proposed "The Master Bakers Association," and Mr. ECKERSLEV reeponded. Mr. RATHBONE proposes" The Visitors." In responding Mr. SPEAKMAN alluded to a visit he recently paid to the 00-operative bakery at Copenhagen There the employees worked eight hours per day and received 355. 6d. per week. One reason of the success of the bakery was that the profits had not been paid away in dividends. He could not see whythat Union.in- stead of waiting for the Government to improve their conditions, could not subscribe £4OO or £5OO and start a trade union co-operative bakery. If they did he ventured to say that within five years success would wait upon them. During the evening songs were creditably rendered by Mr. E. Pownall, Mr. J. Willett, and Mr. Thompson Jones.
