div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. THOMAS • TUNSTALL. FuneraFfeiterday.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. THOMAS • TUNSTALL. FuneraFfeiterday.

Very many of our readers will regret to hear of the death of Mr., Thomas Tunstall, heid and founder of the firm of Messrs. T. and J. L. Tunstall, accountants and commission agents, Warrington, which took place with startling suddenness on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. Tunstall had conducted his business as usual at the Savings Bank, where he had been actuary for a number of years, and proceeded at 4.30 to his office in Bewsey Chambers. He had ascended the steps leading to the office when he. suddenly fell forward an the mat. A clerk went immediately to his assist- ance and Dr. Adams was promptly called in, but on his arrival life was extinct. Mr. Tunstall was a victim of heart disease, and only a week ago he consulted a specialist respecting his complaint. His, condition was not such as to indicate that the end was so near and his death caused a painful surprise to the townspeople. His long business connection with Warrington had made him very well known in the town, and his untimely end at the comparatively early age of 54 years, closes a use- ful and honourable career. In view of Mr. Tunstall's recent attendance on a medical man, an inquest was not considered necessary and the body was removed the same evening from his private office to his resi- dence, Brook House, Penketh. Mr. Tunstall leaves a widow and three children—two dauighters,and a son. He was the eldest son cf the late Mr. John Tunstall,of this town. • Two brothers of Mr. Thomas Tunstall's (Mr. H. G. Tutistall and Mr. Wilmot Tunstall) and a sister (Mrs. Deacon) survive him. For over thirty years, Mr. Tunstall had conducted busineSs on his own behalf in Warrington. He com- menced in a small office.in Sankey-street,as an auction- eer and appraiser, and subsequently he proceeded to larger premises in the old Masonic Rooms. His brother, the late Mr. John Laverock Tunstall entered into partnership with him and they removed their business to Bewsey Chambers, where it has been conducted with niarked success ever since. Mr. Tunstall 'fre- quently gave evidence on behalf of the Corporation at arbitrations, 'particularly in connection with the acquirement of property in Bridge-street, and was a valuable witness. In addition to his duties as actuary of the Savings Bank, Mr. Tuns tall was officially con- nected with a large number of local companies and organisations. •

div.head: LAND GRABBING IN LONDON.
div.p: LAND GRABBING IN LONDON.
"Nobility is not in dignity and ancient lineage ; not great revenues, lands, or possessions; but in wisdom, knowledge, and virtue. Honour ought to he given to virtue, and not to riches."—ANAcHAßsis.

If the old Scythian philosopher who uttered these pious sentiments had been living in our own day he would not have been a worshipper of the Dukes of Bedfordand Westminster, and the other great manorial lords who have appropriated all the land in London, and grown rich beyond the dreams of avarice by the unearned increment from the labours of the people. He would have showered his honours and lavished his praises on the men who have withstood oppression and wrong-doing, and who have vindicated right against might in many a sturdy conflict. I.—LONDON HAS SUFFERED MORE THAN ANY OTHER CITY IN THE COUNTRY FROM THE / GREED OF ITS LANDOWNERS.

From the earliest times it has been the happy hunt- ing ground of the festive landgrabber, and every rood of its ground has been stolen over and over again. The Romans captured it, when it was little more than a clearing in the vast primeval forest, and built a wall and a fortress, in what is now the veryheart of the city Afe centuries later it fell into the hands of the Saxons, and then it was pillaged and burnt by the Danes,and finally it was annexed by the Normans. The abbots, and monks, and archbishops, and bishops of the Middle Ages nibbled at it, and begged it, till nearly every foot of it came into their possession. They held it till the dissolution of the monasteries by Henry VIII., and then it changed hands once more. In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries the ecclesias- tical land-grabbers were in clover. It is more than twenty miles as the crow flies from Westminster to St. Albans, and it is more than fifty miles from Lambeth Palace to Canterbury, and there were religious houses at all these places, so you can easily guess what happened These holy men made the.!wills, and whitewashed the souls of the rich sinners, so the church managed to ap- propriate all the land for miles around. You could walk from St. Albans to Westminster,and from Lambeth to Canterbury, and you could find traces of the clerical land-grabber every mile of the road. After the dissolution of the Monasteries a surprising quantity of the old monastic lands fell into the hands of the Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Bishop of London, and the Dean and Chapter of St. Paul's and the various religious charities, and endowments,and schools of the city. The bulk of this land now is under the sontrol of the Ecclesiasticaland Chatity Commissioners. The Bishop of London was lord of the manors of Stepney, and Paddington, and Westbourne. The Dean and Chapter of St. Paul's awned vast tracts of land from Hackney on one side to Paddington on the other. The Archbishop of Canterbury's domain started at Lam- beth Palace, and]went for miles over the Surreyj hills and away among the hop gardens of Kent. These clerical land-grabbers tithed the crops, and saddled their neighbours with Church Rates, and cap- tured the charities, and filched the commons, and con- trolled the schools, and chivied and persecuted the Dis- senters, and fought as lustily as the monks of old for the privileges and perquisites of their own trades union. Between the old order and the new there was hardly a pin to choose. IL—WHEN LONDON BEGAN TO GROW THERE WAS. A PERFECT EPIDEMIC OF LAND-GRABBING.

So long as there was only one bridge across the Thames and the City could only be reached by miry lanes and open commons, the land was of little value, and nobody wanted it. But when half-a-score of new bridges were built, and highways and roads multiplied, the ground landlords began to close ancient footpaths, and fence portions of the commons, and claim public land as their own. And whenany public-spirited citizen dared to protest against these iniquities he was chivied and persecuted to make him hold his peace. One of the best examples of these land-grabbing enterprises is the story of a fight between a poor cobbler and King George 11. about a right of way through a royal park. Bushey Park is a fine estate of a thousand acres,lying lbetween Kingston-on-Thames and Hampton Wick. A rcentury or two ago it was a popular resort for the people of London, and there was an ancient footpath right through the park that enabled the people to enjoy its famous avenue of chestnut trees, and its mighty oaks, and its sylvan glades to their hearts' content. First one Soveieign and then another had tried his hand at filching portions of the neighbouring common and shutting out the people entirely from the park, but ' somehow they all came to grief. Cromwell did steal part of the common, but he got into such a nest of hornets that he was glad to make his peace with the angry commoners by giving them another piece of land in exchange. George It. went one better than Cromwell, for he closed the ancient footpath through the park, and made his neighbours go a mile or two round for his pleasure and convenience. But Timothy Bennett, the village shoemaker, objected to this little arrangement, and pledged his Nord that he would "mace Master George open that footpath again." So he went to the ablest lawyer he could find, and asked what it would cost to make the King do right. "I don't mean to cobble the job "said he, " for I have about £7OO of my own, and I would give the awl to prevent the great folks getting the upper leather wrong- fully." Acting on his lawyer's advice he warned Lord Halifax, the ranger of the park, that he intended to assert his right of way by walking over the ancient footpath from Hampton Wick to Kingston, and if necessary ho would fight it out in the law courts. "Who are you that you presume to meddle in this affair?" asked Lord Halifax in a towering rage. "My name, my lord," said the cobbler, "is Timothy Bennett, shoemaker, of Hampton Wick. When I was a young man people passed my shop going to Kingston Marker, and now you force them to so round about through hot and saniy roads ready to faint beneath their burdens. I meddle in this affair because I am unwilling to leave the world worse than I found it. "Begone! you im- pertinent fellow," roared the ranger, in a passion, and then he sought relief in profanity. Timothy then carried his complaints to the British public. He told his neighbours and friends that he in- tended to assert his rights as a citizen by walking over the ancient footpath through the perk in spite of the King. If this act should bring him to ab;ect poverty, and cost him his liberty he was quite prepared to suffer for righteousness sake. Now when any honest man comes to this frame of mind he is a very dangerous plaything for tyrants and oppressors. George IT. was one of the most unpopular Kings that ever sat on the Englisk throne, and Timothy Bertnett's grievance had done the King no good. Still he was as obstinate as a mule, and he swore the cobbler should be prosecuted for defying the King.' The law officers of the Crown, and the unscrupulous judges were eager for the fray, and they had their minds made up about the verdict before they had heard the evidence. But somehow that trial never came off. The Ministers of the Crown would not risk an unpopular judgmept that would make a cobbler a martyr, and a King into' a mean contemptible thief. They did not know who was behind Timothy, helping him, and prompting him, and undertaking to find the money to fight out this question to the bitter end. They did know that George 11. had a very tottering throne, and that he was mighty unpopular, andi if he persisted in closing the footpath and then fell into the clutches of a London mob, he would probably get torn limb from limb. So Timothy did, not get prosecuted after all. He com- pelled the King and his Ministers to open that footpath again, and he lived long to enjoy his triumph over a corrupt Court and a dishonest Ministry. lII.—THERE WAS A FIERCE FIGHT ABOUT FILCHING THE ROYAL FORESTS.

And the story of that conflict is too good to be lost. for it lasted many years' and it was conducted with great vigour and spirit, both in the law courts and in the King's hunting ground, and it ended in a great victory on the part of the democracy. Epping Forest was originally a royal hunting ground in Essex, consisting of about six thousand acres of ancient forest land, to which several parties had well defined rights. The King had the right to hunt and preserve his deer in it. The commoners had the right to pasturage for their sheep and cattle, and they were free to cut their own firewood, or dig their own turf, or wander about the forest wherever they pleased,with- out asking anybody leave. It is true that seventeen neighbouring landlords claimed manorial right over the Forest, but as they had no power to dispossess either the King or the commoners nobody took them seriously.

But 9, little more than a century ago Epping Forest began to melt like snow. The manorial lords did not go to Parliament for an enclosure Act, because they I could not agree among themselves about the division of the plunder' and the commoners were prepared to light to the death for their rights. So each manorial lord began to enclose portions of the forest for himself, and fence round the stolen lands with massive barriers of timber, so that he and his retainers might stand a siege when the angry Commoners rose in their wrath. As to the morality of this land-grabbing, Butler in his Hudibms very wittingly says : The fault is great in man or woman, Who steals a goose from off the common; But who shall plead that man's excuse, Who steals a common from the goose? The quarrel about the fate of Epping Forest caused a good deal of excitement among the citizens of London. Unfortunately they +lad no commoners rights over the estate, and therefore, they had no gale right to meddle in the dispute or to claim any portion of the spoil. But about half a century ago the Corporation of

London, by a special Act of Parliament, obtained a- portion of the forest, for a cemetery at Aldersbrook. By this lucky purchase the citizens of London became "Commoners of Epping Forest," and therefore entitled to all the rights and privileges of the freemen .of the- forest. As soon as the average Cockney realised that he was a partner in that concern he began to take a very lively interest in its welfare, and he asserted his rights so vigorously that he soon came into collision, with the manorial bailiffs, and gamekeepers and rangers. Severel free fights occurred between the bailiffs, and. the Cockney Commoners, and these shindies usually ended in the Police Court. But if the Cockney could prove that he was a citizen of London, and had merely been asserting his rights as a Commoner, he invariably- won his case. Several meetings were held, and some- strong resolutions were passed against the manorial lords and their retainers, and finally it was resolved that all the newly erected barriers had got to come • down. And then the fun began. Mr. George Burney took three omnibus loads of navvies armed with crowbars, and pick-a xes, and sledge- hammers, and turned them loose in the forest, with orders to level every fence,aild break down every barrier, while thousatals of London crtizens went out that day to assert their rights, and spank the gamekeepers, and see the fun. You can imagine what a high old time they had, but the battle did not last long. The bailiffs, and keepers, and rangers got it hot, and after the first exchange of civilities they took to their heels and fled. The navvies worked as they never worked before, and those massive timber barriers came down a thousand times faster than ever they went up. When the crowbars and pick-axes had redhced all the barriers to firewood, and the forest was thrown open and free once more, the timber was piled in a heap and sprinkled with paraffin and petroleum and set on fire. The Commoners celebrated their victory by a huge bon- fire and made congratulatory speeches till a late- hour that night.

The n-ext stage in the conflict was a costly law suit, i,n which the land grabbers wwe badly beaten by a verdict that all enclosures made since 1851 were illegal; and therefore the Commoners were justified in destroy- ing the illegal fences and barriers. Finally the matters in dispute were settled by arbitration, and 5,600 acres of forest land were preserved as a pleasure ground free to the public for ever. I know it is the fashion in some quarter to denounce men like Timothy Bennett and George Burney as agitators and mischief-makers and firebrands, but they are the salt of the earth. We owe all our liberties to such men as these, and I pray God the time may never come when the race will be extinct. We cannot spare the humble heroes who are honestly striving to leave this world better than they found it, and who are fight- ing freedom's battles single-handed against the forces of the mighty.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
THE RUSSIAN-JAPANESE WAR.

NO FRESH OFFICIAL NEWS. At the Japanese Legation,. in London, yesterday after- noon, there was no confirmation of the report that a large body of Russian troops were marching towards Seoul.. Indeed no news of any kind has reached the Legation from Tokio.

div.head: Land Operations. ENORMOUS RUSSIAN PREPARATIONS.
div.p: The Land Operations. ENORMOUS RUSSIAN PREPARATIONS.
Exodus from Port Arthur.

The Harbin correspondent of" Le-Matin," says the exodus from Port Arthur continues, and. heavily-laden trains are pouring out useless refugees, who will con- sume the provisions required by the troops. KOREA TO BE THE SCENE OF ACTION. Reuter's correspondent at Seoul reports that two• thousand Russian troops have arrived at Wiju, and. 8,000 at Chin-liencheng. A collision with the Japanese is expected somewhere in the province of Phyong-yang-ping-yang. Phyong-yang lies almost exactly half-way between. Wiju and Seoul. It was the scene of the first great battle between the Chinese and Japanese in the last war, and is a large and flourishing town on the Ta-doncr River, with a population of about 60,000 people. 7 A RUSSIAN ARMY OF 400,000. The Thirbin correspondent of the" Matin " says : A hundred and twenty thousand men of the Corps d'Arm4e from Moscow, Kieff, and Poland were expected and within twelve clays there will be in Manchuria 400,000 Russian soldiers.
Two hundred Japanese disembarked on Tuesday at Talienwan.

div.head: Junior Conservative Club.
div.p: Junior Conservative Club.

A successful smoking concert was held at this club, on Thursday evening and was largely attended. Mr. E. Draper presided- and alluded to the fiscal debate in Parliament, which resulted in a majority of 51 for the Government. At present, the policy practi- cally resolved itself into retaliation, but they in War- rington would have liked the policy to have gone a bit further.—Alderman Bennett de- livered an address in support of Mr. Chamber- lain's proposals, expressing the opinion that Mr Chamberlain. was convinced that his policy would be for the well-being of the country. The. speaker quoted figures to surport his arguments in. favour of preferential tariffs,pointing out that in many English possessions, including Canada, goods from this country were already imported at preferential rates.--A very enjoyable musical programme was sub- mitod, and the gathering concluded -with the usual votes of thanks. Women's Employment Sureau.

A women's -employment bureau was opened on Tuesday at the Gymnasium. For some time it has been felt that there is a great need in the town for an. office where women in search of work, or who wish to take lodgers, can have their names registered, and where those who wish to employ them can go to make inquiries. As the result of the deliberations. of a committee of the Town Council who discussed th o scheme with Mrs. Clay - (guardian of the p -or), Miss Broadbent and Inspector Hackett (N. S. P. C. C.), it was decided that a room in the Gymnasium should be set apart for the purpose, to be open to the women applying for work every Tuesday and Thursday after— noon from two till four. It was also arranged that Inspector Hackett should call ence a week and Write in the register what he knew of the appli— cants and whether they were clean and respectable. Mr. Hayes, who has charge of the register, will be at the Gymnasium from 9 to twelve and from 2 to 4. every day, with the exception of Friday and Saturday when he will be there from 9to 12 only. Ladies can call any time between these hours to see the book. If when suited they will send is. to Miss Broadbent, the treasurer, it will make the office self-supporting, as. the expenses will only come to about ;I:3 a year.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTION 1904 TO THE ELECTORS OF THE A.PPLICIO'N DIVISION. LAMS AND GENTLEMEN At the Triennial Election of Members for the Cheshire County Council which will be held on the sth day of March you will be called upcia to elect a Representative for the Appleton Division. You were kind enough to honour me with your confidence at the Bye-election which occurred some two and a half years ago, when I was elected without opposition. I venture 3nce more to place my services at your disposal assuring you that the interests and requirements not only of this Division in particular but also of the County generally shall always receive my best attention, and that, if again elected to represent you, my earnest efforts shall be devoted to the carrying out of the duties imposed upon me. Thanking you for your past kindne.s and soliciting a re- newal of your support, Believe me to be, Ladies and Gentlemen. Faithfully yours, ROGRR CHARLTON PARR. Grappenhall Hayes, February 18th, 1904.
CLA.RA BUTT.

The, New Sanatorium. A mentinc, of this Council wls held on Tuesday even- ing in the Board Schools, Great Sankey. Mr. W. Taylor presided and their were also present : Messrs. G..' Thompson, J. Fulton Smith, H. Singleton, and J. Smith (clerk). ADDITIONAL POSTAL FACILITIES. The Clerk reported that in accordance with the reso- lution of the Council he wrote to the postal authorities, asking them to erect a pillar box at Penketh Lane I End. Mr. L. E. Tennent, of the Warrington Post Office, wrote that he had received authority to comply with the Council's request and the box would be erected at an early date. Mr. W. Roche, of the General Post Office, London also wrote that he was directed by the Postmaster General to state that instructions had been given for the erec- tion of a letter box at Penketh-Lane End with collections at 7 a.m., 4 p.m. and 8.50 p.m., on week days, and at 8.50 p.m. on Sundays. Mr. Thompson stated that the letter box had been erected. He proposed that the Clerk write to the postal authorities acknowledging their promptness in meeting the wishes of the Council. Mr. Singleton seconded and the proposition was carried. A "DANGEROUS" FOOTPATH. The Clerk referred to a letter received from the Penketh Parish Council in which attention was drawn to "the very dangerous condition" of the footpath leading from Heath-road, Penketh, to Liverpool-road Great Sankey. The Penketh Council asked for the matter to be taken up with a view to the condition of the path being improved, and stated that Mr. Fred T. Kelsall, who was the tenant of the land through which the path passed in Penketh had been requested to re- pair it. Mr. Thompson proposed. Mr. Singleton seconded,and it was agreed that therlerk should write to the Penketh Parish Connell saying that the Sankey Council could Rot see its way to interfere in the matter. MORE LIGHT WANTED. The Penketh Pariah Council wrote suggesting the advisability of erecting two lamps in Cemetery-road. The Penketh Council proposed to erect one lamp if the Great Sankey Council would also erect one lamp. On the proposition of Mr. Thompson it was decided to leave the matter to the new Patash Council to be elected in March next. NEW COUNTY RATE BASIS. TEE ASSESSMENT OF THII NEW SANATORIUM. The Clerk produced the new county rate basis for Great Sankey. The gross assessable value of the town- ship was £12,326 145., against £11,868 ss. a year ago, showing an increase of £458 Os. The Clerk pointed out that the new sanatorium had been assessed at £2OO. Mr. Singleton asked whether that assessment was not a very low one? Mr. Thompson thought that having regard to the cost of the building it ought to have been assessed higher. The Clerk stated that the cost of the sanatorium was about £9,000. Mr. Singlet on thought it was a "scandalous shame' that a building oo sting such a large sum should only' be assessed at £2OO. Mr. J. Fulton Smith proposed that the overseers inform the Assessment Committee that in the opinion of the Council the assessment was too low. The Chairman seconded. Me. Singleton supported and the proposition was carried. THE ENCAMPMENT OF GIPSIES. The Clerk read a letter from Sergeant Schofield, acknowledging the receipt of a communication from the Parish Council with reference to the encampment of gipsies in the neighbourhood, and stating that he had instructed the constable to move them on whenever he found them." . Mr. Thompson stated that on Saturday and Sunday last two gipsy vans were encamped on the public high- way near Huntlpy-street and were a nuisance to the neighbourhood. It was decided to write a letter of complaint to Police Sergeant Schofield. THE ANNUAL COUNCIL MEETING. jlt was decided to hold the annual council meeting on the 7th March, just prior to the annual parish meeting. , DROWNING FATALITY NEAR NEWTON. Severe Censure by Coroner Brighouse. Tie county coroner, Mr. S. Brighouse, held an in- quest on Tuesday, at Lowton on the body of Joseph Geraghpy, 25 years of age. a labourer, of Mount Tabor, Lowton, who was found drowned on Highfield Marsh on Sunday morning. James deraqhpy stated that his brother had been drinking heavily for some time,but had suddenly ceased a week ago. Peter Clarke, a collier, of Lowton, stated that on Sunday morning he was walking on Highfield Marsh when his dog commenced to bark. He looked round to ascertain the cause' when he found deceased lying face downwards in a ditch in about two feet of water. He did not touch the body, but went for the police. The Coroner: Why did you not lift the body out? Witness: I would not have touched you, had you been there. The Coroner: I don't think I have ever heard such gross ignorance before. He might not have been dead. Witness: He did not move. The jury returned a verdict of found drowned, and ordered Clarke to be censured. The Coroner said he hoped the press would give the fullest publicity to the unmanlyconduct of Clarke. He (the coroner) was perfectly astounded to hear Clarke say that he would not have touched him(the coroner) if he had been in such a predicament.He hoped there were not many Englishmen like Clarke' who would rather turn away than give a helping hand. Clarke had stated that in future ise would not touch a body but walk away and say nothing, but if such a thing did occur, he (the coroner) would search the Act of Parliament and see if Clarke could not be severely punished for it. He was perfectly astounded at such gross ignorance bein,, shown y any man.
